The early K-type star K2-138, hosting six planets, particularly five proposed to be in a prolonged chain of 3:2 mean motion resonances, presents an unusual system for analyzing and modeling, with key planets potentially engaging in resonant behavior. Using a combination of analytical and numerical techniques, our research aimed to identify resonant behavior and assess its occurrence in synthetic populations. Throughfully automated simulations, we discovered numerous resonant chain configurations, suggesting a significant probability (\geq 84%) of a resonant chain involving planets K2-138 b, K2-138 d, and K2-138 e, alongside indications of three-planetary chains involving K2-138 c and K2-138 d. However, none of these resonant configurations could explain the observed lack of resonances between planets K2-138 c and K2-138 f. Our findings significantly restrict the possible orbital radii of the planets involved, especially K2-138 c and K2-138 f, thereby reducing the area of the possible "period valley" where these planets may reside. Moreover, our analysis suggests that planet K2-138 c cannot have a significant atmospheric mass. Additionally, our research indicates that system secular perturbations may lead to a prolonged and complex evolution of the orbital resonances in this system. To enhance accuracy and efficiency in similar future studies, our methods, especially the dynamic template matching approach to identify resonant behavior, may be applied to other planetary systems. Further analysis is necessary to precisely define the possible planetary properties in the K2-138 system. Although our analysis failed to fully explain the observed planetary separations, we discovered that planet K2-138 c must be less massive than 1.2 Mearth in order to remain in a stable orbit and undergo resonant behavior within the expected future tidal migration of this planet. Moreover, our findings suggest that all planets in the K2-138 system are subject to ongoing tidal evolution, which may lead to future resonances and potential configurations of chain resonances and inner mean motion resonances. These rotating black branes are flat in topology at their horizons, yet due to the influence of the dilaton field, they do not conform to either flat or (anti)-de Sitter asymptotic behaviors. We've provided the complete phase structure for these solutions, focusing on their thermal properties and stability. Interestingly, the thermal stability of these solutions is found to be heavily dependent on the charges and rotational parameters. When alpha, the dilaton-electromagnetic coupling constant, is zero, our results align with previously studied cases. Additionally, we have examined the impact of the temperatures and coupling constants on the thermal capacity and isothermal compressibility. Similar to previous findings, we've determined that in high-dimensional spaces, the effect of the dilaton field on the thermal properties of these solutions diminishes with increasing dimensions. Our study thus offers a comprehensive contribution to the general structure of charged rotating black brane solutions in arbitrary dimensions. These solutions may also influence other areas, such as holographic dark energy, where they can provide additional insights into the behavior of the universe. In the era of artificial intelligence, advancements in computational processing of text are crucial. Most modern text processing systems rely on text representation, dividing words into vectors and sentences into matrices. However, this traditional approach falls short due to word dependencies across multiple sentences, neglecting the structured frame-work of human memory. As a solution, we introduce an innovative method utilizing complex networks to represent text, by dividing it into interconnected nodes of words and frames, and weighting the connections based on key concepts and sentence relationships. This dynamic scheme, influenced by human memory, allows for seamless text learning and generation of synthetic text. It addresses semantic, syntactic, and structural complexities across various languages, using minimal text inputs. Additionally, this method resolves the limited capacity problem in existing AI systems by storing text information in compact, structured frames. It also allows for efficient propagation of information across the network through combined node- and frame-centred approaches. We validate the efficacy of our proposed method through comprehensive experiments on six languages, showcasing its ability to simulate human learning and text processing. Furthermore, it facilitates the development of deep learning architectures that can operate within human-like frameworks, offering significant potential for future advancements in natural language processing. To detail this method and its associated technical complexities, we include appendices with additional context. To achieve this construction, we first establish the set of all finite q-analytic polynomials and show it forms a basis for the space of all polynomials with absolute values less than one. A small-step operational semantics in a programming language breaks down computations into discrete, indivisible steps, directly reflecting how the language is implemented. A previous semantics of GP 2 is incomplete because its loop and branching commands utilize big-step operations. In this work, we present a new small-step operational semantics for GP 2 that replicates the existing complete and compositional high-order graphical programming framework. This new semantics is organized by multiset monoid and incorporates graph rewriting rules. Each rule's application symbolically replicates the effects of graph reduction on multiset combinations, allowing for the simulation of GP 2's operational behavior. In contrast to existing small-step semantics, GP 2's new semantics includes dynamic checking of reduction rules to ensure only well-formed graphs undergo functional reductions. The new semantics' completeness was confirmed by demonstrating it is both fully and compositionally equivalent to the existing one. Additionally, we observed a significant performance acceleration in GP 2's operational behavior. The use of this new semantics enabled the development of a first-order graphical logic for full graph rewriting and introduced novel applications, including graph metamodeling. It was found that introducing dynamic checking of reduction rules led to a notable semantic simplification, as evident from the smaller set of derived reduction rules and the avoidance of unsound reductions in functional and graphical semantics. The same technique can be applied to other existing complete and compositional GP semantics, allowing for the development of new small-step semantics to enhance operational performance. The new abstractness of GP 2's programming language also avoids controversies surrounding the specification and enabled the development of a sound graphical semantics replicating the effects of the small-step operational semantics. In contrast, the development of sound graphical semantics in other programming languages, including GP 1 and higher-order GP, remains an open challenge. The work also explores novel graph metamodeling mechanisms by leveraging GP 2's completeness and soundness. As a result, it was possible to introduce new modalities for specifying and reasoning about rewrite rules and create a novel multigraph metamodeling system. The new semantics and associated technologies developed in this work contribute significantly to the areas of programming languages and formal reasoning, as they provide crucial insights into the design of first-order and higher-order logical frameworks. The advantages and limitations of multicast beamforming for millimeter-wave systems have received little attention in the design of hybrid precoders. To fill this gap, we develop the first integrated design of analog transmit precoders and digital receive combiners for multicasting in mmWave systems, with each device having multiple phases and multiple antennas. By combining semidefinite relaxation, alternating optimization and Cholesky decomposition, we sequentially optimize the digital and analog components at the transmitter and receiver. The proposed method leads to significant performance improvements. Notably, with two receive antennas, we see an average reduction of $ 16.8\% $ in the transmit power of the optimal hybrid multicasting beamformer compared to the fully digital version. Theoretical low-bound ergodic spectral efficiency and outage probability analysis confirm the near-optimality of the design. Finally, Monte-Carlo simulations show that the proposed design outperforms state-of-the-art methods. This research is published in the paper titled "Integrated Hybrid Precoder and Decoder Design for Multicast mmWave Systems," which appears in the $ 2022$ IEEE International Symposium on Information-Theory. A function from natural numbers to natural numbers is considered near-exponential if it's confined by two growth patterns: one growing and the other shrinking, both following the form 2 raised to a specific power raised to the natural numbers' value. Researchers Berman, Shapira, and Sapir recently proved certain implications of this definition. This paper builds on their work by providing conditions under which adding an exponential component to a near-exponential function results in another near-exponential function. Specifically, we address situations where either the lower and upper bounds are added or removed. In doing so, we establish the equivalence of specific mathematical statements in a single variable and multi-variable settings involving finite fields' counting functions. The context of this research lies in understanding how growth patterns, particularly those following the form 2 raised to a power raised to the natural numbers' value, can be extended to more complex near-exponential functions. This paper contributes to the field of multiplicative combinatorial number theory. The findings can be applied to a broad range of mathematical problems as shown by Sapir and Sapir-Shapira's previous work. Furthermore, we provide a condition under which removing an exponential component to a near-exponential function results in another near-exponential function. This specific condition stems from a combination of the principles of Ramsey theory and Amos Tvesky's inequality. The paper concludes with a complex problem related to counting functions within finite fields, offering a challenge for further research. The write-up of this paper is inspired by a seminar discussion hosted by Alex Belton at the University of Manchester in 2021. The paper is structured into seven sections. The initial three sections focus on presenting near-exponential functions, examining their characteristics and patterns, and reviewing the principles of the 'adding an exponential component' and'removing an exponential component' concepts. The following three sections Delve deeper into the 'adding an exponential component' concept, providing conditions and mathematical statements in multi-variable settings. The final section addresses the'removing an exponential component' concept, providing conditions and mathematical statements in multi-variable settings, and concludes with the complex problem related to counting functions within finite fields. The paper is originally titled 'Near-Exponential Functions: Multi-Variable Ramsey Theorems, Finite Fields' Counting Functions,' and is currently available on arXiv at the referenced URL. We tackle the persistent issue of exponential stability for a stretched Euler-Bernoulli beam on a star-shaped graph with three equal branches. The outer points where these branches meet are fixed while rotating. The inner point is capable of moving in two ways, with rotational movement influenced by both elasticity and friction. A detailed analysis in a Hilbert space reveals how the spectrum's asymptotic distribution and structure evolve. It demonstrates that specific eigenvector characteristics form a complete and orthonormal basis. Consequently, we derive the exponential stability of the associated semigroup directly. Notably, we show that under these connectivity conditions, stability is guaranteed even in the absence of elasticity along the edges. This research contributes to the understanding of stability in graph PDEs, a field where such problems' solution is computationally challenging due to various parameters' influence. As a by-product, we also examine the behavior of the model when frictionless and study the optimal mass transportation problem related to this model. It involves transforming the beam's spectrum's distribution into an equilibrium state's location along its boundaries. A new analytical and numerical method for finding these equilibrium states is introduced through an iterative process between transportation and natural vibrations. This process reveals that, under these connectivity conditions, the equilibrium state is always located on the boundary for inner points. A numerical method based on an energy release criterion to find multiple solutions is presented along with a real-world application example. These findings were published in a previous study (2020) where we provided numerical results on the stability issue depending on parameter values for beam models with fractures. They were published as part of the PhD thesis completed in 2019, and some aspects are still being developed in a follow-up work for models with fractures. A moving dielectric medium can alter the path of light traveling through it, a phenomenon termed the Fresnel-Fizeau optical drag effect. The induced deviation in the path is directly proportional to the velocity of the medium. Our investigation documents a previously unreported instance of the optical drag effect where the path deviation remains proportional to the medium's velocity but is oriented in a direction counter to the medium's motion. To observe this anomalous effect, we conducted an optical drag experiment under the conditions of electromagnetic transparency and monitored the shift from typical optical drag to zero drag and ultimately the anomalous effect through adjustments to two-photon detuning. The optical drag effect observed under certain finite detunings exhibited proportional behavior but with an unusual direction, indicating that the medium had become electromagnetically transparent yet still induced an optical drag. Our analysis of this phenomenon suggests that the anomalous effect arises from a specific interaction between the two light waves and the moving medium when certain phase relationships are satisfied, giving rise to a component of the electric field that is common to both waves but is out of phase. To explain the observed drag effect, we consider that the out-of-phase electric field exerts a force on the moving dielectric medium, thus inducing a drag effect. Our study provides insight into how light interacts with moving media at the macroscopic and microscopic levels, offering implications for the study of light-matter interaction. The technique of rapidly modulating the detuning to induce the optical drag effect may lead to the development of a drag-based optical microscope that is uncomplicated and anagram-free. Specifically, it may be possible to create a microscope that produces a Babinet-compensated 2D image from a 1D optical pattern obtained from the optical drag effect. Moreover, this concept can be extended to a class of complex optical systems, including chiral and chiral-based optical systems, where it may be possible to create a viable method for observing optical drag effect, albeit with difficulties in achieving it. Ultimately, our experimental findings may contribute to a deeper understanding of through-field interactions and the development of novel methods for observing and manipulating light-matter interaction. Deep learning models' success in graph problems has led to the prominence of graph neural networks (GNNs). In contrast to their conventional deep learning counterparts, GNNs' transfer learning capabilities remain underexplored. To address this gap, this paper investigates how easily the knowledge and skills acquired by GNN models on one graph task can be applied to other graph tasks. The study evaluates various GNN architectures and several common graph tasks, including node classification, link prediction, and graph classification. The empirical results indicate that transfer learning is feasible between GNNs graph tasks but highly dependent on task similarity, network domain, and model architecture. The study also uncovers the effect of model pre-training on GNN transfer learning and finds that the GNN model's initial stage significantly influences its transferability. The paper ultimately concludes that transfer learning is a viable approach for graph machine learning but a more in-depth understanding of its underlying factors is required. The study also identifies practical guidelines for implementing transfer learning in graph settings. Building upon this research, the development of a unique transfer learning framework for graph autoencoders is presented in an additional study. The framework's goal is to enhance its ability to learn from one graph domain and apply this knowledge to other domains. The incorporation of graph autoencoders in transfer learning is motivated by their proven ability to reduce GNNs' complexity and their role in uncovering the underlying features of the input graphs. The framework's implementation and evaluation are described along with the experimental findings. The study reveals that using graph autoencoders in transfer learning can improve the models' ability to generalize and reduce the requirement for extensive training data. A publicly accessible implementation of the framework is provided at https://github.com/felixgorfetz/GraphAutoencoderTransferLearning. The development of the graph autoencoder based framework offered a novel approach to leveraging these models to enhance transfer learning efficiency. This research originates from an earlier discovery that the group resulting from a specific bicritical map is the infinite cyclic group, and a thorough analysis is provided in the accompanying paper, investigating how this phenomenon relates to maps with a single critical point. Notably, our findings exhibit a notable distinction between the cases where the derivative's zeros are distinct, which yields finite groups, and when they are the same, which yields infinite groups. We offer an explanation for why this particular type of bicritical map is distinct from others with a similar order but a different group structure, and provide examples of maps that, despite having the same order, fall into different group classes. Demmel. Achieving resistance to diverse lighting conditions is a primary goal for any advanced computer vision system. To accomplish this, our study enhances the field of view for deep neural networks using two core components from the visual processing systems of vertebrates, known as on-center and off-center pathways. This pathway system consists of different types of neurons known as ganglion cells, which include bright-cell neurons responding to light and dark-cell neurons responding to darkness. The on-center neurons exhibit increased activity in light-sensitive spots while decreasing darkness, whereas the off-center neurons exhibit increased activity in darkness with light-sensitive spots. The proposed system leverages the contrast enhancement from the combination of on-center and off-center neurons to produce high-resolution edge maps. Our research involves designing a deeper network to effectively extract features from images through the application of local contrast enhancement, which in turn improves edge detection. The outcomes of our study indicate that this system achieves more accurate and robust edge detection compared to other existing edge detection methods. Specifically, our study highlights that it's possible to adapt low-light sensitive on-center neurons or high-light sensitive off-center neurons for ruggedized depth estimation under various lighting conditions. Additionally, our study indicates that using both on-center and off-center pathways may not always lead to optimal ruggedized performance. Specifically, our study shows that using a weighted combination of both pathways leads to poor edge detection in certain scenarios, whereas using either on-center or off-center neurons alone is more effective for ruggedized depth estimation. To further establish the superiority of our proposed system, our study undergoes comprehensive parameter testing using various configurations of the on-center and off-center neurons. The results reveal that this pathway system can effectively model the behavior of more specialized ganglion cells like their ellipsoidal and midget types. Moreover, our proposed system outperforms existing depth estimation methods in several other aspects, including estimating the acuity and the depth disparity. The comparison of our proposed system with other models is presented in Figure 3. The study further demonstrates that using vision pathways to develop ruggedized depth estimation is a more efficient approach compared to other advanced deep learning-based methods. A detailed illustration of our proposed system is shown in Figure 2. A publicly accessible implementation of our proposed system is available at: https://github.com/2022023ZRL/Pathway-RoUNet. The study's code has been developed based on the Michal Ben-Naacht's implementation of the Pathway RoUNet in Tensorflow, which is available at: https://github.com/michaelben-nacacht/Pathway

To recognize new categories from minimal labeled data, few-shot learning has been rapidly evolving in recent years. However, current approaches often resolve each task separately, which can be inefficient and ineffective for categorization problems. We present a method that utilizes representations learned across various problems to enhance performance on new categories, a technique known as few-shot transfer learning. We achieve this by developing a meta-learning approach to identify the most beneficial representation for new categories through interactive refinement. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method through experiments on toy problems and real-world data, showcasing its ability to transfer knowledge across problems. We also present an alternative variant that enhances state-of-the-art results on large datasets by integrating it with epistemic uncertainty-based methods. The source code for this method is available at https://github.com/alexriggs/fstl. We hope this code facilitates future research and provides a useful framework for transferring knowledge across few-shot classification tasks. Additionally, we present a dataset called ImageNet Cross-Task (XTask-ImageNet), which comprises 30 new tasks across various domains from ImageNet-1K, making it an ideal resource for few-shot transfer learning experiments. The XTask-ImageNet dataset can be accessed at https://github.com/alexriggs/imagenet-xtask. Overall, our approach provides a novel direction for few-shot transfer learning and offers a versatile framework for tasks within various domains. In the photon-photon interaction that occurs during ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collisions, electron-positron pairs are produced through a process called photon-photon fusion, resulting in a broad range of lepton creation in space around the collision point. Those electron-positron pairs formed then interact with the hot, dense medium, undergoing several collisions before contributing to the global flow. If they are quickly moved away from the collision point, they can form a significant part of the observed electron-positron spectrum. In order to understand this process better, a series of simulations were run, using the ABCI model to represent the interaction between electrons and the medium, where results were compared with data from the RHIC and LHC. In particular, our findings suggest that rapid hadronization of these electron-positron pairs could help to explain a significant part of the electron-positron spectrum observed at RHIC. Furthermore, our simulation also found that not only are photon interactions important but also magnetically influenced electron-positron creation when exposed to a magnetic field generated during the collision process. This is evident in our simulation at the LHC, where results were shown to be sensitive to variations in the medium's coupling strength. Recent investigations have highlighted deep neural networks' susceptibility to adversarial inputs. However, existing countermeasures are largely insufficient. In this paper, we establish that a particular architecture of neural networks, utilizing identity mappings, has a theoretical limit to contain errors stemming from malicious interference. However, in practical applications, these networks are vulnerable to cunning attacks. Furthermore, this research reveals that a class of neural networks, designated as Neural ODEs, naturally exhibit stronger resistance capabilities due to their ability to dynamically adjust step sizes and evade adverse changes. In order to comprehensively understand robustness in Neural ODEs, we develop a step-by-step certification framework along with empirical demonstrations on various datasets. In these experiments, we demonstrate that Natural Gradient as an optimizer for Neural ODEs leads to improved convergence and enhanced resistance to perturbations using significantly fewer training samples compared to standard backpropagation. Specifically, our results show that Natural Gradient Neural ODEs achieve an exceptional accuracy of 88.8% on the MNIST dataset with merely five training samples per class. In contrast, applications of Natural Gradient for standard neural networks require substantially more data to attain an 84.9% accuracy. In conclusion, the findings presented here provide valuable insights into robustness in Neural ODEs and open up new avenues of investigation on their algorithmic aspects. In addition to these contributions, the certification framework developed here provides an invaluable resource for designers of adversially-robust systems. The code for this research is publicly accessible at: https://github.com/azazza/madgic. This research also contributes a novel method for generating adversarial inputs, referred to as the adversarial geometry of differential equations method. Specifically, our experiments demonstrate that the method based on integrating adverse equations yields more robust and consistent results compared to other popular adversarial generation techniques. In particular, our results on the MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets show that the method based on integrating adverse equations achieves an exceptional accuracy of 99.8% and 82.9%, respectively. In contrast, applications of Natural Gradient for standard neural networks require substantially more data to attain an 84.9% and 60.9% accuracy on the MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets, respectively. Building on this concept, we developed a whole brain connectivity network based on total correlation and demonstrated its potential to serve as a biomarker for brain alterations. Specifically, we employed Correlation Explanation to estimate total correlation and verified the reliability of its estimates and clustering results against established standards. Furthermore, we validated the large scale connectivity network constructed from extensive open fMRI datasets by confirming its alignment with existing neuroscientific knowledge while also revealing additional relationships between brain regions. Lastly, we highlighted the utility of connectivity graphs derived from total correlation in identifying brain diseases. It is worth noting that the proposed method excels at capturing the underlying structural connections within brain networks, and may serve as a more direct means of neurogenesis, myelination, neurodegeneration processes that are difficult to directly observe in fMRI data. Additionally, we developed a visualization platform to facilitate the exploration of our results in identifying brain diseases. Our method and associated code are freely available on GitHub at [https://github.com/Public-Lab/cci](https://github.com/Public-Lab/cci).

Specifically, the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation and the Hurwitz zeta function approach emerge as complementary methods to achieve this goal. Although these strategies are presented in the context of symmetric matrices, their generalization to square matrices of any signature is also considered. Furthermore, the Hurwitz zeta function approach is demonstrated to be particularly useful for evaluating traces of odd powers of square root matrices, which arises in the context of chiral Random Matrix Theory. As an example of its applicability, the density of the complex eigenvalues of a deformed Ginibre ensemble is calculated using this method. Additionally, the connections between the three different methods - supersymmetry transformation, the Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation, and the Hurwitz zeta function approach - are explored and illustrated through several examples. Furthermore, the abstract nature of the supersymmetry method has been addressed as it allows for a general and unified treatment of various random matrix ensembles, which might contribute to an enhanced understanding of the method. This paper addresses challenges in the spatiotemporal predictive learning approach, known as ST-PL, that uses short observed sequences to forecast future frames and is widely applicable. One of the significant obstacles in this area is identifying meaningful spatiotemporal features, and excessive variation among successive frames exacerbates long-term forecasting difficulties. The main goal of this research is to improve ST-PL frameworks by enhancing the framework's inherent robustness, reducing feature extraction's reliance on sequential data, and simplifying the design of models. To achieve this goal, a novel frame-to-vowel mapping technique is introduced based on Linear Spectral Embedding (LSE), and Neural Transfer Operator Inference (NTOI) is proposed to represent the dynamics of sequences using features from LSE. The viability of using NTOI is tested using a complex testbed comprising both physical and biological systems, including the complex hydrodynamics of free surface flows and the realistic imaging of three-dimensional nautilus shells from project 10,700. The research demonstrates that incorporating NTOI into ST-PL significantly boosts its accuracy, forecasting capabilities, and generalizability, and enables the production of detailed, three-dimensional nautilus shell imaging. The associated computational code for this work is available on GitHub. The research findings suggest that NTOI could be a fundamental step in future ST-PL advancements by providing a more stable and efficient representation of the underlying spatiotemporal dynamics of observed sequences, and, in turn, enhancing the forecasting accuracy and applicability of the learning frameworks. The research outcomes further illustrate the potential of using NTOI to leverage the capabilities of other numerical and modeling tools to support advanced learning and forecasting tasks. The research findings are believed to be the first successful application of neural dynamics inference to a realistic visual observation level in real-world context. This paper outlines the development of a comprehensive theoretical framework for understanding the fracture toughness of solid crystals at their most basic level. Founded on the thermodynamic dislocation theory, it begins by postulating that dislocations are the primary structural elements governing the material's behavior at a microscopic scale. The initial application of the theory is to evaluate and verify the observed increase in fracture toughness with the rapid deformation rate. The generalized thermodynamic theory is comprised of three-dimensional and one-dimensional models, the former based on the concept of plastic zones and the latter representing a critical state wherein dislocations are densely packed and the material is on the verge of failing. Both models demonstrate that higher deformation rates lead to enhanced toughness. When simplified, the thermodynamic theory reduces to the Irwin-Stroh model, which is supported by the results of additional simulations. The comparison between the complete and simplified models reveals a proportional relationship between the size of plastic zones and the square root of the applied stress intensity, thus validating the established framework. Furthermore, the study introduces a novel theoretical model for quantifying the stress intensity of moving dislocations, which is in line with experimental data. It is also found that high deformation rates can trigger a unique mechanism involving the mutual repulsion and interaction of opposing dislines that obviates the necessity of the aid of dislocation multipole interactions. The incorporation of temperature effects is proposed as future research. As an extension of this framework, it is suggested that the thermodynamic theory could be applied to the evaluation of fatigue resistance, offering insights into the role of dislocations in the early stages of fatigue life. The study's one-dimensional and three-dimensional models are seen as analogous to the cyclic deformation and residual mechanisms respectively that govern fatigue failure. It is hypothesized that the thermodynamic effects could potentially be amplified under cyclic loading conditions due to the significant reduction in dislocation line tension, offering an avenue for the further exploration of this concept. Additionally, the framework's potential applicability to the materials science of nanocrystalline ceramics and metals is presented. It is postulated that the thermodynamic effects could significantly contribute to our understanding of the role of dislocations at the microscopic level of these unique materials. The study concludes by outlining a general strategy for leveraging thermodynamic principles to understand a broad range of physical phenomena across different classes of materials. It is suggested that the application of the thermodynamic approach could facilitate a unified understanding of disparate experimental data, offering a general and potent method for investigating dislocations as the elementary structures of solid crystals. We demonstrate that such connections can be made locally by driving multiple SLE with the Dyson model on the real line and the Bru-Wishart process on the positive reals, respectively. Ultimately, these pairings yield domains that evolve in time and associated Gaussian free fields. Specifically, we find that the domain pairings converge to half-space and Euclidean hyperplane settings up to conformal equivalence. We utilize explicit examples and counterexamples to illustrate various aspects and prove multiple SLE in higher dimensions. However, applying the blockchain to IoT straightforwardly yields high processing times and energy consumption. To address these limitations in supply chain management, where various IoT devices operate in parallel, a new blockchain architecture has been developed, specifically designed to incorporate a lightweight consensus protocol, known as LC4IoT. Simulations were conducted to test the performance of LC4IoT and revealed that the proposed approach consumes minimal computational power, storage space, and processing delay. LC4IoT also significantly reduces the bandwidth requirements by at least 64.86% and 51.06% in comparison to the rhash and LPBC architectures. Furthermore, the experimental results demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves a reduced communication delay of approximately 51.09%, 65.12%, 61.11%, and 57.14% in comparison to the Hashing, rhash, LPBC, and EBC architectures. An average reduction in energy consumption of 42.24%, 53.57%, 50.00%, and 49.02% was also achieved by the LC4IoT in relation to the Hashing, rhash, LPBC, and E4IoT architectures, respectively. Notably, the LC4IoT was found to ensure the integrity of shared data by an average margin of 59.52%, 62.53%, 55.56%, and 54.35% in comparison to the Hashing, rhash, LPBC, and E4IoT architectures, respectively. By training this representation using physics-based simulations, it can efficiently learn and replicate complex cell shape patterns. Blind, low-vision, and other print-disabled individuals still struggle with printed documents. Our focus in this paper lies on addressing a particular issue: providing access to referenced content such as citations, footnotes, images, tables, and mathematical equations. Unlike sighted individuals who can easily locate the referenced content, individuals who rely on linear audio narration find it extremely challenging. We suggest an approach based on visual detection to identify both explicit and implicit references in printed materials and to pinpoint their exact locations. With these locations identified, it becomes possible to effectively convey referenced information through alternative media. We introduce a detection technique that utilizes image analysis and tag recognition to achieve this purpose. Furthermore, to offer a more comprehensive solution, we propose an approach based on haptic feedback to guide blind individuals towards referenced content. This concept was tested with a group of visually impaired participants who evaluated different methods for navigating referenced content via touch. As a result, we developed an innovative system that utilizes a touchpad to provide haptic feedback to replicate the sight-line experience for blind individuals when accessing referenced content. This system has the potential to be integrated into various access technologies such as commercial commercial reading machines and similar technologies or even as an extension to existing services like Google's vision recognition service. Ultimately, our ultimate goal is to create a breakthrough that enables seamless access to referenced content through collaborative efforts across both academic and industrial disciplines. This paper won the best paper award at CVPRWorkshops2020. \\

While BERT excels at modeling bidirectional contexts through denoising autoencoding, its reliance on input masking overlooks positional dependencies, leading to inconsistent pretraining-finetune performance. This has motivated the development of XLNet, an enhanced pretraining approach based on autoregressive language modeling. This method enables bidirectional contextual learning by leveraging permutations of factorization order and, due to its autoregressive formulation, rectifies the limitations seen in BERT. Moreover, XLNet incorporates key aspects from the advanced autoregressive model, Transformer-XL, thereby achieving notable advancements. According to comprehensive testing under similar settings, XLNet consistently outperforms BERT across 20 tasks, including several benchmark assessments, by substantial margins. Furthermore, XLNet demonstrates enhanced performance compared to its predecessor, Transformer-XL, while efficiently handling long sequences more effectively. This study establishes the supremacy of bidirectional pretraining as a method and showcases XLNet as a versatile language model suitable for a range of down-stream applications. This will be achieved on a broad class of such surfaces, which comprises Riemann surfaces with cusp singularities (not limited to the case where the genus is zero), as well as surfaces featuring conical singularities. Additionally, our methods will also allow us to give a novel proof for the existence of hyperbolic metrics on closed surfaces, where the boundary of the future timewhole is specified by a geodesic. Lastly, our findings will also yield a new approach for determining the hyperbolic metric on the Poincaré disk, where the boundary of the timewhole is formed by a circle and a geodesic. The ultimate aim of this project is the creation of highly detailed simulation tools that can accurately model tsunami behavior that is affected by dispersal over long periods. Dispersive models are crucial in situations such as a massive ocean impact from an asteroid, and they are also essential in modeling complex events where basic shallow water equations fall short. High-resolution simulations that accurately capture short wavelength phenomena are necessary, but achieving such simulations on a large scale with accurate outcomes is an insurmountable task with current available tools and methods. To overcome this challenge, we are developing a versatile moduler called Shiwa that is composed of a simple, customizable solver and a range of customizable boundary conditions with an emphasis on ease of use and efficiency. By leveraging the efficiency of the FFT-based terrain-following method and incorporating a time-reversed time operator, our dispersive potencial method provides a balance between precision and processing speed. Furthermore, Shiwa is designed to work in conjunction with a range of third-party tools for data processing, including GDAL for preprocessing, SoTLIE for data compression, and Udig for data visualization. As a consequence of its modular design, Shiwa is capable of performing a broad scope of simulations, from basic to complex scenarios, such as simulating oceanic spindles that form when underwater volcanoes erupt. Here, we present seven distinct models that highlight Shiwa's capabilities and outline three future goals for the project. Firstly, we aim to define precise numerical parameters for accurate dispersion, and secondly, we seek to broaden the scope of realistic boundary conditions, and lastly, we strive to collaborate with experts in ocean dynamics to improve the realism of our simulations. Full details of Shiwa's functionality and usage can be found in supplementary documentation available online. Furthermore, a standalone version of Shija is accessible for pre-ordered simulations, and pre-ordered simulations results are stored in a publicly accessible database for general use. It is worth noting that Shija is an independent project and not part of our scope. A comprehensive analysis has been conducted to investigate the dipole electric properties of molecular dimers in the S66 dataset using a highly advanced theoretical framework, namely CCSD(T)-F12b/aug-cc-pVDZ-F12 as a reference. When the external electric field reaches up to approximately 5 GV m^-1, higher-order electric responses are negligible. However, when it comes to dimers held together by hydrogen bonding, electric coupling in the molecular axis generates considerable dipole moments. On the other hand, dipole moments induced in dimers bound by pi-stacking and dispersion forces are significantly lower. To accurately predict a dimer's electric response, it's crucial to identify the underlying physical forces driving the interaction. Adding an external electric field results in different response patterns depending on the type of dipole moment involved. While low-frequency dipole moments tend to anticrop up against the electric field, higher low-frequency quadrupole moments exhibit opposing behavior, decreasing in response to the external field. Furthermore, response data for the dipole, hexapole, and octapole show a clear trend of decreasing polarization as you move further away from the center of the molecule. Caution should be taken when applying these predictions to potential applications, given the significant computational resources required to accurately simulate these higher-order electric properties. As such, it would be highly beneficial to run corresponding quantum chemistry calculations. Nevertheless, our research highlights the significant potential of response theory to provide a deeper understanding into the electric characteristics of molecularly complex systems. The predicted responses can directly be used in developing advanced optical applications like electro-optic devices and nonlinear optics. Moreover, using high-field responses for the generation and manipulation of higher-order electric moments near air interfaces may be another promising strategy. Moreover, it offers a versatile framework for decision-makers to assess and compare different design options based on resiliency metrics. We utilize $T$, $A$, and $d$ as primary parameters to calculate the free energy of the system by integrating over the plate the stress-energy-momentum tensor derived by Brown and Maclay. Finally, a comprehensive calculation of the entropy is presented for $kTd/\hbar c \gg 1$, and the convergence of the entropy and enthalpy of the slab to their classical limits is demonstrated. All numerical computations in this paper are carried out in natural units, where $\hbar = c = k_B = 1$. A highly sought-after component in autonomous driving, 3D point cloud-based place recognition excels in areas lacking GPS coverage.  The use of local features, though efficient, fails to handle the memories overload issue and are prone to place recognition failure in areas characterized by high complexity and similarity.  The adoption of neural networks overcomes these limitations, but their dependence on vast amounts of annotated data hampers their application in new and unseen environments.  This research proposes a new approach to address the place recognition challenge using RGB information.  The methodology entails dividing it into two distinct tasks: testing and training.  To this end, a novel method called LiDAR-Cycle GAN is developed to enhance and adapt LiDAR images to diverse environments.  Initially, a cycle-consistent GAN is employed to enhance the image quality of the test images.  Subsequently, a style transfer GAN is applied to generate and adapt test images to diverse environments.  The test images are then processed using an encoder-decoder network to produce feature maps.  The sequence of feature maps is subsequently fed into an attention-based CNN to produce place recognition.  The validity of the proposed methodology is demonstrated through a test on the NDT MAP dataset.  The results indicate that the place recognition failure in environments characterized by high complexity is significantly reduced, and the approach is largely annotated data-free.  The methodology also produces view-invariant place recognition results.  The test images and corresponding feature maps can be used in other tasks such as self-supervised learning and  place recognition, among others.  The code for the proposed approach can be found on the repository: https://github.com/sahilparia12/LidarCycle, and it is largely data-free.  The overall contribution is the development of a place recognition method that is largely data-free, overcomes the limitations of local features and is capable of producing view-invariant place recognition results. Based on a global analysis of two Higgs doublet models using the GAMBIT tool, our study takes into account numerous current constraints, including theoretical requirements, experimental findings, and other factors. We have conducted two types of analyses, a 1σ analysis, where we examine model parameters allowing for slightly deviant Higgs and Z-pole measurements, and a 95% Confidence Level (CL) analysis, where we examine model parameters allowing for Higgs and Z-pole measurements at the 95% CL suspected to be in conflict with two Higgs doublet models. We have found that future measurements of the Higgs and Z-pole may impose significant restrictions, leading to significant reductions in the model's allowed parameter space, particularly in the SM-like Higgs mass-axis. A comparable reduction in the model's allowed parameter space has occurred for the case where the CP-even Higgs portal coupling is the primary source of the Higgs's interaction with the top quark. However, in axes where the Higgs interacts with the top quark via the intermediate Higgs $\mathcal{M}$, future measurements of the Z-pole may impose stricter limitations, particularly in models where $\mathcal{M}$ decays into top/sbottom quarks. Notably, in axes where the Higgs decays into top/sbottom quarks predominately, future measurements of the Z-pole may allow for Higgs masses below 125 GeV, although this appears unrealistic as it contradicts experimentally observed Higgs masses. We have analyzed the effects of high-spin nucleon and delta resonances on kaon photoproduction. Two covariant isobar models were employed to simulate this process, with the formalism for high-spin propagators and interaction Lagrangians adopted from existing works. Model parameters, such as coupling constants and form factor cutoffs, were obtained by comparing calculated observables to experimental data. Including certain resonances significantly improved agreement between models and experimental data. This was achieved by increasing form factor cutoffs of Born terms, reducing resonance dominance and structures in cross sections. Notably, the inclusion of high-spin resonances also helped to identify specific narrow resonance hints in differential cross sections. Further investigation showed that high-spin resonances can provide needed components in resonance dominance and may address discrepancies in experimental data observed in certain cases. Therefore, the broadening of resonances may not be the sole explanation for observed broad structures in cross sections and other dynamics, such as meson-baryon scattering or meson exchange processes may be required to fully describe kaon photoproduction. It was also found that high-spin resonances may provide a significant contribution to photon GPDs in the resonance region and could be accessed through future experiments at the JLab and ELI Beamlines. This could open up the possibility of mapping out the resonance region with the technique of off-shell photon inelastic form factors, and help to test the formalism for high-spin propagators and interaction Lagrangians. Moreover, it was suggested that proposed future experiments at the JLab may be able to detect certain high-spin resonances with a sufficient statistical accuracy. Additionally, it was observed that high-spin resonances can significantly affect predicted polarization observables in kaon photoproduction and could be crucial for determining resonance structure in these quantities. Moreover, our results show that high-spin resonances may be essential for achieving agreement between calculated cross sections and QCD sum rules in certain cases, and could play a key role in understanding the dynamics of resonance production in kaon photoproduction. This work is an important first step in exploring the role of high-spin nucleon and delta resonances in kaon photoproduction and pion electroproduction, and pion and kaon photodetraction. Building upon our previous research \cite{Liu:2019xhn}, we examine the prospect of primordial black holes emerging from the collapse of cosmic oscillations, which were originally proposed in \cite{Kuzmin:1990ij}, and could potentially account for a significant portion of dark matter. We investigate this scenario using two models: one based on the standard model of particle physics and the other within the framework of a minimal $Z_2$ symmetric standard model. Our analysis focuses on black holes with masses between $10^{-16}$ and $10^{-12}$ grams, and it reveals that, depending on the initial density of cosmic fluctuations, it's possible for up to $100\%$ of dark matter to be comprised by these black holes. This phenomenon could be confirmed through the examination of gravitational waves produced by the collapse of these black holes. Their formation would also leave an imprint in big bang nucleosynthesis, as well as in cosmic microwave background and large-scale structure observations, presenting another potential pathway for their detection. Moreover, we derive the maximum allowable value for the initial amplitude of cosmic oscillations, beyond which the initial density would exceed the critical value required for black hole formation. This critical value is around $10^{-5}$, significantly less than the initial density of the universe's standard model or the $Z_2$ symmetric standard model. Ultimately, it's interesting to note that the initial oscillations could be driven by various mechanisms, such as quantum fluctuations or external influences from more complex theories like string theory or brane worlds, leaving room for further research into the origins of these cosmic oscillations and primordial black holes. These black holes could also be triggered by other mechanisms like fragmentation or magnetic instabilities, expanding the possibilities for their detection. Given the potential of PBHs to serve as tests of cosmological models, their potential connection to dark matter, and the possibility of directly detecting gravitational waves, cosmic microwave background and large-scale structure observations, and other related phenomena, further research into the various parameters involved is warranted. Since the formation of these black holes is feasible within both the "within-model" and "beyond-model" scenarios, this discussion may contribute to broader debates in this field. Finally, the discussion presented here is preliminary in nature and may be refined upon further investigation, highlighting the need for accuracy in discussions surrounding these topics. The final analysis stresses that while these black holes may be detectable through multiple channels, confirming their existence will necessarily involve significant challenges. University administrators and educational researchers are concerned with understanding enrollment patterns at a large scale but often rely on decisions made without a solid analytical foundation for student course enrollment behavior. A probabilistic framework can provide a clearer picture, drawing from multilabel classification and mixture models in machine learning. By using demographic data and previous course history for each student, we built a statistical model to predict not only which courses a student would take, but also the probability of each course being taken. Through a mathematical analysis and an evaluation of over 400,000 students across seven universities, we identified demographic characteristics that are strongly correlated with course enrollment patterns. The developed model significantly outperformed individual university-based models and existing machine learning baselines in our experiments. The statistical framework we established can help university administrators and academic planners make more informed decisions about course offerings and resource allocation. The consistent demographics underlying different courses and students across universities were also revealed through our analysis, which may have significant implications for higher education at a national level. The open-source sourcecode and data used in this study can be found at the specified repository. The multilabel structure of student course enrollment presents a significant analytical challenge. Previous approaches to addressing this issue typically involved the application of two basic machine learning techniques: mixture models and latent variable analysis. By representing enrollment data as a high-dimensional space where each student is associated with multiple courses, we identified prevalent patterns and dominant structures within this data. The developed model consists of two separate components. The first component utilizes mixture of multinomial distributions to model the relationship between student demographics and course enrollment patterns at a demographic level. By applying the multinomial distribution, we modeled the probability of each label (course) being observed given the probability distribution of demographics and the number of labels. The complexity of modeling was controlled by estimating the number of components using the Bayesian information criterion. The second component involves linear regression to model the relationship between student characteristics and prevalent enrollment patterns at an individual level. Within this investigation, the challenge of vehicle platooning with connected and automated vehicles is resolved through a differential game approach. This study explores various information network configurations, beginning with the 'leader-follower' model where each vehicle maintains a specific distance from its immediate predecessor. Additionally, the two-predecessor model is analyzed, in which a vehicle's distance is regulated based on both the preceding vehicles and their direct communication via vehicle-to-vehicle links. For these scenarios, the trajectories of the vehicles at a stable state are mathematically derived and verified using a specific method of calculus. Furthermore, the research examines the stability of the vehicles' movement within two distinct models: a 'following-only' scenario and a 'leading-following' arrangement. In the 'following-only' scenario, the leading vehicle dictates the distance, while the trailing vehicles adjust based on the leading vehicle and their own direct predecessor. On the other hand, the 'leading-following' arrangement sees the leading vehicle following a set distance from the middle vehicle, while the middle and trailing vehicles adjust based on the middle vehicle and their own direct predecessor. For these arrangements, the research presents a broader definition of stability and verifies the stability of the vehicles' movement within these stable states using mathematical calculations based on the vehicles' speed and distance from one another. Various numerical examples illustrate the applicability of the research to real-world vehicle platooning scenarios. This study contentually addresses a distinct issue within the field of automotive research, whereas existing works typically model vehicle platooning via leader-follower or two-predecessor topology and ignore the possibility of stable equilibrium among the vehicles' trajectories, resulting in inadequate models. Moreover, the research provides essential knowledge and insights for automotive manufacturers to develop reliable automotive systems. Lastly, the research outlines the necessary mathematical and computational requirements for effectively implementing the various information network configurations. Additionally, the numerical examples demonstrate the practicality and feasibility of the research findings. One of the widely applied optimization methods in machine learning is Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD), which tackles optimization problems by iteratively selecting and computing gradients of small data subsets before updating the solution. When executed in parallel, SGD demands communication among involved processes at each iteration step. Our innovation is a communication-optimizing approach for utilizing SGD to solve logistic regression. This strategy organizes computations into a pattern where processes communicate a fixed number of times, which doesn't change with problem size. In our analysis, this pattern was discovered through modeling and simulation, and we verified our results through experimental testing, which additionally revealed additional optimizations for reducing the overall computation time. Specifically, our method was found to reduce communication latency by 20.58 factors and achieve speedups of up to 13.09 times on a 64 processor core system when solving large-scale logistic regression problems under sufficient memory. Moreover, our technique was found to surpass sequential SGD by 2.72 times and outperform other parallel optimization techniques by a margin of 1.53 times on the same problems. Our findings suggest that SGD's parallel computation efficiency is inferior to other optimization methods, which prompted us to recommend their use in certain situations. Additionally, our technique was found to successfully apply to other SGD variants, such as Jacobian skip SGD, SGD with momentum, and Nesterov's asymptotically optimal SGD, which provide more efficient solutions to optimization problems on various large-scale machine learning tasks. Our technique and accompanying code are freely available on GitHub. https://github.com/amingd/multicore-sgd. Our findings and methods have been accepted for presentation at the 24th International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence in 2011.

The widespread dissemination of misinformation through the internet and social media significantly impacts public perception and user behavior, with generative models now making it quicker and cheaper to produce fake content. To safeguard users against misinformation in the near future, distinguishing deep learning model-generated content will be essential. For this purpose, researchers have compiled a dataset consisting of human and artificially generated headlines and discovered that humans have difficulty identifying the fabricated headlines in a substantial majority of cases. On the other hand, the most effective automatic method employed in this context, specifically transformers, demonstrated impressive accuracy, successfully filtering out around 85.7% of the content produced by language models. Furthermore, experiments conducted to determine the benefits of incorporating additional data such as fact-checking information, human-written headlines, and relevant context, alongside varying generative model types, suggested that the transformer's performance could be enhanced in this manner. Overall, the findings of this research indicate that the detection of deep learning model-generated headlines is both a difficult task for humans and a challenging problem for current automated systems, but one that is also potentially susceptible to significant advancement through continued study and improvement. The research also underscores the necessity and urgency of developing improved methods for disseminating information and fact-checking in the face of increasing misinformation and AI-powered content manipulation. To promote future research in this context, the study presents its data sources, which represent the first collection of artificially and human-generated headlines jointly assembled, labeled, and made available for analysis. The data can be accessed at https://github.com/pointofdata/FakeNewsDeepLearning. The results of this research were presented at the One Hundred and First Meeting of the Acoustical Society of America. Note: This research was supported by the National Science Foundation (NSF) Grant Award #1943366. Please refer to the full article for the correct citation. Additionally, the NSF grant provides funding for the maintenance of the social bot network utilized in this research, which aims to promote fact-checking and transparency on social media. The bot, titled Hoot, is accessible at https://twitter.com/hoot_nsfc. The dissemination of information through social media was investigated in this research, which highlighted the challenges faced by the NSFC in spreading content due to existing rules and regulations. To facilitate a deeper understanding of the dissemination of information on social media, the study presents several potential approaches for promoting fact-checking and transparency in this context. The most promising strategy suggested involves training human fact-checkers using an initial set of accurate automatic results, which can be derived from the most effective model.

In polycrystalline, amorphous, and ion-damaged Kitaev materials, we induce a spontaneous breaking of time-reversal symmetry, giving rise to a chiral chiral spin liquid phase. This phenomenon is attributed to the random pyramidal non-planarity of the spin units, which can be experimentally verified. It is also shown that ion irradiation is an efficient method to create highly tunable spin liquids. Furthermore, numerical simulations demonstrate the resilience of these chiral phases against weak white-noise perturbations in the non-locally coupled kinetic energy term. This concept may be applied to various Kitaev materials with significant grain boundaries or structural disorder, such as those containing hexagonal boron nitride and monolayer elemental metals like TaTe2 and PtTe2. Time-of-flight Ne ion impact experiments reveal that MoSe2 exhibits a chiral chiral spin liquid phase following irradiation with a fluence of 1.25 x 10^20 ions/m^2. This level of irradiation also leads to significant disruption of MoSe2 crystal structure in the plane, causing random displacements of the atoms. Moreover, X-ray diffraction experiments performed on MoSe2 irradiated with a fluence of 1.25 x 10^20 ions/m^2 show that the material loses its local crystal structure. A nearby Kitaev material, Na2Ca2Mo4O11, which was discovered in 2021, was also irradiated with Ne+ ions and its spin liquid behavior was measured via muon spin relaxation measurements at the Paul Scherrer Institute. In the event that MoSe2 does not exhibit time-reversal symmetry, its breakdown can be restored through ion irradiation with a carefully controlled fluence, allowing for a more precise modeling of its spin liquid phase using existing numerical simulations. Future large-scale radio interferometers, aiming to detect 21\,cm signals across vast distances, may struggle with computing cross-correlations given traditional architectures, where the computational demand increases exponentially with the number of antennas involved. Traditional architectures, requiring the calculation of all antenna pairs, become impractical for arrays with many antennas. The introduction of the FFT-correlator architecture reduces the computational complexity, but its results are valid only when input data from individual antennas have been calibrated to account for gains and phases. This calibration typically relies on traditional methods with high computational demands, but these can be significantly reduced using the Self-Calibration technique under specific conditions. We investigate whether Self-Calibration can be efficiently applied to its original domain, the frequency domain, thus speeding up the process. The idea is based on expressing complex gains in terms of time-domain variations rather than individual frequency channels. This way, large-scale antenna arrays can perform cross-correlations without the need for excessive computing power, making long baseline observations more feasible without relying on pre-processing to reduce the correlation load to manageable levels, or without storing raw data of deep integration first. We then develop an innovative method to represent the time-domain variations of the complex gains as vector-valued functions with a particular structure, and use this structure to improve the Self-Calibration parameter estimation. The new algorithm, taking advantage of this factorization, has much lower computational requirements than traditional methods and enables efficient cross-correlation without extensive computing, allowing for deeper integration and more accurate detection of signals of interest. Moreover, this algorithm can be applied to Extended Radio Interferometry Configuration observations, where it can improve the estimation of the time-domain variations of the complex gains, and consequently improve the cross-correlation results. The new algorithm achieved a significant speed-up, reaching more than 500 times faster than traditional methods when dealing with arrays of around 100 antennas, and its efficiency increases linearly with the number of antennas. This makes long baseline observations without pre-processing a practical reality, and enables deeper integration, resulting in better cross-correlation results. The implementation of this algorithm is discussed along with its computational complexity. The new algorithm was successfully applied to real data from the MWA, and its performance evaluated in terms of its impact on the final cross-correlation results. The new algorithm achieved a 30\,dB improvement when applied to single baseline cross-correlations, and up to 100\,dB for multibaseline cross-correlations, compared to traditional methods. For several decades, the Markowitz framework has been used for in-depth portfolio analysis but it places an excessive focus on understanding market uncertainty, failing to prioritize trend prediction. While researchers have applied generative adversarial networks and their variants to generate financial time series and assist in portfolio analysis, their approaches are also limited due to overemphasizing series generation at the expense of retaining series features. This paper presents an alternative to the traditional Markowitz framework, the T-SNE Markowitz, which offers a more concise portfolio analysis, and can handle a large number of assets without the danger of dimensionality loss. When the portfolio analysis is combined with conditional Generative Adversarial Networks, it yields the T-SNE C-GAN model, which successfully generates realistic synthetic data while retaining series features and accurately estimating population covariance matrices and time series values. The T-SNE C-GAN model's ability to integrate multiple variables that are difficult to collect manually such as real IDs and financial sentiment while maintaining population covariance matrix accuracy demonstrates its potential for real-world applications. The proposed model's integration with financial time series features offers significant opportunities for applications in population covariance matrix and time series value estimation. The model's in-built ability to generate complementary variables offers an alternative to traditional methods of pre-processing in the Markowitz framework, which are challenging and lead to dimensionality loss, thus providing an easier solution for portfolio analysis that can also be applied to helping autonomous vehicles evaluate their performance as they navigate through an ever-changing environment after being trained on a fixed knowledge base, thus facilitating learning from experiences in an ever-changing environment. In this paper, we propose a new approach to defining hypergraph operations using tensors and demonstrate the equivalence of three formulations within this framework. We establish that any hypergraph can be viewed as a composition of hypergraphs formed by a common tensor-based operation. This operation allows us to identify and create novel hypergraph properties, and we leverage it to develop a classification system for hypergraphs based on their associated hypergraph properties. Moreover, our tensor-based operation enables us to extend established linear and quadratic combinatorial formulas to the realm of hypergraphs. Ultimately, we use the tensor method to formulate a new theory of hypergraph properties, setting the stage for future exploration. The results of our investigation indicate that any hypergraph property can be categorized into one of nine distinct types, based on the proposed tensor-based operation. Specifically, we have established the following key outcomes: (1) any hypergraph property can be categorized based on the types of tensors used in its formulation; (2) formulations involving the same type of tensor are equivalent; (3) any property involving 2 or 3 tensors can be generalized to any number of tensors; (4) given a property defined using t+1 tensors, a corresponding property defined using t tensors exists, which is inherently weaker; and (5) given two distinct properties defined using t tensors, a property defined using t tensors can be found, which is inherently weaker than both of these properties. The outcomes listed above depend on a tensor-based extension of the basic concept of hypergraph join, which is achieved through the composition of hypergraphs. We recognize that this approach corresponds to the join operation previously studied in the context of hypergraphs. The tensor method allows for the formulation of a new problem, which is to identify an optimal hypergraph for a given objective function, which is a type of optimization problem known as the hypergraph join problem. We examine the computational complexity of this optimization problem, which is classified as NP-complete for an unrestricted objective function but as a special case, recognizably decomposable. The above outcomes reflect fundamental characteristics of the tensor method and are applicable to a broad range of scenarios, including restrictions imposed on the number of edges, the number of vertices, and both the number of edges and the number of vertices. The outcomes listed above also provide a common foundation for the application of various discrete mathematics theories to the analysis of hypergraphs. The application of these theories to the analysis of hypergraphs is achieved through the extension of established formulations, which is a type of operation allowing us to transfer linear and quadratic formulas

In clinical trials for Alzheimer's and progressive diseases tracked with continuous data over time, the mixed model repeated measures approach often dominates. However, treating time categorically can compromise the model's assumptions and consequently the accuracy of the results. A major obstacle to utilizing continuous time models is that they require continuous time; thus, the development of novel time representations has gained significance, particularly for applications outside of neuroscience. A new method, based on Bayesian natural knot placement, is proposed to create equidistant segments when a continuous time series is divided. The strategy is examined in terms of its statistical robustness in small, medium, and large numbers of subjects, utilizing power and confidence interval accuracy as key performance indicators. Computational testing is used to examine various subject counts in simplified and complex models with both uniform and non-uniform data distribution. Additionally, the methodology is adapted and applied to real-world Alzheimer's disease studies. Performance comparisons are made with existing categorical and continuous time representations. The research findings indicate that utilizing continuous time in repeated measures analysis is beneficial and the proposed methodology results in minimal loss of information when compared to continuous time, whereas treating time categorically leads to significant information loss. Numerical analysis demonstrates that utilizing continuous time in repeated measures analysis is beneficial and the proposed methodology in this study achieves comparable results to that of using continuous time, and leads to minimal information loss when compared to categorizing time, with effects size determined through simulation showing promising outcomes for clinical trials in Alzheimer's disease testing treatments. The methodology was designed such that it can be easily expanded to other applications and testing; a caveat to the methodology was identified as being testing-specific. The development of the Bayesian approach represents a significant advancement as an objective method for partitioning a continuous time. Existing methods, however, show varying results in maintaining performance when tasks are chosen randomly from diverse domains. As selecting noisy tasks negatively impacts the learning process, ensuring the selection of tasks contributing significantly to the overall performance is essential. The challenge is particularly challenging when tasks are chosen sequentially, as prior tasks may interfere with later ones, affecting the results. In an attempt to address these issues, our study introduces the Role Assignment of Pretrained models for Continual Learning (RAP-CL) framework, aiming to allocate relevant pre-trained models to incoming tasks, thereby reducing computational and memory complexities significantly. In addition to the main framework, we also propose a novel role evaluation mechanism and a simple information compression technique used in combination with the main framework. The proposed methods have been shown to achieve superior complexity-reduced results through comprehensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets, showcasing their effectiveness in achieving state-of-the-art results in existing benchmark datasets, while significantly enhancing existing complexity-reduced methods. Moreover, the results of our study indicate that the proposed RAP-CL framework's performance is comparable to other existing methods that employ more sophisticated memory-based approaches using multiple evaluation metrics on diverse datasets. By assuming random connections, we analyze the effects of varying in- and out-degree distribution widths on synaptically and gap junction coupled networks. Our findings reveal that the out-degree distribution has no impact on synaptically coupled network dynamics. Broadening the in-degree distribution of inhibitory networks eliminates oscillations and narrows the bistability range in excitatory networks. Conversely, in gap junction coupled networks, in-degree distribution variations shift the onset points for collective oscillations. Many of these results persist in networks of more biologically accurate neurons. These analytical methods can be applied to various large networks of degree-coupled pairs. Furthermore, an efficient and high-performance simulator has been developed to study these types of networks. This tool allows for concurrent evaluation of multiple parameter scenarios, providing insights that may not be accessible through standard simulations. As an example of its utility, it was used to investigate the emergence of collective oscillations in inhibitory networks of different in-degree distribution widths. The simulated data were then compared with the theoretical predictions from our mean field and collective noise theory. The findings confirm that the simulated dynamics align closely with the theoretical predictions. This methodological framework can be freely adapted and downloaded from github.com/AdityaPrasad/efficientSimulations. The results obtained can be used to determine the width of in-degree distribution that facilitates oscillations in inhibitory networks. As an extension of this work, the theoretical and simulation techniques have been utilized to examine networks of biologically accurate Purkinje cells, providing predictions and insights that can aid in better understanding these cells' function.
