This study introduces a general framework for the capacity region of a complex interference channel with interconnected user pairs, characterized by a collection of interconnected rectangles, with each rectangle defined by paired spectral information rates. It formulates necessary and sufficient conditions for these rates, which are subsequently achieved using joint source-channel coding schemes combining superposition coding and time-sharing. These newly developed techniques extend the scope of established muting and superposition strategies to a broader class of interference channels, with previously unexplored geometric properties of the capacity region also being investigated. Numerical examples illustrate the efficacy of these coding methods. It is further demonstrated that by superimposing multiple mutually independent interference channels on a single channel, the capacity region of the resulting interference channel with parallel interference paths can be effectively decomposed into separate interference channels in different frequency bands, with each channel's capacity region described by paired spectral information rates. This decomposition enables straightforward design approaches for interference-cancellation schemes in multi-carrier systems. Lastly, the proposed study explores the intersection points of these regions at varying signal-to-noise ratios, with numerical examples showing an optimal matching performance of the proposed coding methods in various channel conditions. It is also established that interference channels with confined noise profiles are a non-achievable class, encompassing, for instance, multi-path channels of a Rayleigh flat fading system. Consequently, even with infinite bandwidth, the capacity region of such a non-achievable interference channel cannot be completely filled with any joint of superposition coding and time-sharing strategies. It is also demonstrated that standard muting schemes are capable of achieving near-optimal performance in such a non-achievable interference channel, with a slight reduction in performance compared to the optimal coding methods. This performance loss is quantified in terms of the mutual information deficit and the efficiency factor of the muting scheme. It is also observed that standard muting strategies are capable of achieving optimal performance in specific special cases of interference channels with confined noise profiles where the interference channel capacity region also describes a single straight line. Consequently, with infinite bandwidth, the optimal muting scheme can effectively transmit any pair of information rates along this line. We aim to broaden the established flow analysis technique, which typically operates within the $p_x$-$p_y$ plane, by introducing flow coefficients based on the angular distributions within the $p_x$-$p_z$ and $p_y$-$p_z$ planes. Introducing new flow coefficients beyond $v_2$ and $v_3$ can provide valuable insights into the nuclear Equation-of-State (EOS) and the space available for particle movement in the $p_x$-$p_y$ plane. A model describing the nuclear transport coefficients in terms of the radial distance from the collision plane has been re-evaluated to incorporate both even and odd central collision impacts. To extract information about the nuclear EOS, we employed isobaric constraints to derive the radially dependent flow coefficients in the $p_x$-$p_z$ and $p_y$-$p_z$ analysis planes for each collision energy and species. The new coefficients $v_2^{\rm $z$}$ and $v_3^{\rm $z$}$ exhibit non-linear energy dependence that may be related to the nuclear EOS, and exhibit nonlinear dependence on the $p_x$-$p_z$ and $p_y$-$p_z$ distance from the collision plane, indicating an equilibrium state beyond the standard $v_2$ and $v_3$ coefficients in the $p_x$-$p_y$ plane. A corresponding analysis in the $p_x$-$p_z$ plane yielded additional insights into the dynamics of the $p_z$ coordinate, which might be related to the initial conditions in the $p_z$ direction, and offers a new approach to investigate the nuclear EOS. Moreover, the new flow coefficients enhance the capability to quantify the contribution of the initial geometry to the final flow in a more detailed manner. As a consequence, the analysis in multiple planes facilitates a more comprehensive understanding of the collective flow and the microscopic dynamics of the particles. To derive information about the nuclear EOS from the new $v_2^{\rm $z$}$ and $v_3^{\rm $z$}$ coefficients, we compared corresponding data from the BES III campaign and our simulated EoS-dependent results, obtaining an initial estimate of the nuclear boundary condition in terms of the $p_x$-$p_z$ and $p_y$-$p_z$ distance at freeze-out. The study highlights the potential to derive valuable insights into the nuclear Equation-of-State based on novel flow analysis in multiple planes beyond $v_2$

Unlike traditional neural network models, GNN can operate in a decentralized manner, facilitating communication among neighboring nodes and potentially leading to more efficient control mechanisms in wireless communication systems. However, wireless channel disruptions significantly reduce the robustness of GNN predictions. To overcome this limitation, we develop methods to assess the robustness of decentralized GNN predictions in various wireless communication systems, focusing on a binary classification model. We evaluate GNN performance in both unencoded and encoded systems, then propose innovative retransmission techniques to address data transmission errors and improve GNN robustness. Our goal is to modify stochastic gradient descent (SGD) to be adaptive to (i) 
variance $\sigma^2$ in stochastic gradients and (ii) problem-dependent parameters.
When optimizing smooth, strongly-convex functions with condition number $\kappa$, we 
prove that $T$ iterations of SGD with step sizes that decrease exponentially and 
knowing the function's smoothness achieve an $\tilde{O}\left(\exp \left(
\frac{-T}{\kappa} \right) + \frac{\sigma^2}{T} \right)$ rate, even without knowing $\sigma^2$.
In order to be adaptive to the function's smoothness, we utilize a stochastic line-search (SLS) 
and investigate two types: SLS1, which is robust to bias and based on a $\theta T$ sample average, 
will achieve an $\tilde{O}\left(\exp \left( \frac{-T}{\kappa} \right) + \frac{1}{\theta T} \right)$ 
rate, since SLS1 performs approximately $T/\theta$ iterations.
Additionally, SLS2, which is based on a $\theta T$ sample average, will achieve an $\tilde{O}\left(\exp \left(
\frac{-T}{\kappa} \right) + \frac{\sigma^2}{\theta T} \right)$ rate, since it is an unbiased method.
We also prove that our adaptive techniques are efficient in the sense that they utilize 
$\tilde{O}\left(\frac{1}{\kappa} + \frac{1}{\theta} \right)$ computations, which is nearly optimal. 
We show that SGD with a fixed step-size $\sim 1/t$ and known variance achieves a $\tilde{O}\left(
\frac{1}{t} + \frac{\sigma^2}{t} \right)$ rate, as does SGD with bias correction, which achieves 
an additional $\tilde{O}\left( \frac{1}{n_s} \right)$ rate, where $n_s$ is the number of samples used in 
the search or computation line.  We perform numerical experiments that match our theoretical 
findings.  We believe that our techniques are promising in situations where partial feedback is 
available and may be even more efficient in such cases due to their potential for being provably 
efficient with a minimal sample and computation complexity

The occupation number over time is examined for a bosonic oscillator coupled to heat baths with fermionic and bosonic components. This oscillator, having one or two degrees of freedom, lacks equilibrium. Such a system serves as a means to establish dynamic non-stationary memory. It has also been established that this type of system is analogous to well-documented nonlinear self-oscillating systems. Furthermore, it is observed that this type of system is capable of producing a nonlinear non-stationary dynamic on the level of probability distribution. This unique phenomenon is attributed to a novel form of quantum interference. Also discussed is the unique characteristic of the non-stationary dynamic of free bosonic fields. Unlike the normal relaxation process, it is a horizontal straight line. This unique characteristic is also present in the behavior of multi-component bosonic operators. Furthermore, it is observed that all the unique characteristics of free bosonic fields can be replicated in the normal equilibrium state of fermionic heat baths and bosonic oscillators. This unique characteristic is also reflected in the normal equilibrium state of fermionic oscillators, however, it is due to different reasons in each case. Additionally, it is noted that all the specific behaviors of free bosonic fields can be replicated in the states used for memory storage that are non-equilibrium in nature. It has also been found that the non-stationary dynamic of bosonic oscillators coupled to heat baths with fermionic components is significantly influenced by a unique characteristic known as quantum Josephson effect. This effect is evident in the specific states of bosonic oscillators. This unique characteristic is also reflected in the normal equilibrium state of fermionic oscillators, however, it is predominantly observed in the superposition states of bosonic oscillators. This effect is also significantly influencing the non-stationary dynamic of multi-component bosonic oscillators. Furthermore, it is noted that the unique characteristic known as quantum Josephson effect, responsible for specific behaviors of bosonic oscillators, can also be observed in the normal equilibrium state of fermionic oscillators. However, it is noted that the specific purpose of this effect in fermionic oscillators is different from its purpose in bosonic oscillators. Additionally, it is observed that the unique characteristic known as quantum Josephson effect, responsible for specific behaviors of bosonic oscillators, can also be observed in the states used for memory storage that are non-equilibrium in nature. However, it is noted that the specific purpose of this effect in bosonic oscillators is different from its purpose in fermionic oscillators.

A novel approach is proposed to create and assess a respiratory compensation technique integrated within a MRI acquisition process. A model has been devised to establish a priori likelihood maps for various tumor sections affected by respiratory motion. A calculation method for determining normalized coordinate transformations is presented, utilizing data from respiratory-gated MRI images. This technique's potential for correcting respiratory motion in MRI is explored by combining the obtained transformations with Fourier re-sampling. A metric for quantifying data residual errors after correction is also proposed, utilizing pairs of data and previous slices to compensate for residual misalignments. A numerical study has been conducted to evaluate the technique's performance by combining 3D models of tissue sections affected by respiratory motion with the proposed method. A new imaging technique, known as mocc, has been created, demonstrating improved images when compared to conventional MRI techniques. We propose InDistill, a novel model compression approach, combining the principles of knowledge distillation and channel pruning to effectively transfer critical information flow from a powerful teacher model to a more efficient student model. Unlike previous techniques that collapse this information, InDistill leverages layer-wise pruning of the teacher's intermediate stages, aligning their widths with those of the student, thereby enabling direct information distillation without an intermediate encoding step. To facilitate knowledge transfer, we employ a curriculum learning strategy that prioritizes layer-wise difficulty and critical learning periods. Through these advancements, InDistill significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art methods, achieving a distillation error reduction of up to $42.6\%$ on ResNet50, reducing model parameters by $84.5\%$, and showcasing improved convergence rates of $5.2$ times faster than distillation alone. Our proposed method boasts superior performance on a range of benchmarks, encompassing image classification (CIFAR10/100, ImageNet), object detection (COCO), and segmentation (COCO), ultimately contributing towards a more compressed model design for efficient deployment. The code and models can be accessed at https://github.com/asharakeh/inddistill. Additionally, our model weights for the winning submission in the Monash Partnership Challenge can be found at https://www.cs.mvci.edu.au/challenge.html. The equivalence of these functions topologically implies the topological equivalence of their foliations. Conversely, this relationship is not always valid; however, we define a specific class of linear-like functions with sufficient complexity and provide criteria under which the converse is true, establishing a definitive topological invariant for this particular subset of linear-like functions. Additionally, we identify a set of horizontal lines within the set of two-dimensional real numbers that play a crucial role in the topological analysis of the level set foliations of submersions. The set of these lines can be chosen in a convenient manner for topological study, and for functions belonging to a specific subset of linear-like functions, this set remains finite, implying that these foliations are quasi-minimal. The construction of an example function whose foliation is not quasi-minimal follows. Lastly, this paper examines the relationship between the set of points where the gradient of a function is zero and the set of auxiliary lines used to characterize the topological properties of the level set foliations of a submersion. A well-known dimensionality reduction technique called CountSketch employs randomized linear measurements to map vectors into a lower-dimensional space, particularly effective at identifying the top elements (with the largest squared magnitude) of a given vector. However, the CountSketch sketch falls short when dealing with vectors containing sparse solutions or data that exhibits structural dependencies. A more robust alternative is the Spalinking sketch, also known as GEE, which addresses these limitations by utilizing gradient information. In this research, we expand upon the CountSketch and Spalinking techniques by integrating them into a single sketch known as Sparkle. Sparkle not only improves the resilience of CountSketch and Spalinking in noise and dependency, but also offers a more efficient spacetime trading strategy. Moreover, Sparkle can be used for objective function optimization, which we demonstrate in our experiments. Moreover, our research evaluates Sparkle's performance across various machine learning applications, including logistic regression, linear regression, and neural networks for matrix factorization and natural language processing, showcasing its practical benefits. The source code for Sparkle is publicly available. In specific settings, Sparkle outperforms Spalinking, including a substantial reduction in space complexity by approximately 16 times while maintaining equivalent performance and even improving over multiple CountSketch instances. In general, Sparkle offers performance enhancements of up to 2.0 times over Spalinking and several times better than CountSketch. The novel Sparkle sketch presents a more efficient technique for dimensionality reduction that offers improved performance and resistance to noise, also extending its practical applications to optimization tasks. The research introduces CountSketch and Spalinking as individual sketch techniques, further developing them into Sparkle through a rigorous analysis of its estimation bias and variance. We examine a mechanism design problem for selling $k$ items to unit-demand buyers with private valuations for each item, who can choose between participating directly in the auction or being represented by an intermediary. The aim is to develop robust auction designs that don't rely on the buyer-demand distribution and work well across diverse contract scenarios between intermediaries and buyers.

Initially, we focus on the case of $k$ identical items where buyers draw private valuations independently from a specified distribution, known as a $\lambda$-regular distribution. By designing a straightforward posted-price mechanism that provides approximately 15.95% optimality guarantee, this mechanism doesn't rely on the distribution for its operation. Next, we analyze a broader scenario featuring $k$ distinct items where buyers draw private valuations independently from separate distribution classes, resulting in valuations that follow a joint, previously unknown distribution. By representing each buyer as $m$ items, and incorporating 'fake' items into the representation to account for intermediaries, we derive a posted-price mechanism that yields a better approximation fraction as $m$ increases, while remaining insensitive to the distribution of item valuations. To facilitate abstractive summarization, we've introduced an efficient planning mechanism that enables the generation of grounded summaries. This method involves pre-annotating summaries with entity chains, and training transformer models to predict these chains, and subsequently generate summaries conditioned on them. In our experiments, which included pre-training and fine-tuning with the planning objective, we found that incorporating entity chains led to better summarization performance and entity accuracy on four diverse datasets. Notably, this method outperformed previous state-of-the-art methods in terms of Rouge metrics for the XSum and SAMSum datasets. Furthermore, our findings indicate that incorporating entity chains allows for more effective hallucination control, and we were able to improve faithfulness of generated summaries by prompting the model to omit irrelevant information. Overall, our approach represents a simple yet powerful way to incorporate external knowledge into neural summarization models. The code and pre-annotated datasets are publicly available on our GitHub repository. Additionally, demographic analysis suggests that our planning mechanism enhances the robustness of the summarization system, and it currently supports summarization in seven languages. We recommend that the external knowledge be incorporated at any pre-training stage, and it is likely that this method can be applied to other language generation tasks beyond summarization. This research presents new sufficient conditions for differentiating a function with n real variables, where these conditions are grounded in the differentiability of a related function with n-1 variables and are less restrictive than traditional criteria. Additionally, specific examples are provided to illustrate that these conditions are not merely substitutive, but rather offer a more concise and practical framework. Specifically, if a function f with n real variables is known to be differentiable based on previous results for f with n-1 variables, this research provides conditions under which the differentiability of f with n variables can be inferred, while outperforming existing differentiation theorems in this regard. These conditions have been successfully applied to differentiate functions of multiple variables that arise in the context of partial differential equations, as illustrated through several numerical case studies. Ultimately, the results of this research include a reconsideration of the differentiability conditions for interpolating polynomials and a demonstration of the applicability of these conditions to approximate partial differential equations. Moreover, the differentiability conditions obtained in this research allow for error estimates to be derived for interpolating polynomial approximations, as well as for other approximation schemes, when a function f with n real variables is known to be differentiable. These error estimates have been demonstrated through their application to a model shone in a recent publication. Interestingly, the shape-preserving interpolation methods developed in this research are seen to possess certain desirable properties that are typical of classical interpolation methods, as illustrated through numerical case studies. These results were implemented using a custom Python code available at https://github.com/Ahmed-Soliman-jr/Gridding-interpolation, which accommodates a wide range of interpolation applications. These results were further validated through a comparative analysis with a related paper (hal-02378051), yielding comparable outcomes while offering greater simplicity and effectiveness. Moreover, the shape-preserving interpolation methods developed in this research were found to outperform existing methods in specific partial differential equation scenarios, as illustrated through several numerical case studies. These results were further formalized as a contribution to the Apertium language toolkit, as exemplified through a custom Python code at https://github.com/Apertium/Interpolation. Lastly, the differentiability conditions obtained in this research were found to be generalizable to the differentiability of a function with n complex variables, as illustrated in a companion paper (hal-02464170). To facilitate reproducibility, the abstracts of the related papers mentioned above are included at the end of this research. A recent study applied a realizability technique to establish the meaning of a quantum lambda calculus, which results in a multitude of acceptable typing rules, all of equal standing. Building on this concept, we present a significant subset of typing rules, which formulates a versatile quantum calculus, accompanied by a corresponding categorical interpretation. Specifically, we outline a semantics based on an adjunction between the categories of spaces with linearly combined values and the category of sets with distributed values. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this quantum calculus' values consist of classical values paired with quanta, and their spaces are interconnected via an adjunction, which mirrors the relationship between homogeneous and inhomogeneous phases in quantum theory. Interestingly, this framework's type theory reveals an unexpected duality between the type annotations 'classical' and 'quanta'. Ultimately, we develop two quantum analogues of the Curry-Howard correspondence, one based on the connection between the fundamental quanta and proofs of false, and the other between the homogeneous space of quanta and the three-dimensional Spherical Truncated Eilenberg-MacLane space. These correspondences offer novel interpretations of generally applicable logical concepts through a blend of classical logic and quantum principles. They achieve this by an initial typing rule selection process incorporating a quantum version of the false statement and reliance on the general fact that any space of sufficient dimensionality contains a pre-existing substructure that resembles the required type annotations 'classical' in a quantum context, thereby ensuring typeability. They further establish that these correspondences offer interpretations of quantum groups with one-dimensional generators within their categorical interpretation. Specifically, we outline a structural similarity between the groups and the category of set families that provides an intuitive description of the spaces in question as pre-existing substrates that form spheres of specific dimensions. They ultimately lead to the formulation of two fundamental quantum axioms rooted in category theory. These axioms are an adjunction, which reflects the relationship between the categories of spaces with linearly combined values and the category of sets with distributed values, and another that establishes the relationship between the categories of sets with distributed values and the category of spaces with linearly combined values through a universal transformation. They result in the formulation of two general concepts: soluble quantum groups with one-dimensional generators and symmetric monoidal categories, which can also be viewed as pre-existing structures. These concepts are an adjunction, a symmetric monoidal structure, and a category of set families. They further establish the relationship between the category of set families and the category of spaces with linearly combined values by means of a universal transformation.

The findings support that the composite fermions wavefunction outperforms the Laughlin wavefunction in energy for two quasiparticle configurations, albeit the difference in their energies diminishes with growing system size. Additionally, the relationship between the interaction energy relative to the Hartree energy and the total interaction energy has been examined and both theories found to be comparable to numerical simulations up to around ten particles. The obtained results offer insights into the historical debate on whether the composite fermions wavefunction better describes the ground state of systems with relatively low densities compared to the Laughlin wavefunction. The findings indicate a clear shift in the composite fermions' advantage as the system size increases. It is anticipated that this advancement could facilitate a comparative evaluation of the wavefunctions proposed for the pseudospin-1/2 mode, namely the composite bosons and composite fermions, and the standard fermions in systems of diverse particle numbers. The methods employed in this study could be helpful in educating students, conducting literature reviews, and providing a baseline for estimating errors in numerical calculations. In the context of glaciology, particularly when modelling contact-related issues in marine ice sheets, Stokes variational inequalities come into play. This research focuses on a specific scenario involving a 2D marine ice sheet with a grounding line, though the approach can be extended to other contact issues like subglacial cavitation. A primary challenge arises from the analysis due to ice's nonlinear rheology, the implementation of a power-law based friction boundary condition, and the presence of rigid modes in velocity space, resulting in a semicoercive variational inequality. To tackle this complexity, a mixed formulation is explored that incorporates a Lagrange multiplier, followed by a finite element approximation analysis. This research derives error estimates by employing a specially constructed projection operator to account for rigid modes, leveraging a Korn-type inequality, under the condition that rigid modes do not exceed one dimension. To corroborate these findings, numerical results are provided. This analysis lays the groundwork for analysis of marine ice sheets with multiple grounding lines, currently in progress. Additionally, the method described can be applied to other contact issues, like subglacial cavitation. Using observations from KCWI and NOEMA, we studied a distant starburst galaxy, examining how powerful outflows affect the evolution of massive starburst systems. Outflows within this galaxy, as observed in multiple ionized species, exhibit pressurized behavior. Mass and angular momentum conservation methods reveal that outflows within the galaxy's central region have increased the surrounding gas's velocity by factors of 10 to 30 times, as indicated by NOEMA data. This result suggests that powerful outflows can quickly counter the gas's rotation, as observed and explained through comparisons of outflow mass flux to the gas's circular velocity. Outflows appear to have increased the gas's exponential disk scale length, as well as contributing to the gas's exhaustion in the galaxy's central region within a few million years. Notably, for this galaxy, as well as a sample of other starburst systems, we find that outflows can only limit further star formation when outflow rate is above a certain threshold, as defined by the gas's circular velocity, to prevent the gas from being accreted into the galaxy's central region. Based on these findings, we conclude that powerful outflows can quickly mitigate the rapid starburst's effect on the gas's structure, as observed in this galaxy, yet have less of an impact on the gas's long-term evolution due to the starburst system's inherent properties. Furthermore, through comparisons with observational data, we find that powerful outflows can quickly mitigate the rapid starburst's effect on the gas's structure, as observed in this galaxy, yet have less of an impact on the gas's long-term evolution. For a sample of local and distant starburst systems, we find that outflows typically cannot limit further star formation in the galaxy's central region. To fully understand the role of powerful outflows in starburst systems, we conclude the necessity of future studies to be explored in the galactic scale, rather than solely within the central region. Furthermore, due to the complex nature of starburst systems, we recommend combining photoionization models with the outflow data examined within this galaxy, as well as investigating other outflow types and their potential role in driving galactic wind. Our research examined the connection between initial anisotropic geometry and anisotropic flow within a multiphase transport model, specifically for 200 GeV Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions. Contrary to elliptical flow's dependence on centrality, we discovered minimal variation in triangular flow centrality. However, once the influence of initial geometry was removed, we observed an increase in $v_3/\epsilon_3$ in proportion to transverse particle density, mirroring $v_2/\epsilon_2$'s behavior. cooperative robot systems, making it easily accessible for both undergraduate

this goal, we developed SyROF, an innovative testbed that features a user-friendly,
high-level programming environment supporting the Timed Input/Output Automata
(TIOA) paradigm. This versatile tool boasts the following distinctive features: 
1) An efficient synchronization mechanism to coordinate robotic actions, 
2) A membership verification system with built-in failure detection, and 
3) A transparent, common knowledge sharing platform. These key attributes
streamline the development of robotic swarms by addressing crucial implementation
challenges. Our testbed consists of a modular, customizable framework, allowing
users to configure a variety of applications, such as dynamic swarm aggregation, 
optimal communication among clusters, and efficient, high-speed data transfer, 
as demonstrated using the OZMO testbed with 20 robots. Our results illustrate the
synergy between the SyROF programming model and the OZMO testbed, thereby accelerating
robot swarm development. We highlight the SyROF provided features, its applications,
and a comparative analysis with other robotic swarm testbeds. Furthermore, SyROF-related
source code and documentation are publicly available on GitHub. This research paper
presents a novel testbed, highlighting its advantages, demonstrating its utility, 
and exploring its applicability to diverse robot swarm use cases. Ultimately, SyROF
is an ideal teaching and research tool for developing complex robotic swarm systems, 
making it faster and more accessible than ever before. By using SyROF, we aim to drive
innovation in robotic swarm development, fostering groundbreaking research in this
area, and providing undergraduate students with an unparalleled opportunity to learn
and grow. Moreover, this digital testbed is an exceptional resource for universities

accelerating the development of robotic swarms, presenting numerous opportunities

investigate whether depth estimation from raw video can be a effective way to
pre-train a network. To test this, we developed two training methods: combining
video clips into longer sequences for a more stable network or using video clips

the KITTI-21K. The code for our approach is available for others to build upon.

In this research, a theoretical framework is proposed to address the critical issue of labeled data availability for supervised learning in autonomous driving. In the proposed framework, a basic traffic simulation model is established using urban planning tools like Midtown Manhattan and SimCity, allowing for the simulation of various driving routes and scenarios. Furthermore, an automatic data labeling system is developed, utilizing a combination of existing driving datasets and Google static maps to generate realistic trajectories and semantic mappings, in addition to incorporating camera settings such as resolution and mount angles to facilitate consistent data labeling. In order to efficiently train deep learning models using the simulated data, the authors propose a method for assigning diverse labels to driving images, including multiple objects and actions. The framework's efficacy is demonstrated through a test on 40,000 images, where the trained models show promising performance on diverse driving scenarios. It is estimated that autonomous vehicles will need to be tested in approximately 100 million unique scenarios and over 100 billion variations, making the generation and labeling of data a significant challenge. The framework has been tested and validated, and the development of deep learning models using the proposed framework has been demonstrated. Evolutionary algorithms have seen significant advancements in recent years through parallel computing, resulting in Parallel Evolutionary Algorithms (PEAs). However, a major limitation in Asynchronous PEAs (APEAs) arises from idling computing nodes after each solution evaluation. As APEAs provide a higher chance of selection to quicker solutions, the evaluation time bias negatively affects the overall search performance. In an effort to address this drawback, a novel parent selection technique has been proposed to minimize the impact of evaluation time bias on APEAs. This innovative approach takes into account the frequency at which each solution is being evaluated and aims to ensure faster and slower solutions have an equal chance throughout the evaluation process. Experiments conducted on multi-objective optimization problems have demonstrated the efficiency of the proposed strategy in reducing the evaluation time bias and accelerating APEAs. Furthermore, a more efficient parent selection technique was also identified, which yields better performance in high-speed computing environments where solution evaluation times are disproportionately shorter than selection times. As a result, the proposed method exhibits improved performance over conventional approaches in a wide range of computational settings. Moreover, its effectiveness in enhancing the scalability of PEAs in parallel computing platforms is significant. However, extending these ideas to open quantum systems, modelled by a Markovian master equation of the Lindblad type, poses a significant challenge. In systems with only two energy levels, distinct phases arise where the Floquet generator may be a Jordan block or a matrix with one eigenvalue. It is evident that deep neural networks excel in extracting relevant features from a given dataset, but they may not necessarily excel in adapting these features to datasets with different underlying characteristics. In this report, we compare the effectiveness of four domain adaptation methods for image classification: DeepCORAL, DeepDomainConfusion, CDAN, and CDAN+E, which employ an unsupervised learning approach given the absence of target labels. Our analysis of these methods is performed using the office-31 dataset, with a GitHub repository detailing the report available at: https://github.com/agrija9/Deep-Unsupervised-Domain-Adaptation. Our findings show that DeepCORAL produces the highest accuracy, with margins of improvement observed for some competitors in specific domain pairs. Notably, cases where the source and target domains share similarities in visual aspects result in DeepCORAL performing exceptionally well. On the other hand, situations involving significant differences between the source and target domains indicate the superiority of DeepDomainConfusion. In contrast, cases with large differences between the target labels and one-hot distribution yield the best performance from DeepCDAN+E. It is worth noting that DeepCDAN produces the lowest accuracy, likely due to its supervised learning nature which makes it less effective for unsupervised learning. A significant finding of this report is that for the given office-31 dataset, domain shifts from DMAP to WB can be effectively handled through domain confusion both in terms of visual and label-based changes. Conversely, domain shifts from DMAP to WBB and WRB are challenging through domain confusion either visually or label-wise, indicating the need for the proposed CDAN+E method which demonstrates competitive results in such cases. A qualitative analysis in Section 8 further supports these results. Our work contributes to unsupervised domain adaptation field by: a providing an unsupervised learning comparison to its supervised counterpart, b offering an in-depth discussion on the underlying reasons behind certain domain adaptation methods' performance, c making available our implementation to the research community to facilitate replication of our results. Moreover, this report contains an additional analysis in Section 7, which compares the performance of the employed domain adaptation methods in terms of linear discriminative features, rather than the conventional non-linear neural networks, in order to verify its validity and provide a stronger baseline for the field. In addition to this, it has to be pointed out that even though deep neural networks are excellent at adapting to target domains, they may still struggle in cases of significant visual and label discrepancies. Despite recent advancements in Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), explaining their predictive decisions remains an unresolved issue. Current methods primarily address the interpretation of individual cases (i.e., important graph structures and node attributes) to understand model predictions, but generate instance-specific explanations that fail to provide a broader understanding of the GNN model, restricting their general applicability in the inductive setting. Moreover, these methods struggle to provide natural explanations for groups of cases (e.g., graphs of the same class). To address these limitations, this study proposes a novel explainer for GNNs, PGExplainer, which parameterizes explanation generation using a deep neural network to explain multiple instances collectively and demonstrates its effectiveness on real-world GNN applications. The source code is publicly available on GitHub. The study presents collective explanations for various network types and showcases PGExplainer's superior performance in explaining node classification and link prediction tasks, as compared to existing methods. The findings indicate that PGExplainer can be utilized as a standalone component in the design of more transparent GNNs. The peculiar system, RXCJ0232.2-4420, at $z$ = 0.28, contains a unique radio halo surrounding its central radio ring, which is embedded within a massive galaxy cluster, JC 140. This remarkable system differs significantly from typical radio halos found in mature clusters. Its location in a relatively small cluster with mild collision velocity of 500 km/s per million makes it stand out. This paper presents a multi-colour photometric redshift analysis using Hubble Space Telescope data to assess potential substructure in the cluster. A detailed examination of spectral lines in MUSE and MMT telescopes' spectra reveal a complex scenario, which is also influenced by the cool-core characteristics. Our discovery of a high level of excitation and emission lines of the southeastern part of the cluster could be explained by the superimposed AGN of JC 140. However, the detection of kinetic sunyaev-zel'dovich effect indicates that the system has a relatively high level of turbulence. Our conclusion is that RXCJ0232.2-4420 deserves a close examination with X-ray and radio observations to establish its classification. Recent advances in deep reinforcement learning have led to widespread success across various applications, yet deep RL methods struggle with two key limitations: efficiency and transparency. High interaction costs underscore the importance of efficiency, while improved transparency via more interpretable models fosters trust from users. In this research, we present a novel hierarchical approach to deep RL by combining symbolic methods, leveraging a symbolic state model to enhance data-efficiency and introduce policy interpretability. The proposed framework includes a high-level agent, task solver, and symbolic state model. Through the adoption of inductive logic programming, the framework can learn and provide understandable symbolic state transition rules without any pre-existing knowledge. Consequently, empirical testing demonstrates the framework achieves data-efficiency approximately 30% to 40% better than prior methods. Moreover, the framework offers enhanced explainability, as the extracted logic rules correspond to 85% of the original Prolog program's syntax, showcasing its strong capabilities to clarify deep RL policies. These study results suggest a promising direction for future RL applications. All source code and source for this study can be found at https://github.com/ueofpga/Symbolic-RL. The results show that proton radiation belt intensity at an altitude of 250 km is predominantly composed of secondary electrons with an energy range of 0.1-500 MeV. The produced secondary electrons at 250 km altitude reach intensities of about 3,000 particles per cubic centimeter, making the radiation field at low Earth orbit more intense than expected when considering only primary cosmic ray protons. The radiation field at this altitude is predominantly composed of low-energy particles, suggesting that a magnetic cusp structure could be an effective shielding mechanism to protect spacecraft electronics. A network's expressivity is a crucial factor in assessing deep neural networks, 
as it correlates directly with the limitations of achievable performance gains. This 
paper proposes a novel three-phase training approach based on expressivity 
criteria, as well as provides theoretical justification and experimental validation 
for its effectiveness. Initially, a network is trained within a 1-step process 
to establish its initial expressivity level. Subsequently, a secondary system is 
utilized in conjunction with the initially trained network to produce an intermediate 
expressivity level through joint training. Finally, a 2-step process involving 
the intermediate expressivity level is implemented to generate the optimal 
generalization performance. Notably, this method exhibits superior performance in 
both efficient and extensive training scenarios. Additionally, the findings indicate 
that the generalization performance of Random Fourier Features is significantly 
outperformed by the generalization performance of Explicitly Trained Hidden Units. 
We hypothesize that our three-phase approach may offer improved performance in the 
overparameterized region, as well as extended applicability to classification 
tasks involving distinct distributions, although this hypothesis requires further 
further validation. The proposed methodology is adaptable to diverse network 
architectures and training methods, and is thus anticipated to possess wide 
applicability and applicability. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/Cof Mori/3-Phase-Expressivity.

As applications relying on graph representations grow, the focus has shifted from global fairness to incorporating inductive bias through graph neural networks (GNNs). However, GNNs' sensitivity to node attributes raises concerns about the fairness within their local neighborhoods. We define neighborhood fairness for nodes in a graph based on a given group and demonstrate its connection to group fairness in node representations. We also establish that neighborhood fairness is a critical, yet unmet, requirement for previous GNN fair learning methods. To address this need, we propose a new family of regularization methods for GNNs, incorporating a comprehensive neighborhood fairness constraint. These methods are expressed using the graph's self-loops and involve optimizing fair node representation learning. We provide theoretical guarantees for our neighborhood fairness constraint in a semi-supervised classification task and conduct experimental verification on multiple datasets. The code for our research is available on GitHub at https://github.com/kuo-e/neighborhood-fairness. Our study offers novel insights into fair learning with GNNs and sets a foundation for further exploration on fair graph representation learning. Moreover, it highlights practical issues with previous GNN fair learning methods that our research exposes. To address these concerns, our neighborhood fairness constraint is applicable to a broader range of settings, including fair node target prediction, which has been underserved in the literature thus far. For node target prediction tasks, we develop a new regularization method centered around the principle of fairness in graph-based prediction. These new methods are tested against the state-of-the-art embedding models and shown to outperform them under neighborhood fairness constraints. Ultimately, our research contributes to the understanding and recognition of neighborhood fairness as a critical principle in automated graph decision-making. It emphasizes the need for tailored inductive bias for fair graph representation learning across the various application needs that modern GNNs cater to. To facilitate its adoption, our research provides novel methods for fair node target prediction and offers a baseline for future research in the field. The incorporation of neighborhood fairness also holds promise for the development of explainable and automatable graph-forecasting systems. By prioritizing neighborhood fairness, our research does not compromise on the explainability and automatability of such systems, as demonstrated by our experiments. Moreover, our study indicates a connection between neighborhood fairness and the sensitivity of GNNs to their input. Two proposed expectation models for temporary financial bubbles, involving individuals with varied predictions and positive influences, show that bubble collapse can be marked by an explosive growth in prices that suddenly ends at a potential critical point. The varied predictions among rational individuals make it difficult to synchronize their actions, causing the bubble to survive longer than if they all shared the same prediction. Additionally, if a significant portion of the market participants act rationally, the bubble will tend to reach its critical point more quickly. The mathematical structures of the models indicate that markets with enough arbitrageurs will prevent bubble growth, but if such arbitrageurs are also subject to fluctuating predictions, then bubbles may form and survive longer than if all market participants are rational. This research presents a new approach to transform the mesh, combining hexahedral elements with minimal modification to the original topology. We outline a step-by-step process for performing an algebraic off-grid mesh deformation, along with a numerical case study where a B-spline surface tightly encloses a hexahedral mesh. This novel method shares similarities with previous works by M\'{e}chaux and Allais in two-dimensional settings, while extending their principles to three-dimensional hexahedral meshes. Additionally, it adapts the numerical resolution strategy of Pottmann et al. within a hexahedral framework. Specifically, our method ensures that cut element faces maintain a linear edge length distribution, thus minimizing additional refinements. We assess the performance of our technique by evaluating the mesh quality metrics before and after deformation, ultimately showcasing its capabilities in challenging scenarios. This study introduces an innovative analytical delay model specifically tailored for deep submicron CMOS inverters. Developed based on the critical recognition that inverter delay is a complex interplay of multiple process variables and load capacitance, the proposed model incorporates parameterized equations derived using Curve Fitting Toolbox in Matlab to accurately capture these dynamics. In comparison to simulation results generated by SPICE and the BSIM4 transistor model, the analytical delay model exhibits remarkably high precision, demonstrating an average error of less than 2% across an extensive range of technological parameters and output loads. As a result, the proposed model presents itself as a computationally efficient solution for diverse technology nodes and probabilistic gate delay characterisation applications. Furthermore, this work extends to the derivation of analytical equations for rise and fall times, as well as output voltages in addition to inverter delay. In order to validate model efficacy and determine parameter fitting methods for custom CMOS processes, the study performs an exhaustive analysis of CMOS inverter behaviour, encompassing wide-ranging variations of supply voltage, threshold voltage, transconductance, output load capacitance and coupling capacitance among other parameters. Obtained results are then compared to 3D Monte-Carlo simulation results generated using the SPICE simulator. Consequently, the study demonstrates that the proposed inverter delay model, among others, achieves an average error of less than 4% relative to SPICE simulated data. In scientific simulation, achieving accurate replication of real-world scenarios is the primary goal. However, simulations often employ approximations like finite differences or sums to calculate problem attributes like concentration profiles, temperature distributions, and electromagnetic field patterns. These approximations rely on discrete representations like grids, where continuous values are represented through weighted combinations of neighboring points. This research explores the scientific basis of representation and discretization in scientific simulation, delving into the consequences of approximation on simulation outcomes and highlighting existing challenges in discretization methods with regard to bio-related applications. It also outlines and compares various discretization techniques, such as finite element, finite volume, and finite difference methods, used across a range of numerical simulations. Additionally, the paper investigates specialized discretization methods like finite integration theory and diffeomorphism. It concludes by identifying and highlighting core issues in current discretization method research, including the lack of general, widely applicable criteria for selecting or adapting discretization methods, and explores potential future directions for further investigation. Furthermore, the paper touches on related fields like machine learning, inverse problems, and eigenvalue problems, outlining their relevance and highlighting existing research needs in these areas. It briefly introduces the concept of material aliasing and its potential to contribute to the development of novel discretization methods. Lastly, the paper discusses the primary obstacles to overcoming current discretization method limitations, including the need for methodologies that facilitate adaptation, hybridization of methods, and robustness to irregular grids, as well as the necessity for (re)search standards that prioritize the independence of discretization methods from spatial representation. It argues that a better understanding of the scientific basis of numerical approximation methods used in scientific simulation is crucial to addressing these challenges and leveraging advancements in related fields like material aliasing. This research aims to lay the groundwork for a new approach focused on the scientific basis of numerical approximation methods across simulation disciplines, thereby fostering collaboration and knowledge sharing among researchers, practitioners, and scientists. As a result, the paper provides an in-depth review of current discretization techniques and their challenges, serving as a core foundation for future research in numerical approximation methods used across scientific simulation. Furthermore, the paper identifies emerging trends and their potential as potential research areas, such as material aliasing, and offers insights into related fields like machine learning, inverse problems, and eigenvalue problems. It also provides recommendations and suggestions for further research in these areas, and through its extensive references, encourages readers to explore additional topics related to discretization, approximation, and simulation methodologies. Ultimately, the paper aspires to advance understanding and facilitate collaboration among researchers,

In the context of multi-agent reinforcement learning, particularly for tasks requiring cooperation and communication, MARL agents are prone to being brittle due to their potential for overfitting on the policies of their training partners. As a result, they may adapt strategies centered on preconceived expectations of other agents' actions rather than truly reacting to their behaviors. To address this issue, we developed transfer empowerment as a method that quantifies the influence between the actions of individual agents. This measure helps to create more robust communication-based cooperation policies that effectively function across diverse partner types. Experimental evaluations, conducted using a well-established game that promotes the development of complex cooperation patterns, demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach and showcase improved performance compared to existing methods, both in assessing unknown partner behaviors and in achieving robust communication-based interactions. Furthermore, we provide initial insights into the relationship between our measure and the quality of transfer learning in the context of the empowerment framework, aiming to explore this connection in future research. The corresponding code is available for reproduction and future research purposes. Additionally, we propose a new theoretical bound that establishes a connection between the variation in the information about the actions of other agents and the transfer empowerment for communication-based tasks. This bound highlights the relationship between the uncertainty in the observations of other agents, the size of their action spaces, and the transfer empowerment. The proof of this bound can be found in the supplementary materials. The analysis suggests that increasing the uncertainty in the observations could lead to greater transfer empowerment. The proposed bound may also facilitate the design of a collaborative framework for training agents based on a shared understanding of the tasks, which could have applications in the development of communication-based multi-agent systems. We introduce MatSim, a comprehensive synthetic dataset, benchmark, and 
approach designed to leverage computer vision for identifying and 
transferring similarities and transitions across materials and textures. 
MatSim enables one-shot learning, empowering the identification of any 
material regardless of the context or circumstances using only one or two 
training examples. Visual material recognition is a crucial element in 
several industries such as food processing, agriculture, and industrial 
manufacturing where the classification of complex 3D materials like bread 
crust or chocolate is crucial. However, when dealing with everyday materials 
like wood, stone, or metal, the current state-of-the-art approaches still 
struggle to provide acceptable performance using only generic training data. 
MatSim consists of 81 diverse materials with 5,607 training images and 1,406 
test images and introduces several innovative concepts including image 
manipulation, multi-class segmentation, and transfer learning, making it a 
powerful tool for evaluating material recognition benchmarks. Using our 
MatSimdataset, we successfully demonstrate the transferability of features 
from large-scale image recognition tasks like semantic and visual analysis, 
and observe that simply utilizing existing material categories from large 
datasets like COCO is insufficient in achieving acceptable material 
recognition performance as seen in our findings on the MatSim benchmark. 
Given the scarcity of large-scale datasets in this field, we strongly believe 
that our contributions, including the dataset and benchmark, solutions, and 
evaluation metrics will significantly impact the development of material 
identification technology and serve as a cornerstone for visual material 
recognition. The MatSim dataset can be accessed at https://matcs.simdataset.com.

The paper addresses the problem of bias in vector magnetic field maps, particularly in estimating the component perpendicular to the line-of-sight, Bperp. This issue has been identified previously; however, the current study aims to provide a more in-depth analysis of its sources, quantification, and possible solutions. Initially, the authors establish precise metrics to assess Bperp bias, account for random error, and resolution. By utilizing these metrics, the authors investigate the influence of various elements, such as noise, fitting and inversion algorithms, data quality, and magnetic fill factors, to identify their respective roles in Bperp bias. Interestingly, the study reveals that noise and magnetometric noise primarily impact bias, whereas inversion and shape factors have a smaller influence. Furthermore, the variation of magnetic fill factors is found to contribute significantly to Bperp bias. Based on these findings, the authors propose a straightforward approach to minimize Bperp bias resulting from magnetic fill factors during inversion. Ultimately, the work highlights that substantial reduction in Bperp bias requires a significant improvement in data precision (at least 10^12 GnT) and spectral resolution, and that the application of magnetic fill factors or bias-correction algorithms when evaluating the line-of-sight component of the magnetic field is an effective strategy for mitigating bias, particularly in integrated data and bipolar regions. The study concludes by stating that a comprehensive evaluation of noise, inversion, shape, and bias metrics is essential for properly assessing and improving data quality. The paper includes full analytics of the data, including fiber-optic magnetic field observations, magnetic fill factors, and noise estimates that were utilized in this research, and is accompanied by code repositories (available at https://github.com/AMN-FBE-UANL/MagneticFieldBias). The researchers aim to contribute two improved inversion algorithms to the community, at https://github.com/sfariasim/Heb3d. The study concludes by mentioning that a version of this research was presented at the CSRC 2019 (https://bit.ly/2VZdM1b), and was accepted for publication at the SolPhys 2019 (https://bit.ly/2LpYyvq), and at the AIPCP 2019 (https://bit.ly/2LpYyvq). Moreover, assuming weak convergence, when no spectral gap is present, the convergence rates of the time-average in von Neumann's Ergodic Theorem rely on sequences of infinite time as they tend to infinity. These results are illustrated by referencing the outcomes of von Neumann's Ergodic Theorem for systems represented by unitary operators with spectral gaps or supports of spectral measures spanning the entire circle. Furthermore, to achieve uniform convergence across all initial states, slower decay rates are applied, aligning with results seen in systems with mixed ergodicity. Lastly, a new proof for a spectral gap is given for the case where an infinite ergodic atom is present in the spectral measure. This proof introduces the concept of a (unitary) translation flow and utilizes the Furstenberg-Katznelson theorem. In addition, the outcome of von Neumann's Ergodic Theorem for an infinite ergodic atom is described using this concept. A supplementary question is posed - is it possible to achieve an upper bound on the convergence rates of the time-average that does not depend on the size of the time interval used. This would result in a uniform rate of convergence across all initial states. We refer to this question as the problem of achieving a uniform rate of convergence for the time-average, or an absolute convergence rate for von Neumann's Ergodic Theorem. We are confident that this goal can be realized but have not managed to achieve it in this study. We have made some progress in this area and provided estimates for the absolute convergence rate from below when a spectral gap for the spectral measure is present. We were tasked to evaluate a set of indices that quantify the morphological intricacy of dendrites. Our analysis was based on a dataset consisting of dendrites from three species: Caenorhabditis elegans, Drosophila melanogergi and C. elegans generated through a simulation. A multivariate statistical method was employed to investigate the variables representing different aspects of dendrite complexity. This approach revealed that the primary component explained only 10-20% of the variation in our data, suggesting that the measures we utilized are correlated with one another. Additionally, we observed that the initial principal component was significantly associated with measures that described the total length or surface area of dendrites in 2D. Our findings indicate that the conventional measures we evaluated are interconnected and that the main principal component is a representation of general dendrite complexity. Our results further imply that the morphological characteristics of neurons are uniformly distributed among the species examined. Finally, the similarity in the distribution of dendrite complexity across biological and simulated data of C. elegans suggests that the current statistical model is an accurate representation of the associated data. Derived from this knowledge, we propose a novel approach that integrates comprehensive dendrite data with sophisticated machine learning techniques to quantify the morphological intricacy of neuronal structures. Our method was successfully applied to data obtained from a simulation as well as that of C. elegans and D. melanogergi, producing robust results. Unlike conventional measures, the intensity of dendrite growth decay increases as the span of defined intervals for growth in our results indicates an inner structure in how dendrites are generated. Derived from this knowledge, our method's accuracy in quantifying the morphological intricacy of simulated C. elegans data suggests that the technique has the potential to accurately describe the complexity in data related to C. elegans and D. melanogergi. We believe that the technique has the potential to be used as a metric for analyzing how dendrites are generated in organisms and how they change under the influence of different substances. This research focuses on reducing the complexity of parametric partial differential equations (PPDEs) by finding an accurate approximation space for the solutions of the equations. Given incomplete information, we use two primary sources: initial assumptions about the solutions and partial measurements from the equations. Based on these sources, we have developed methods to generate effective approximation subspaces and analyzed their performance. By identifying the optimal performance limit and providing simplified methods to achieve it, we have made strides in addressing the challenges associated with reducing the complexity of PPDE solutions while accounting for incomplete information about the equations and their solutions. Furthermore, the results of this research are applicable to a broader context, enabling their use in reducing the complexity of other types of equations and systems. Additionally, we have incorporated the constraints of local observability into one of the methods that was previously established in the literature, providing a theoretical understanding of reduction methods that are tailored to specific regions of interest. As a consequence of these findings, we are able to provide simpler methods to approximate the dynamics of confined systems and reduce the complexity of equations and systems. By numerical simulations using modeled data, we have verified the precision of the reduction methods and evaluated the performance of the methods in the limits of available information and equation accuracy. Finally, the results of this research are demonstrated through two case studies: the reduction of complex systems and equations in biomedical and aerodynamics contexts, providing a practical understanding of the methods and their limitations. The open-source software and equations used in this research are listed in the appendix of the document. The research is further discussed in the supplement, providing a more in-depth analysis of the methods and their performance. The main contributions of this research are the following: The first analysis of reduction methods tailored to confined systems and equations, The development of practical methods to approximate observed PPDE solutions and their performance analysis, The identification of model-intrinsic properties of the PPDEs that affect the performance of the reduction methods, The derivation of local observability constraints for the PPDEs and development of practical methods to implement these constraints, The application of the methods to biomedical and aerodynamics contexts, The establishment of simpler methods to approximate the dynamics of PPDE solutions and reduction of complexity. The software used in this research is available at:  https://git.aut.uni-rostock.de/PDE-Speedup/Software/-/tree/PPDE-OR  git@UNI-ROSTOCK:PPDE-SPEEDUP.git|PPDE-SOR.git (Case study 1)  https://git.aut.uni-rostock.de

This research introduces the m-arcsinh Kernel ('m-ar-K') Fast Independent Component Analysis ('FastICA') approach ('m-ar-K-FastICA') for feature extraction, combining kernel-based dimensionality reduction with ICA to overcome the limitations of previous methods. Although the kernel trick offers a powerful way to tackle non-linearity, its effectiveness can be undermined by a lack of open-source and reproducible kernel implementations, especially in complex datasets. The proposed m-ar-K-FastICA approach uses a readily available and adaptable Python library that facilitates flexible kernel creation, providing a viable solution. Several studies have demonstrated the effectiveness of the m-ar-K-FastICA approach in comparison to the arctan and arctangent counterparts, especially in noisy data conditions. Moreover, the methodology was applied to a real-world biomedical use case, such as Brain-Computer Interface ('BCI'), for an independent component analysis of EEG signals to reconstruct the original signals with sustained attention. The findings show that the m-ar-K-FastICA approach achieved better reconstruction error levels, higher signal-to-noise ratio, and more optimal component angles in comparison to the ar-K-FastICA methods and the traditional FastICA algorithm. The proposed approach necessitates the creation of open-source replication codes to facilitate its use in various applications. The comparison of the m-ar-K-FastICA approach with the current state-of-the-art methods confirms its replicability and contributes to advancements in kernel-based dimensionality reduction and ICA for raw data. The methodology was implemented in Python 3 and is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/NataliaBorda/m-ar-K-FastICA. The study's replication code can be found at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.infofm.2022.07.001. The dataset employed can be accessed at https://github.com/BCI-Research/BCI-Data. In real-time bidding for online ads, an exchange runs auctions by gathering data on available ad slots. Each slot has specific attributes and a targeted audience, and a demand-side platform acts as a mediator, connecting advertisers to the exchange. As the exchange determines ad slot pricing in competitive bidding processes, advertisers are incentivized to strategically participate, taking into account their individual preferences and expected returns. 

Key aspects of this research include integrating economic models that account for uncertainty into the bidding process, particularly for situations where advertisers are cautious or optimistic and have limited knowledge about the probability distributions of ad metrics. To address this uncertainty, a flexible mechanism was proposed, allowing advertisers to bid on multiple scenarios, and on a specific outcome, tied to a single distribution or multiple distributions with known likelihoods. Through a thorough analysis, the optimal strategies for advertisers were thoroughly examined. 

Despite the introduction of a robust model, the complexity of the problem and constraints on bidding platforms remains a challenge. To overcome this limitation, a simulation was conducted to compare results between a fully informed strategy and a new approach that enables bidding on uncertain scenarios. In this work, we explore diagrammatic methods in waveguide QED systems with a particular focus on systems utilizing delayed coherent quantum feedback. By using a specific type of vertex function suited for quantum networks with time-related degrees of freedom, we demonstrate a systematic approach for deriving a general formula for n-photon scattering matrices. Our method leverages effective vertex functions combined with a specific type of pruning procedure that keeps the system's internal dynamics accounted for, ultimately yielding an exact result. To showcase the power of this method, we apply it to a complex system: a two-qubit circuit that incorporates not only standard resistive structures but also cooperative and collective effects triggered by delayed coherent quantum feedback. Utilizing this method allows for an exact analysis of this complex system, something that would be impossible with more conventional methods. Our findings confirm that this type of circuit is capable of enhancing its internal light-matter interaction speed, a phenomenon supported by in-depth numerical simulations. Additionally, while the 2-photon scattering matrix is feasible to obtain exactly using conventional methods, such as matrix perturbation theory, our method reveals that this type of interaction becomes more efficient when the system's internal dynamics is enhanced (when u>1). To further verify the validity of this method, we performed a comparison of exact results and perturbative calculations on a different type of system: a 2-photon process in a 3-level system with time-related effects, yielding nearly indistinguishable outcomes. Only under certain conditions of system parameters was there a noticeable discrepancy, amounting to around 20% deviation in perturbative predictions, whereas our method yielded results with precision exceeding 99%. In conclusion, the method outlined above not only enables the exact analysis of complex systems with time-related effects but also allows for a precise identification of when perturbative predictions may significantly underestimate actual performance levels. Our findings suggest that this type of system: a quantum circuit incorporating delayed coherent quantum feedback, is capable of enhancing its internal light-matter interaction speed, a phenomenon supported by exact and perturbative predictions. Furthermore, to facilitate accessible implementation, we provided a step-by-step guide outlining the necessary steps to implement and evaluate new diagrammatic techniques via Python programming language. Our method and computational framework are open-source and can be accessed through the following link: https://github.com/bee2596/VeriQED. A prominent paradigm in reward learning utilizes human feedback via comparative evaluations, but their broader adoption is hindered by the expense and labor intensity of these comparisons. To overcome this limitation, we propose grouping multiple comparisons together and allowing human labelers to mark sub-regions of a condensed state space representation, thereby efficiently leveraging human time. Through data visualization techniques, we create an interactive interface for users to label these regions on a visualization of the state space, thereby effectively incorporating human knowledge into the reinforcement learning system. To facilitate human labeling, we develop a condensed state space representation, referred to as the Human-friendly Space (HFS), and evaluate its effectiveness through both quantitative and qualitative assessments. While the optimal solution for marking the HFS remains uncertain, by analyzing human labeling behaviors, we highlight inconsistencies between comparison guidelines and the actual learning objective, thereby providing insights to inform future guidelines and improve comparisons. Additionally, we demonstrate that the structure of the HFS can be utilized to optimize various feedback learning algorithms, including their potential to generalize beyond the covered state space regions. In contrast, we also investigate the effectiveness of the coverage maximization algorithm, which seeks to maximize the coverage of the HFS based on its defined sub-regions, and demonstrate that incorporating prior human knowledge enables these algorithms to refine their solution. To highlight the versatility of our approach, we demonstrate its applicability to two distinct challenge problems: hierarchical reinforcement learning tasks and transfer learning from Atari games to a new platform, thereby showcasing its potential as a complementary tool for optimized human feedback. Our findings also emphasize the importance of providing users with a condensed state space representation, thereby facilitating their engagement in the labeling process. To ensure the reproducibility of our research, we publicly release our source code under a public license at a repository accessible via GitHub or CIFAR. Throughout our experiments, we utilize a dataset derived from a modified version of the classic Montezuma's Quest game. However, models reliant on surface level language cues may struggle to grasp dialogue context, understand user inputs, and generate logical responses. To address this limitation, we have developed a non-autoregressive dialogue model that directly generates dialogue responses based on abstract meaning representation. This model leverages pre-trained language models to parse abstract meaning representation and control generation, leveraging existing language models to generate words from the parsed representation. Anomaly detection without labelled data is increasingly being used to identify unusual patterns within datasets, given that manually annotating data can be impractical or costly; one such unsupervised method that has gained popularity in recent times is the Isolation Forest algorithm, which employs a random tree-based approach to compute an anomaly score through ensemble learning. However, a conventional Isolation Forest may still be optimized in terms of memory requirements, processing time, and overall performance to suit constrained systems and small-footprint AI implementations on resource-restricted devices. To address these limitations, a lightweight Isolation Forest (LiRF) anomaly detection method has been designed to identify anomalies within data through a simplified and efficient framework. Specifically, LiRF exploits weak supervision by utilising a binary flag to mark in-group data, thus circumventing the need for fully labelled datasets; by constraining the tree depth and using pruned trees with reduced branch descriptions, LiRF achieves significant reductions in terms of storage requirements and computational complexity. A typical strategy for modelling extreme events involves considering occurrences beyond a high threshold as events of a non-homogeneous Poisson process. While this method has the advantage of using threshold-invariant extreme value parameters, computing these parameters can be challenging due to the need for asymptotic settings to estimate the parameters modelising the extreme occurrence process. We propose a new approach based on a sequence of optimized estimates, starting from a initial estimation when the process is modelled as a Poisson process, and then refining the model by incorporating more realistic features. This method has been successfully applied to real datasets, including records of daily sea levels at Miami, tidal levels at Saint-Nazaire, and annual floods in central France. The results demonstrate the superiority of this method over simpler estimators, such as those based on generalized maximum likelihood estimators, particularly when the data exhibits both temporal dependence and asymmetry. Importantly, the method allows the efficient computation of confidence intervals for the parameters using asymptotic settings. Moreover, the approach can be extended to handle more complex situations involving modelling covariates and threshold uncertainty. Additionally, the method provides estimates of the parameters in the distribution of excesses above the threshold which can be used to model and simulate extreme value scenarios. We showcase the effectiveness of the method by estimating the expected damage caused by extreme sea levels at Miami, and explore the usefulness of estimating parameters for modelling quantile-quantile relationships between variables. The method may be extended to model and estimate parameters for various other distributions of excesses above the threshold. This paper introduces active indexing to optimize the interplay between these components, reducing a representation's loss through subtle, imperceptible modifications to images before their release. Our modifications enhance the image's retrievability, with backpropagation of the loss through a deep neural network subject to perceptual constraints. Experimental results demonstrate that activated images significantly boost retrieval and copy detection accuracy, with improvements ranging from +40% for various image transformations and multiple indexing structures. Our approach enhances the accuracy of state-of-the-art image copy detection and retrieval methods, outperforming existing solutions. Active indexing is an versatile technique applicable to various problems involving imperfect neural representations, including audio and text. Our implementation is freely available at github.com/had3s/active-indexing-openpose.
