Our current research builds upon our earlier findings where we identified acoustic characteristics essential to synthetic speech sounding natural. In this study, we investigate specific voice qualities by examining the perceptual importance of range limits in synthetic speech. To do this, we conducted two listening tests using female speech from various voice models with altered frequency range limits. The first test explored the impact of extending the frequency range of synthetic speech, while the second examined the effects of limiting it. Our results indicate that expanding the frequency range of synthetic speech contributes to an enhanced sense of warmth, achieved through increased brainstem audio likelihood and lower pitch variance. Conversely, limiting the frequency range of synthetic speech is found to increase spectral flatness, associated with a cooler voice perception. Furthermore, findings suggest that reducing the frequency range of synthetic speech is beneficial for listener comprehension, albeit to a minimal extent. Our research highlights the significance of frequency range in imparting voice quality and suggests that optimizing synthetic speech within natural frequency boundaries may enhance its naturalness. Importantly, narrowing the frequency range of synthetic speech is found to improve listener understanding, although only modestly. Our research implies that synthetic speech that stays within natural frequency limits can still convey meaningful information, thus any excessive extension may be unnecessary. The synthetic speech's frequency range should therefore be balanced between natural and unnatural limits. Importantly, these findings validate the proposal that optimizing synthetic speech within natural frequency boundaries is an effective approach. The importance of acoustic diversity in synthetic speech was also demonstrated, suggesting that a diverse range of voice models should be utilized to provide more accurate human-like guidance during listening tasks. In conclusion, our research sheds light on the acoustic characteristics that define the warmth of synthetic speech and provides insights into the importance of frequency range in both voice quality and comprehension. The outcomes of this study may inform the development of more efficient voice synthesis algorithms in the future. Building on the Heisenberg algebra concept of minimal length, a new geometrical approach to the Bohr-Mottelson model for nuclei is explored. By combining deformed canonical commutation relations with the Pauli-Podolsky prescription, a quantized Hamiltonian operator for a nucleus with collective geometric behavior is derived. The resulting operator, along with the creation and annihilation operators for collective modes, forms the core of the deformed BMV model. Employing this framework, the eigenvalues of the Hamiltonian are calculated for even-even nuclei, with the eigenvalues confirming $A^{5/3}$ scaling as predicted by collective quantum mechanics. Furthermore, by treating collective excitations as particles, a spectrum of the deformed BMV model is obtained, in which the first excited state corresponds to a particle-hole excitation, while the degeneracy of the first excited state may reflect the occurrence of symmetry operations within nuclear structure. The model's results for nuclear levels can be found online at the 'Collective Nuclei' website. Additionally, relations to the Cronin molecular model and nuclear pairing problem are investigated. It is shown that the deformed BMV model minimizes the length, along with the collective variance in position and momentum, at minimal geometric collectivity. Consequently, the proposed deformed BMV model is deemed a reliable method for describing nuclear structure. The model's potential applicability to hyperonic nuclei is also examined. Using the energy of gamma vibrations as an estimate for the nuclear pairing energy, the pairing correlation in such a system can be determined. Estimated values of the minimal geometric length for $\alpha$, $degerate$ nuclei as well as for $\alpha$, $\beta$, and $\gamma$ excitations in even-even nuclei of varying mass numbers have been calculated and published online along with the model's results. Moreover, the concept of minimal geometric collectivity has been discovered in compact $K$-islands within even-$K$ even-even nuclei below the deformed shell. The deformed BMV model may be developed into a powerful tool for exploring exotic nuclei with geometric collectivity. The quantum version of this framework is being prepared for application in analyzing data from GRETINA and GEFES, as well as investigating pairing correlations in both atomic and particle systems. A future study will involve deriving the classical version of this framework based on a prescribed classical Hamiltonian, with results to be reported in a following article. Recently, Golay complementary matrices have gained popularity in omnidirectional precoding techniques due to their unique properties allowing beamforming vector coding to achieve non-directional transmission. This led to exploring other COM matrices, such as those introduced by Li in 2017, via equivalent channel responses, and by Xu in 2018, via equivalent pilots, to determine their ability to facilitate Golay complementary codes under limited precoding constraints. Further research discovered a new COM matrix family possessing the same subset COM matrix property as the Li matrix and is also capable of producing Golay complementary codes under the same precoding limitation. Notably, these matrices exhibit higher average power than the Xu precoder and are also more efficient in terms of decoding complexity compared to the Li precoder. Moreover, it was found that this new family is an extension of the Xu precoder and shares a significant number of common non-zero elements. To verify the performance of these codes, simulations were conducted which demonstrated superior error-rate performance when using COM matrix-based precoders over precoders utilizing orthogonal codes. Finally, it has also been proven that this new family of precoders can also produce four-element subset COM matrices and is an extension of a specific subset COM matrix precoder introduced by Chen in 2020. The research findings were validated through experiments demonstrating the superior quality of the proposed precoders over those using four-element orthogonal codes. To further compare the performance of these codes, another experiment was conducted which showed that for precoders capable of producing four-element subset COM matrices whose elements have an average power of 1, it is possible that Li's precoder will have the lowest error-rate performance among this class when compared to other precoders, including those proposed in this study and by Xu and Chen. However, it is worth noting that this precoder will also have the lowest average power among this class. Experiments were also conducted to explore the relationship between Li's and Xu's precoders and to assess their overall compatibility. The findings revealed that first, Li's precoder was found to have a significant number of common non-zero elements with Xu's precoder and is also an extension of Xu's precoder. It was also discovered that both precoders can facilitate four-element subset COM matrices and is also capable of producing 16-element subset COM matrices under certain precoding limitations. On the other hand, it was found that Xu's precoder is an extension of Li's precoder and is also capable of producing this code under specific precoding constraints. A comprehensive study examines the connection between residual entropy and viscosity using an extensive, high-accuracy dataset. The concept was first introduced by Rosenfeld in 1977; this research demonstrates that scaling leads to a nearly linear correlation between residual entropy and reduced viscosity across a broad range of substances (argon, methane, CO2, and several others), including different model potentials. The initial "universal" correlation of Rosenfeld was found to be limited, yet adjusting the density can successfully relate the viscosity of many fluids to their residual entropy, with the condition of comparable reference states being essential. A preliminary classification system based on intermolecular potential types (hard-sphere, square-well, and 6-12 potential models) was also established, highlighting distinct viscosity behavior for each group. The viscosity of fluids belonging to the 6-12 potential type displays the most notable anisotropy. The concept of scaling was found to be effective in studying entropy, but not viscosity; the examination of viscosity showed that it is significantly influenced by the specific type of intermolecular potential. The measured reduced viscosities of fluids at their boiling points were found to be close to one another for different substances. The effectiveness of the "entropy correlation" approach was discussed in comparison with the "viscosity correlation" approach. The initial models used to derive the entropy and viscosity correlations were found to be insufficient; a refined set of parameters was proposed to improve the accuracy of predictions. The research highlights that although the initial "universal" correlation of Rosenfeld was inaccurate, the concept of residual entropy remains a valuable tool for understanding and analyzing the properties of molecular fluids. The study further clarifies the origin of the anisotropy of viscous forces in molecular fluids. The analysis of the viscous torque component in the spheroidal shape "particle-torus" model demonstrates that the force causing particle rotation is the gradient of the potential, not the entropy. A theoretical "unentropic" viscosity correlation was formulated and found to be successful only at high densities, as consistent with the initial "universal" correlation of Rosenfeld. The analysis of the anisotropic force component allows for a clear explanation of the interparticle transfer of angular momentum, revealing that this transfer is linked to a slip mechanism, with the accuracy of entropy-based predictions being enhanced by its inclusion. The research confirms that the configuration of particles influences the origin of the anisotropy of viscous forces; the efficiency of entropy, not viscosity, is significantly enhanced by this anisotropy effect. The possibility that our Universe undergoes a periodic cycle of expansion, slowing down, reversal, and asymptotically approaching static equilibrium is investigated in this research. We've found that a reasonable approximation of this phenomenon can be achieved using a single, complex scalar field governed by a particular version of the Einstein-Hilbert action, supported by a unique, time-dependent dark energy potential. These findings indicate that the field's kinetic and dark energy components are evenly distributed at static equilibrium points, ensuring the Universe remains static. When the Universe begins expanding, both components are predominantly kinetic. Key milestones of the dynamical phase are identified, including points where the field reverses direction, passes through stationary points, and contributes significantly to dark energy. We've also derived a set of equations that govern the dynamics of the system and analyzed its behavior using numerical methods, particularly with regard to the points where the field changes direction and approaches static equilibrium. These findings provide insight into the fundamental dynamics underlying the proposed cosmology and pave the way for further modeling of the reversals and asymptotic phases of the phenomenon. As a result of this research, the proposed cosmology has been shown to be both theoretically feasible and intriguing, suggesting the possibility that our Universe may undergo multiple cycles of expansion and growth in the future. As an extension of this research, the implications of periodic cosmology will be explored in the context of our current understanding of the Universe. It is proposed that the earliest expansion of the Universe, characterized by a deceleration parameter of approximately 0.5, could be identified as a phase of periodic cosmology. This phase occurred about 8 billion years ago, during the epoch of deceleration, and is supported by observations of supernovae Ia. These findings suggest that the light emitted by these supernovae was produced during a previous cycle of the Universe, in which the luminosity of the objects was reduced by the effects of cosmological expansion. As the objects erupted as supernovae, their emission was timed to coincide with the onset of the accelerating phase of the Universe, at a point where their observed luminosities were predicted to increase by a factor of approximately 100. This timing, coinciding with the onset of the accelerating phase at a distance of approximately 1000 Mpc, is remarkably consistent with the distribution of observed luminosities, in agreement with the predictions of periodic cosmology. A new superdeterministic theory of quantum mechanics known as Invariant-set theory is being proposed. This idea brings concepts from smooth ergodic dynamics into the realm of quantum mechanics, utilizing the inherent ideas of duplication and non-locality seen in Bell correlations. Despite initial similarities with other superdeterministic ideas, this theory has a unique difference - it doesn't try to explain away the predictions of quantum mechanics. Instead, it enhances them by creating a broader range of possible outcomes. We examine how a common argument against superdeterminacy on the grounds of "Hubble-scale" superdeterminacy holds up against the new framework. We show that this argument's effectiveness varies depending on how one defines "relevance." Also explored is the potential for Invariant-set theory to be tested, with a possible test related to how individual systems fall into states within their quantum environments. We conclude that this test offers no clear evidence in favor of the new theory but also no strong evidence against it either. The same test, however, does support an alternative solution to the Bell correlations, known as the "dummy-worlds theory," more strongly than Invariant-set theory does. Finally, some thoughts on how Invariant-set theory might be considered "post-quantum" are presented. These ideas raise questions about whether and how much a smooth, non-quantum system can fall into a state of quantum nature. The same inquiry applies to how many "dummy-worlds" it's possible for the universe to have. The question of these ideas might lead to new avenues of research, with a potential challenge being to develop a post-quantum Invariant-set theory. The ideas presented include a possible solution to this challenge, with a universe described as being composed of a quantum system and a "dummy-world" and a mechanism established for how the quantum system interacts with its environment. The effectiveness of superdeterministic ideas like Invariant-set and dummy-worlds might ultimately need to be evaluated by considering their ability to explain how the universe behaves at large scales. These ideas could then inform and be refined by a broader range of relevant observations at these scales. Specifically, it achieves higher accuracy with 20% lower latency and traffic than the current state-of-the-art. Our compact CNN also surpasses other notable NN architectures such as VGG16 and Shopee in terms of efficiency. Our proposed method is evaluated using the Google Speech Commands Dataset. In recent years, the needs of embedded systems have grown more complex.  These systems not only require reliable, hard real-time capabilities but also diversified functions like network capabilities.  Implementing virtualization using hypervisors has emerged as a suitable solution, however, existing hypervisors have been ineffective in achieving the required mix of hard real-time and virtualized services.  To resolve this issue, T-Visor, a lightweight hypervisor, has been developed to offer mixed criticality real-time capabilities, making it more suitable for the mixed criticality embedded real-time system.  Through its unique structure and the support of specific drivers, T-Visor is able to offer superior performance when compared to other hypervisors, making it an ideal choice for the mixed criticality embedded real-time system.  This paper will discuss how the lightweight hypervisor, T-Visor, can effectively support the mixed criticality embedded real-time system.  The performance evaluation results show that T-Visor's overhead is significantly lower than that of Xen and VMware hypervisors, making it an ideal solution for the mixed criticality embedded real-time system.  The support of the mixed criticality real-time capabilities and T-Visor's low overhead enable the coexistence of hard and soft real-time tasks as well as non-real-time tasks and Linux's embedded system functions on a shared host machine.  This allows the development of systems where real-time capabilities and non-real-time capabilities such as network protocols can share resources efficiently.  This capability is known as hypervisor assisted scheduling and enables the coordination of hypervisor driven task scheduling between the kernel and the hypervisor, enabling the interoperation of real-time and non-real-time tasks at the level of the operating system and the hypervisor, providing a mixed criticality real-time scheduling solution. This approach treats tunneling time as the average time at which electrons in a sample approach equilibrium, calculating this time based on the fluctuations of electron spin in a population of two-level systems. This concept is tested in an experiment involving a two-level system in transition, where the tunneling process is investigated under different conditions. However, the theoretical model assuming a well-defined tunneling time is found to be inconsistent with the observed fluctuations in quantum phases under the influence of random processes. This discrepancy suggests that the tunneling process is better described as part of a coherent process involving wave packet transmission, rather than the model of particles transitioning through classically defined times. To reconcile this, a modified model is proposed that addresses both the average tunneling time and the fluctuations surrounding the phase of precessing spins. This model assumes that the two-level systems begin transmitting packets of quantum information at random intervals. The simulations based on this model accurately predict both the average tunneling time and the fluctuations in quantum phases observed in the experiment, demonstrating compatibility with the principles of quantum mechanics. This approach effectively eliminates the concept of tunneling time, instead emphasizing the average tunneling time as a measure of the transmission rate. The simulations further reveal that the average tunneling time can be determined not only by the transmission rate but also by the degree to which the two-level systems deviate from equilibrium, which in turn is influenced by the height and location of the potential barrier as well as the temperature. The theoretical model proposed provides a quantitative explanation for the observed average tunneling times and the fluctuations in quantum phases, offering an alternative to classical models of tunneling time. The theoretical framework developed may be applied more broadly to the study of quantum tunneling in a variety of scenarios. The proposed approach may be particularly valuable for assessing the quantum tunneling coefficients in electrostatic barriers and barriers influenced by time-dependent potentials, where fluctuations in phases may provide direct insight into incoherent tunneling rates. This work introduces a novel approximation technique for a broad category of zero-sum-free cooperative games related to both variable differential investment and variable reinsurance. In the initial stages of this research, the distribution function of a general diffusion process is approximated using a free-boundary problem involving the Black-Scholes equation and a reflecting boundary, which is then used as the basis for calculating reinsurance levels. Subsequently, the distribution function of a general Wiener process is approximated using a partial differential equation (PDE) involving the reflecting boundary of a linear combination of conjugate variables. The resulting approximation errors are quantified and demonstrated to be asymptotically normal under certain conditions. The technique is further validated by numerical case studies involving investment-reinsurance scenarios, which highlight its practical utility. Lastly, the potential of partial differential equations (PDEs) to provide accurate approximations is explored via numerical case studies. The research findings indicate that when the mean variance process is a Wiener process with a H\"older continuous drift and linear volatility, the approximation error can be precisely described using a Wiener process and constants. By extending the complex domain without considering complex scaling, Deep Complex Networks (DCN) is limited, whereas SurReal achieves scaling invariance but discards complex information. In contrast, we approach complex scaling as a distinct co-domain transformation and create neural network functions tailored for this unique operation. Compared to DCN and SurReal on datasets MSTAR, CIFAR10, CIFAR100, and SVHN, our co-domain symmetric classifiers exhibit enhanced accuracy, improved generalizability, increased robustness, reduced bias and variance with significantly fewer model parameters. As the scaling operator covers diverse transformations, the corresponding classifiers cover many more classes than just the class label set, resulting in lower bias and variance. A novel machine learning framework addresses the challenge of prediction bias resulting from the omission of relevant variables known to the algorithm but not included in the observation. This bias is demonstrated in the context of a matrix completion problem where a learning algorithm is aware of some but not all item characteristics. As an example, a mixed signal representation is proposed, incorporating both the available data and the missing item information. Subsequently, two methods for generating the required missing signal estimates, inspired by Bayesian inference and maximum likelihood, are presented and discussed. Experimental results confirm that our approach effectively mitigates prediction bias in the absence of irrelevant features. Additionally, the framework's practical applications extend beyond matrix completion to cover a broader spectrum of machine learning problems involving missing data. Source code for the implementation is available on GitHub at https://github.com/guillaumeRichard/missing_signal. Our associated notebook can be found at https://github.com/guillaumeRichard/stochastic_completement_for_wass. Lastly, the theoretical underpinnings of our framework are detailed in supplementary materials prepared for NeurIPS 2022. Subsequently, the results of our research were presented at the conference. To address the bias, the framework incorporates both the available data and the missing item information as a mixed signal representation. The results of our experiments confirm that our approach effectively mitigates prediction bias in the absence of irrelevant features. We investigate numerically charge-neutral collective excitations in fractional quantum Hall systems, focusing on two specific Jain states, ν=2/7 and ν=2/9. An analysis of the interaction-induced corrections reveals that these magnetoroton Hall peaks at finite temperature are distinct from those observed at ν=1/3 or in the ground state. Specifically, in addition to Hall conductivity plateaus, spectral representations show a series of oscillations at finite temperature. Calculations using both the RPA approximation and the conventional finite temperature perturbative approach are conducted with a diluted two-dimensional electron gas, involving the effects of electron interaction, Coulombic potentials, and Landau levels. A detailed analysis of the traditional perturbative approach reveals its shortcomings and inconsistencies, which become apparent both in its convergence towards the continuum limit and in its ability to describe magnetoroton Hall peaks. It is found that including higher-order contributions in the traditional perturbative approach leads to a convergence towards the continuum limit, which in turn enables the description of magnetoraton Hall peaks based on a fermionic representation. On the other hand, in the context of the spin-polarized ground state, an explicit calculation shows that a representation based on the quasiparticle and quasihole density matrix is successful in describing magnetoroton Hall peaks. Furthermore, in the thermodynamic description of these magnetoroton Hall peaks at finite temperature, a representation based on the quasiparticle and quasihole density matrix in the vicinity of these peaks shows a discontinuity, which becomes apparent beyond the continuum limit. It is found that this discrepancy is effectively addressed by representing the interaction-induced corrections to the collective excitations based on the adiabatic expansion of the Luttinger liquid, specifically the extended Kalmeyer-Lainé Lagrangian. Consequently, in the context of the description of magnetoroton Hall peaks, both the representation based on the quasiparticle and quasihole density matrix and the extended Kalmeyer-Lainé Lagrangian are found to be essential and necessary at finite temperature, specifically beyond the continuum limit. It is hoped that this success in describing magnetoroton Hall peaks at finite temperature may serve as an inspiration for developing new numerical and theoretical approaches to describe magnetoroton Hall peaks in the continuum limit. Epidemics on massive contact networks with millions of individuals pose significant challenges for analysis due to their immense scale. Furthermore, conventional epidemic models fail to account for critical nuances present in real-world outbreaks, such as age and temperature readings. To overcome these limitations, researchers have developed a new approach that involves grouping individuals into smaller, manageable clusters to study the spread of epidemics. By using basic contact networks within those clusters, the new model is able to capture the intricate dynamics of the outbreak. One such model, the SIS model, has been modified to incorporate this clustering approach, which is shown to be independent of the choice of cluster formation. When applied to simulations of a novel coronavirus outbreak, the average error of this model relative to simulations without clustering remained below 20%, despite varying cluster sizes and the number of individuals. The study demonstrates that clustering can be an effective strategy for analyzing and understanding epidemic outbreaks on extremely large scales. To further validate the approach, the researchers were able to reproduce simulation results using a reduced-order model, with an average error of approximately 0.1% when comparing simulation sizes. Through a measure called the Barber and Netto score, the reduced-order model was able to replicate key characteristics of the original simulations across various epidemic parameters. By using a clustering strategy to derive the reduced-order model, the researchers were able to obtain an error of less than 0.25% when simulation sizes differed by five-fold. Ultimately, the study highlights the potential for clustering to bridge the gap between large-scale simulations of complex systems and reduced-order models that can provide insights into the fundamental dynamics of the original system. Furthermore, the approach offers the promise of allowing researchers to derive reduced-order models of general size from simulations of arbitrary scales without being limited by computational constraints. To obtain the full benefits of the clustering strategy, the study suggests that future work could focus on optimizing parameters such as the number of clusters and the size of those clusters to facilitate reduced-order model derivation. To allow researchers to quantify the relationship between clustering and model accuracy, the study offers a new score called the clustering score. To facilitate the application of the clustering strategy, the study provides an open-source library called DeriveRO, which offers a range of implemented clustering and reduced-order model algorithms. DeriveRO also includes simulated contact network generation, as well as a range of SIS model simulation tools to enable the evaluation of various clustering and reduced-order model derivate strategies. The maximum likelihood estimator used in CMB map-making provides optimal, unbiased results as long as the underlying data model is accurate, but inaccuracies often arise due to sub-pixel structures, instrumentation flaws such as time-varying gain and pointing errors, leading to model inaccuracy in practice. When errors occur, this estimator becomes biased, causing distortions to spread across the scanning pattern through correlations in noise. A notable effect of this phenomenon is the creation of 'X' shapes surrounding strong point sources in typical scanning patterns. This paper examines why such distortion occurs and introduces both established and novel techniques for mitigating or eliminating the effects, including accompanying Python tools for TOD simulation and map-making. The investigation further reveals that the primary cause of the distortion is the unrealistic assumption that instrument glitches are randomly distributed within the scanning pattern, as analyzed mathematically in terms of signal to noise ratio, under the $1B$ signal power condition. Understanding why this distortion occurs and presenting mitigation methods reveals key lessons for CMB data analysis, primarily centered on instrument characterization and sampling patterns. The discussed methods include EAL (effective instrument calibration), DPAI (direct pixel estimation), and PAUL (using an instrument simulation to find new pixels), all of which are driven by the desire to minimize the effects of this distortion, aiming to provide near-unbiased maps with reduced 'X' shape distortion around strong sources. The experimental results indicate that EAL, requiring an extra set of rings, can restore up to 90% of unbiasedness, whereas DPAI, needing an extra set of pixels in each ring, can restore up to 99%. PAUL, an algorithm yet to be fully optimized, shows potential in further improving DPAI. The authors are not aware of any previous discussions on this distortion, these techniques or their quantified performances within the CMB community. The presented work primarily focuses on understanding a general distortion mechanism, as the treated case involves a randomly fluctuating solenoid time varying gain, as the investigated PAUL is generally applicable across instrument types. The work is set to expand into exploring the underlying statistical physics of this distortion in a future publication. The developed Python library for TOD and map-making is named 'MBTA', short for map making with bias removal and artificials. The tool includes functions to simulate TOD, estimate instrument effective pixels, find new pixels through an instrument simulation, and map-making with established and novel methods, as well as statistical analysis of the identified distortion, as shown in our accompanying paper figures 16 and 17

Interpreting teaching instructions with natural language can be compromised by the complexity of meaning, often leading to misunderstandings. Learners may misinterpret the intentions behind teacher-provided information when object characteristics are ambiguously described, a problem known as referential ambiguity. We explore how principles from cognitive sciences, such as teaching strategies (tailoring instructions) and adapting to agent preferences, can mitigate referential ambiguities through induction. Our experiments involve training two artificial agents to accomplish a simulated robotic task (block-stacking) and demonstrate that incorporating these ideas increases the learner's sample efficiency. The results suggest that natural language can be effectively taught, but doing so may necessitate complementary learning mechanisms. The project's code is available online. The Ramsey sequence serves as a prime illustration of quantum phase measurement for a spin qubit, and its efficiency in measurements can be enhanced by strategically choosing the duration of phase accumulation, $\tau$. A sequential Bayesian experimental approach is employed to determine this duration in low-accuracy Ramsey measurements, and its results are compared to a prior adaptive heuristic method and a randomly selected setup. An efficient process that enables simultaneous measurement-taking and design calculations has been developed and implemented using an FPGA platform. When the precession frequency is the primary factor influencing the results, the Bayesian method surpasses the adaptive heuristic by achieving lower standard deviations in measurement estimates compared to the random setup. Nevertheless, when the initial qubit uncertainty plays a significant role in the results, the Bayesian method and the adaptive heuristic method exhibit similar performance, and both outperform the random setup by a considerable amount. The Bayesian method achieves an estimate standard deviation that is roughly $2.6$ times lower, and the qubit fidelities associated with the Bayesian method and the adaptive heuristic method are $95.56\%$ and $95.32\%$, respectively. The presented measurement strategies can be further extended and applied to magnetic resonance, a widely used technique, as well as other spin-based quantum sensors and computing devices. Moreover, the employed Bayesian approach may have a broader range of practical uses in experimental instrumentation. The presented work aims to create general methods for enhancing the efficiency of quantum measurements by leveraging maximum likelihood estimation techniques. An estimation strategy based on MLR has been developed and tested in a recent experiment where an estimate of the position uncertainty in a micromechanical oscillator is acquired. The estimation strategy employs a minimum number of measurements as only $5\%$ of the total measurements, and the results show a standard deviation that is $3.0 \times 10^{-21} {\rm m}$. The estimation strategy has been proven to be effective in dealing with a variety of quantum sensors and can potentially be used as a general strategy for different measurement set-ups. The strategies have been designed to work on existing experimental infrastructure and the results can be readily applied in different measurement procedures. Future implementations of the strategies have been planned for optical measurements in different contexts. The optimization of the measurement process and the resulting estimation strategies have been carried out in different physical contexts including optical, mechanical, and electrical systems.

Network centrality metrics quantify node importance using various geometric and diffusive characteristics, focusing on distinct scales. From a geometric perspective, a multi-scale centrality is defined by a node's tendency to lie close to shortest paths within its surrounding area. The Gromov centrality metric gauges importance at different network scales based on the size of the neighborhood and recovers well-known metrics as limiting cases. It's demonstrated that the Gromov centrality is sensitive to geometric and boundary constraints of the network, enabling the identification of various node types within random and real-world networks. A data case study illustrates the practical value of the Gromov centrality metric in analyzing air traffic networks. Computational methods for calculating the Gromov centrality have been developed and validated at different scales. The results show that breaking the triangle inequality yields a meaningful boundary between central and peripheral nodes. Additionally, a node's influence on shortest paths is reflected in its Gromov centrality value, especially at small neighborhood scales. In contrast, the Gromov centrality asymptotically converges to degree-based metrics at large neighborhood scales. Moreover, the Gromov centrality has the potential to enhance diffusive processes by favoring nodes located near the boundary of the sampling area. As such, the Gromov centrality offers a novel multi-scale approach to node importance, complementing existing metrics, and holding promise for real-world applications. While shortest paths centrality tends to capture geometric properties, the Gromov centrality is capable of removing this restriction and converging to other metrics as limiting cases. Consequently, the Gromov centrality provides significant geometric and boundary flexibility. It's worth noting that current computational methods exhibit a time complexity of O(|E| α + |E| β ) where α and β are exponents depending on the neighborhood size and Gromov centrality values, respectively. They also demonstrate an overall improvement of at least a factor of 10 compared to existing shortest paths centrality metrics. To further increase computational efficiency, the development of more efficient algorithms, at least for large-scale networks, would be beneficial. Lastly, while the proposed approach shows promise for real-world applications, the characterization of node importance in air traffic networks requires the integration of other diffusion-based methods for a more comprehensive understanding. The source code for calculating the Gromov centrality is available at the following GitHub repository https://github.com/jmvega1/GromovCentrality for reproducibility purposes. From a purely non-relativistic perspective, we derive the Poisson equation solution for empty space in a scenario with a rotating gravitational system, analogous to the Sun, and consider the implications of this solution for the behavior of test objects within its gravitational field. The general solution to the Poisson equation, expressed in terms of the distance r and angle θ, is shown to exhibit properties consistent with Newton's inverse square law of gravitation to the lowest order approximation. This analysis yields two significant outcomes: firstly, the observed linear increase in the Earth's orbit, and secondly, the reduction in the test object's velocity, both of which are in accordance with Newton's laws of physics. Additionally, we provide a theoretical explanation for the fluctuations in the Earth's orbit, attribute mass loss in the Earth-Moon system to the thermal energy released during the spinning process, and propose a mechanism for the observed increase in the Earth's rotational inertia. Furthermore, we make a predictive claim regarding a minimal velocity correction of approximately 0.0304 times c for test objects within the Sun's gravitational field. Finally, we draw a connection between the conceptual framework of this work and the theoretical framework of General Relativity, highlighting their distinct theoretical underpinnings. The equation derived for the velocity correction is formulated as Δv = (2.0346 ± 0.0074) (G M_solar / (r_c))^2 (T_solar / (2 π))^2, where the given values are for the Earth and the Sun, and the error margin is significantly lower than one percent. This analysis highlights that the velocity correction can be significant even at low velocities, providing a new understanding of the phenomenon and suggesting the applicability of this work to a broader range of celestial systems, including binary star systems. Ultimately, the core idea of this work is a simple yet fundamental concept, rooted in the basic principles of physics, yet provides a unique and innovative perspective on the study of planetary motion, and may serve as a primer or introductory suite for students and colleagues new to the field of theoretical physics. The numerical values and parameters derived in this work are compared to those available in the public domain, and any discrepancies are attributed to existing data limitations. A final review is provided on the one-to-one correlation between the derived time parameters (T_solar, T_earth) and the established specific gravitational time parameters (tau_solar, tau_earth) available in the public domain. Sets of matrix pencils sharing the same Kronecker canonical form are classified under strict equivalence into infinite groups called bundles. Introduced in the 1990s, this concept is an extension of the earlier idea by Arnold in 1971, relating to matrices under similarity transformations. Despite substantial research on the topology of bundles of matrices, real matrices, and linear polynomials, there is limited understanding of bundles of matrix pencils. Our research contributes to a comprehensive classification of bundles of matrix pencils of real rank, and we outline the challenges posed by those of rank zero. We demonstrate that particular cases of such bundles, encompassing rank-one matrix pencils and matrices, as well as pencils of quadratic polynomials, are comprised of isolated, distinct points. In contrast, we reveal that every non-zero finite bundle of rank k matrix pencils can be transformed from a particular infinite group known as the 'trunk', through a series of singular transformations, and that this 'bundling process' can be applied even to random matrix pencils, including those of real rank. These findings are displayed in a graphical analysis for up to rank-3 matrix pencils, showing how each bundle is connected to the 'trunk'. Lastly, we outline possible future research directions. These include investigating the properties of bundles of matrix polynomials of higher degrees and expanding our understanding of bundles of matrices. The implementation of the presented ideas is illustrated in a newly developed Python program. This computational tool is expressed in terms of the Syrma library, an open-source MATLAB and Python framework for the study of matrix pencils. The abstracted code is accessible through syrma.github.io or https://github.com/syrma.assistant/research/tree/main/matroid-bundles. Specifically, the program enables the computation of bundles using the Syrma function 'pencil-bundle'. In conclusion, the contribution of this work is a deeper understanding of the infinite groups of matrix pencils, as well as computationally practical tools and programs that can be utilized for a general classification of bundles of matrix polynomials. The findings and computational developments presented are aimed at promoting further research in this field. The programs developed are intended to be practical and easily expandable to related problems, and the goals outlined are intended to be finite and achievable within a reasonable timeframe. The classification of bundles of matrix polynomials is a complex problem that has been ongoing for decades, and the research presented hopes to make a meaningful contribution toward its eventual resolution. The $C^*$-algebra formalism of topological T-duality developed by Mathai and Rosenberg is applied to a broad class of topological spaces encompassing torus bundles, nilmanifolds, and other examples from string theory. By constructing T-duals from commutative $C^*$-algebras with ${\mathbb R}^n$ action, we establish a general framework that produces almost abelian solvmanifolds as key components for the algebraic description of T-duals. The method involves a new T-duality construction that starts with an abelian principal bundle and uses its $C^*$-algebra cross-section to find the dual algebra through a $C^*$-algebraic twisted Bott projection. We demonstrate the utility of our approach with non-trivial examples of metrized torus bundles that can't be captured by the current Limit, and show that certain non-solvmanifold T-duals have extra structure as unitary duals. By analyzing the duals of the standard real line, of the 3-torus, of the Rayleigh surface, of the Bieberbach group, and of the Fubini-Study manifolds, we test the theoretical description and evaluate its accuracy against existing knowledge. A comprehensive survey of the algebraic description of classical T-duals based on $C^*$-algebras concludes the paper. Given that many known T-duals are solvable and can be described as $C^*$-algebras with group action or, more generally, as Morita equivalence classes of $C^*$-algebras with group action, we argue that our general framework is indeed comprehensive. The construction of the dual algebra as a subalgebra of a twisted Bott bundle $C^*$-algebra also arises naturally in the context of non-commutative T-duality within the current Limit, as observed in an example related to non-symmetric unimodular quasitopological groupoids. A final note alludes to non-commutative T-duality consequences that might be drawn from the $C^*$-algebra description proposed here. By generalizing the non-commutative T-duality conjecture of Mathai and Rosenberg to the realm of impure groupoids, we derive a description of the dual impure $C^*$-algebra and its action by ${\mathbb R}^n$. For C1-smooth discrete-time systems exhibiting strong monotonicity, the prevailing long-term behavior of linearly stable cycles is established in a probabilistic framework. This research then extends to periodic parabolic equations and reveals new findings regarding the ubiquity of periodic solutions and asymptotic stability at the periodic regime. The presented examples offer a model for population dynamics where periodic factors are predominant over random elements. The study ultimately shows that under certain conditions, the asymptotic behavior of these systems is marked by uniform persistence. The accompanying companion paper will delve into hyperbolic systems and examine the emergence of periodic behavior facilitated by random forces. Furthermore, that paper will investigate the prevalence of rare or delayed dynamics in models of population size, focusing particularly on models involving periodic coefficients and those defined on narrow strips of the phase space. In contrast, this investigation will primarily address linearly stable systems, identifying scenarios where rare or delayed dynamics are improbable yet may manifest substantial positive effects during rare or extended periods. The closing section of that paper will be devoted to problems and challenges that the author is endeavouring to resolve. These challenges include obtaining sufficient conditions for rare or delayed dynamics, developing methods to approximate the measures centred around periodic and virtually periodic trajectories, and establishing the ubiquity of virtually periodic discrete-time systems possessing smooth coefficients. In the process of this research, the author draws upon advanced mathematical concepts and techniques from the fields of smooth ergodic theory, bifurcation theory, and hyperbolic dynamics, as well as probabilistic methods involving the existence of SRB measures and the construction of conditional entropy functions. The companion paper will expand on these mathematical tools, as well as present additional research undertaken in [4], [17] and [27]. The current work, on the other hand, presents primary findings, as opposed to the companion paper which presents secondary findings. The research reported in this preprint is based on a presentation given by the author at the workshop on differential equations and dynamical systems, held at the ECM in July 2006. The corresponding companion paper is currently under review and is also available at http://mat.ufrgs.br/jpereira/. The potential of using noisy intermediate-scale quantum computers with the variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) lies in molecular simulations, where accurately constructing an ansatz using a shallow quantum circuit is key to successful implementation. Instead of employing fermionic-excitation evolutions to create ans\"atze, our approach utilizes qubit-excitation evolutions, which adhere to qubit symmetries, resulting in more robust and noisy-resistant constructions. This qubit-excitation approach is demonstrated in two chemical reaction studies: the hydrogen molecular bond breaking and the dihydrogen molecule's dissociation. Our results show improved qubit excitation accuracy in the VQE ansatz, which translates to reduced computational costs and diminished sensitivity to noise in chemical reaction predictions. A key characteristic of deep generative models is the interaction of representation, its distribution, and a neural network mapping, with techniques like variational autoencoders (VAEs) often applied, but posing significant optimization challenges. Specifically, the inclusion of an encoder introduces complexity and potentially poor performance. The proposed deep generative decoder (DGD) offers an alternative, grounded in a theory specifying the distribution of the hidden state, thus removing the need for an encoder. Using laplacian distribution losses, the DGD is shown to achieve better results than VAEs on both optimized and non-optimized bases in various experiments. Although simplified, the approach presented opens up new avenues for research in a simplified model, while highlighting potential improvements for more complex generative models. The source code is available at https://github.com/galgebra/galra/tree/dgds. Furthermore, the potential of the DGD as a generative model for graphics simulations is explored using the Cesium engine at https://cesium.galra.io/dgds. The discovery of a common-spectrum process in recent NANOGrav findings has led to the hypothesis that a primordial stochastic gravitational-wave background could be evident in 2020 datasets from several other telescopes. If the gravitational-wave frequency were increasing, it would mean the universe has been expanding slower in the past, matching a trend seen in recent observations of cosmic microwave background fluctuations and redshift-dependent velocity. We found the NANOGrav result supports a slower universe in its early stages, but the interpretation is uncertain due to possible anisotropy in the background and non-Gravitational-Cosmology signals in the NANOGrav dataset. Additionally, we discuss how current models fail to fully match the observed universe speed in the early stages and the primordial background amplitude. The models we looked at couldn't account for slower universe speeds early on, unless there's a significant difference between the gravitational-wave frequency at 200 MHz and 290 MHz, or if gravitational waves aren't the only factor influencing these observations. Given these uncertainties, we conclude that a larger dataset from multiple sources is needed to confirm the presence of a primordial stochastic gravitational-wave background. Such a dataset could provide crucial evidence both for a slower universe in its early stages and for how the universe speed changes over time. We found the gravitational-wave frequency at 200 MHz would need to be lower than 1.97*10^-6 Hz for it to not have been the main factor influencing the observed universe speed changes. We found the gravitational-wave frequency at 290 Mpc would need to be higher than 4.78*10^-6 Hz, under the same conditions. We found the universe speed changes both for a slower universe in its early stages and for how the universe speed changes over time could be explained if the gravitational-wave spectrum contains a peak around 200 MHz, although this would need to be lower than 4.1*10^-4 Hz to not make daily time measurements from radio telescopes unstable. We found several other factors that could be behind the observed universe speed changes both for a slower universe in its early stages and for how the universe speed changes over time. Our study presents the first survey of molecular emissions from a comet's volatile substances. We utilized spectroscopic techniques to analyze the composition of comet C/2015 ER61 (51P) by observing its direct image and spectra during a brief apparition in March-April 2016. The comet's volatile substances water, carbon monoxide, and carbon dioxide were detected in its bright coma. Notably, we identified, for the first time in a comet of this type, the emission lines of ethane, ethylene, and ethylene oxide, which are essential in understanding the interstellar delivery of organic compounds to Earth. The ethane and ethylene emission ratios were found to be greater than those observed in the outer solar system comets, providing insight into their formation and evolution processes. The discovery of high levels of hydrogen chloride and the low ratio of hydrogen cyanide to water in C/2015 ER61 add more information to these findings, contributing to a new knowledge base for the comet ensemble. Moreover, a fully detailed dataset, including the raw information and its analysis, is accessible at https://www2.valil.org/datasets/di-54/. We propose an unsupervised speech synthesis approach that builds on recent research in automatic speech recognition and existing neural-based speech generation methods. Employing only raw, unlabeled audio and text data, as well as a dictionary, our technique enables high-quality speech synthesis without requiring a prelabeled dataset. Human evaluation confirms the synthesized speech produced by the unsupervised system is comparable to that of a traditionally trained model in terms of its naturalness and ease of understanding. Moreover, the unsupervised model we developed achieved a reasonable average opinion score and only required several hours of computation to train, despite being built with only 200 hours of speech data. The unsupervised model we developed achieved an average opinion score of 70.65% with respect to its similarity to human speech. Conversely, the supervised AlexTS model we developed achieved an average opinion score of 67.38% when evaluating its ability to accurately convey text information. The unsupervised model we developed achieved an average opinion score of 62.46% when evaluating its ability to easily understand the speech it generates. In addition to these findings, we also developed and evaluated a range of existing neural-based speech generation methods and a traditional statistical approach to automatic speech recognition. The results of our evaluation suggest that the unsupervised system we developed outperformed all of these alternative methods in terms of its ability to easily understand the speech it generates. The unsupervised model we developed achieved an average improvement in its WER score of 43.5% when compared to the range of alternative methods we evaluated. While our approach has many advantages, it is clear that the unsupervised system we developed still falls short of the high-quality speech synthesis achieved by traditionally trained models. When creating a perfect fluid model, using the Friedman equations for this added component results in two possible outcomes, contingent on whether the energy density's fractional value exceeds one or not. If the value exceeds one, the description does not represent a real universe. When the added component's twin is paired with a positive mass energy term, the added component's behavior mimics dark energy's behavior and a cosmologically significant "acceleration period" can be observed. However, in the event of both components having negative mass energies, the behavior can be characterized as a "dark matter-like" scenario with two consecutive acceleration periods. On the other hand, when both components have positive mass energies, the behavior can be seen as a "single" acceleration period. When the added component's twin is not included in the general energy-momentum tensor, the equivalent energy density value can be attained using a negative constant, referred to as the "cosmological constant equivalent". Multi-objective mixed-integer non-linear programming problems frequently arise in real-world contexts, notably in mechanical engineering. A novel approach, combining multi-criteria branch-and-bound and non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm 2, is proposed for approximating Pareto fronts for such problems. A computational study, comparing this proposed hybrid method to non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm 2, demonstrates its efficacy with real-world and test cases. A new performance metric, investment ratio, assesses solution quality in relation to computation effort. Results from evaluating this proposed algorithm on five mechanical engineering and two test problems indicate its competitiveness for solving MO-MINLPs. A publicly accessible implementation, MO-MINLP-bnB, is made available with additional details on parameters, a manual, and the code itself. This open-source package facilitates comparisons with other algorithms and allows for independent assessment of its claimed advantages. We refine and reinterpret the core principles of Lie theory, specifically Lie groupoids, through the lens of internal groupoids in synthetic differential geometry. Key concepts are re-expressed, including path sources and integrated $A$-paths. The primary findings demonstrate that a classical Hausdorff Lie groupoid's internal connectivity properties mirror those it satisfies as a classical connected Lie groupoid. This has the significant consequence that a Lie groupoid's internal connectedness properties are essentially equivalent to those of its classical connectivity variants. Furthermore, a specific condition, integral path connectivity, is defined, and surprisingly, we find it to be consistent with classical connectivity. The methods employed incorporate Taylor reifications, a form of infinitesimal approximation commonly used in SDGE. The work culminates by using these findings to establish a connection between Lie groupoids and their Lie algebroid counterparts through the concept of path sources. This path source correspondence has the additional benefit of providing a new understanding of integrated $A$-paths, which in turn reveals a path-based equivalence between Lie algebroids and their corresponding integrated Lie algebroids. The key concepts and methods presented in this work have the potential to facilitate the development of a path-based Lie theory, a topic explored in separate articles. The new understanding presented even enables a proof of the integrability principle that does not rely on the use of jets, which are conventional in this context. The approach taken showcases the utility of internal and integrated frameworks in synthetic differential geometry to create new mathematics for the study of Lie theory. The work includes a supplementary appendix explaining its use of composite and Taylor-extended concepts. The methods employed in this work rely on composite and extended notions commonly used in differential geometry, such as composite maps and Taylor expansions. The Dynaswap project is focused on developing a robust, trustworthy architecture for safeguarding holistic workflows in cyberinfrastructures, allowing for deployment on virtual machines via cloud services such as JetStream. This cloud platform facilitates user-friendly access to dynamic computing and data analysis tools on demand. Dynaswap's security architecture incorporates role management, hierarchical relationships, and adaptable access control mechanisms. By integrating cutting-edge frameworks like Authentication-Authorization-Accounting and Blockchain technology, Dynaswap aims to balance advanced security features with user-friendly implementation. This paper outlines the core security design of Dynaswap's role-based access control system and presents preliminary findings from a pilot study on its usability. Analysis of the research reveals that Dynaswap's security architecture has inherent properties aligning with the requirements for secure processes, thereby validating the design's adherence to safe computing principles. Furthermore, our user-centered design approach ensured that Dynaswap's implementation of complex security functionalities does not compromise user privacy. We also examined common security threats against Dynaswap's access control and data protection, system operation, and user experience, and verified that the solution can effectively mitigate these security threats. Lastly, our paper outlines potential areas for expanding Dynaswap's security functionalities within the context of cyberinfrastructures. Aspect-based sentiment analysis focuses on determining the sentiment of a particular aspect within product reviews. Approximately one-third of reviews lack explicit opinion words, requiring a different approach for accurate sentiment identification. We refer to this nuanced sentiment as implicit sentiment. This paper outlines a novel method for identifying implicit sentiment regarding a specific aspect, using explicit sentiment cues as a reference point. Specifically, we utilize oriented word pairs, formed by removing stop words, to represent explicit sentiment, and an oriented word pair-based kernel, to represent implicit sentiment. We also introduce a new model based on the oriented word pair kernel, called OriKernel, for aspect-based sentiment analysis. Conventional feature engineering methods, involving negative sampling and oriented word pair orientation adjustment, are employed to support OriKernel. When tested on four datasets, OriKernel demonstrated superior performance compared to the state-of-the-art THUAS-KDE model. The results showed that OriKernel achieved accuracy rates of 92.59\% ($micro$), 89.59\% ($macro$) for the STC dataset; 93.28\% ($micro$), 90.35\% ($macro$) for the ATC dataset; 88.60\% ($micro$), 85..69\% ($macro$) for the Newsgroup dataset; and 79.06\% ($micro$), 77.66\% ($macro$) for the Amazon dataset. Notably, our research introduces the concept of oriented word pairs for aspect-based sentiment analysis. The proposed method has the advantage of being unsupervised, allowing it to be used for domain-specific tasks where labeled data is scarce. The oriented word pair kernel also serves as a means to interpret neural network models. Importantly, our experiments reveal that OriKernel surpasses the state-of-the-art THUAS-KDE model, even when used in conjunction with oriented word pair kernels, in both aspect sentiment and classification tasks. The source code for the OriKernel model is publicly available at \url{https://github.com/Color6/SentimentAnalysisUsingOrientedWordPairs}. All experimental datasets can be accessed at \url{https://github.com/Color6/SentimentAnalysisUsingOrientedWordPairs/tree/main/experiments/datasets}. This is particularly significant when conducting mediation analysis with binary outcome and mediator variables in stratified case-control studies. In such scenarios, using the stratified design enables researchers to obtain estimators for the outcome model, which can be employed in conjunction with a weighted estimation technique to obtain an unbiased estimation of the causal effect through the mediator. Our results derive summation formulas for estimating main parameters, including a parameter that measures the extent to which the mediator causes the outcome. These formulas consider how the stratified design influences the estimation of parameters needed to perform a logistic regression on the secondary outcome. Using real data and simulations, we compare the performance of our estimators with that of a stratified cohort study. Additionally, we apply the developed methods to two medical studies to investigate new questions. One study examines whether a mediator contributes to a secondary outcome in a causal pathway, while the other investigates whether the presence of a mediator enhances the effect of a secondary outcome associated with a primary exposure. Both studies utilize data on whether acute infections (AI) increase the occurrence of a secondary outcome, autoimmune disorders (AID). To address detection bias, we extend our results to a scenario where the detection of the mediator depends on the secondary outcome, which requires an estimator for a logistic regression parameter that takes into account correlation between detection probabilities across strata, based on a summation formula. Using a logistic-normal mixture model, we create a weighted estimation method for a parameter that measures the extent to which the mediator causes the outcome, which is sensitive to the stratified design and detection bias. This conceptualisation is grounded in the current advancements in both cognitive science and the field of few-shot learning. Based on this understanding of cognition, we develop a basic model to facilitate learning through experiences and provide evidence within a simple simulated environment that demonstrates its efficacy. The self-reference framework also enables us to identify factors influencing the ability to learn through experiences and to develop methods for quantifying cognitive abilities and capabilities. Furthermore, we discuss how this framework contributes to the evolution of intelligent systems and address the challenge of measuring unsupervised cognition. The findings of this study are supported by a comprehensive background analysis. Ultimately, we anticipate that our research will play a part in addressing the control problem in artificial intelligence. The majority of this work is implemented as a multi-agent simulation using the Swift Robotics Institute's Birob platform with robotic experiments. The research code is accessible through GitHub, both the theoretical model and the research one. The demographic considerations for the development of intelligent systems and robots have also been taken into account in this study. The research presented here seeks to answer questions such as: Can a cognitive biologically-inspired decision-making system be achieved through experiences and adaptive processes? What is the role of executive function in such a system? How can cognitive functions and abilities be measured and quantified? What is the role of emotions and entropy in the learning and decision-making process? How can control problems in intelligent systems effectively managed using cognitive design principles? The study presents findings in the field of multi-modal, visual, and general cognitive learning capabilities. The research also seeks to answer questions such as: Can a cognitive biologically-inspired decision-making system integrated with a perception system operating in real-time? What is the role of emotions and outliers in the learning and decision-making process? The research aims to derive design principles for the development of intelligent systems and it is expected that the proposed model will contribute to the current debates in the field. A new method inspired by finite volume schemes leverages a cell-average based neural network to solve partial differential equations. By utilizing the weak formulation of these equations, the method trains a feed-forward network to accurately predict solution evolution between time steps, circumventing traditional numerical limitations. After offline training, the neural network model can be used in conjunction with a finite volume scheme, which requires mesh adaptation. One distinct advantage of this approach is its ability to eliminate CFL restrictions, permitting a wider range of time step sizes. Furthermore, when solving the Heat equation, convergence rates and error magnitudes show dependence on the spatial mesh size while being independent of the time step size. Moreover, the neural network model exhibits exceptional performance in simulating shock waves and rarefaction waves within nonlinear hyperbolic conservation laws with negligible numerical diffusion. Successful applications are also demonstrated for the Kelvin-Helmholtz instability and the Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation, yielding highly accurate results. Extensive numerical testing confirms that the neural network model accurately predicts solution values. Detailed analysis of the neural network's optimization process reveals that the majority of error comes from two sources: numerical gradient estimation and neural network out-of-domain generalization. Consequently, an adaptive learning rate strategy is employed to mitigate these issues. Furthermore, a numerical gradient estimator based on the central difference method contributes significantly to reducing error. Overall, the results demonstrate the neural network model's ability to significantly accelerate traditional finite volume scheme solutions for partial differential equations. Moreover, one interesting observation is the neural network's tendency to learn and replicate finite volume scheme properties even when starting from random weights. Consequently, this approach has the potential to accelerate a wide range of existing numerical methods for partial differential equations. By utilizing a similar framework, it is also demonstrated that the neural network model can be utilized to solve eigenvalue problems more efficiently. In particular, the neural network model developed for the Heat kernel reveals a remarkable ability to accurately predict solution values at time t for any initial condition at virtually machine zero error while being independent of the time step size. One notable advantage of this approach is its ability to eliminate the CFL restriction, which was previously a limitation of finite difference methods for solving eigenvalue problems for partial differential equations. Furthermore, the neural network model developed for the eigenvalues of the Helmholtz equation shows accuracy and robustness in the presence of numerical instability and out-of-domain generalization. Utilizing an adaptive learning rate strategy and a numerical gradient estimator based on the central finite difference method contributes significantly to reducing error. The ALICE Collaboration has finalized the upgrade of its detector, with the current phase involving testing to mark the beginning of data collection for LHC Run 3. In conjunction, preparations are underway for ALICE's upcoming run, characterized by the doubling of luminosity and the enhancement of specific measurements. In ALICE's electromagnetic calorimeter, researchers are developing a novel fast read-out based on digital silicon-on-insulator technology to achieve improved time resolution. This new detector will facilitate precise identification of the collision time using the cluster-like hit patterns resulting from electromagnetic energy deposition. Moreover, the adoption of look-up tables to transform analog signals into digital hit information will enable the use of active areas above the beam pipe, thereby reducing data volume and allowing for the use of active areas above the beam pipe. In this paper, the technology and performance of the newly developed read-out is presented, focusing on the time resolution performance obtained with a single module and a full slice of the detector, comprising nine modules. It is demonstrated that the overall time precision is sufficient to allow for the use of the collision time information in ALICE's experiment. In addition to improving the accuracy of specific measurements, the use of the new read-out will also accelerate the data processing, thus increasing the detector's ability to capture events, especially during LHC Run 4. In that stage, researchers will be able to make detailed measurements, such as those on heavy flavors and dielectrons with low masses, utilizing a processed event rate of approximately 10 MHz. This new technology will also facilitate the improvement of ALICE's capabilities in detecting electrons with low transverse momenta, thereby making the experiment more efficient in terms of data processing. In the past, researchers were constrained by the detector's read-out frequency, recording only about 30 events per second, regardless of the event rate. With the newly implemented technology, this value can be increased to 100 events per second. In summary, the adoption of look-up tables in the read-out circuit will facilitate the improvement of specific measurements, increased efficiency in data processing, and the use of active areas above the beam pipe, benefiting both current and future runs of the experiment. In conclusion, the presented phase marks an essential milestone in the evolution of the experiment, dedicated to the study of the collision time using the cluster-like hit patterns resulting from electromagnetic energy deposition in ALICE's electromagnetic calorimeter. In the past, this feature was not utilized due to the detector's read-out frequency, recording only about 30 events per second, regardless of the event rate.

We examine a complex manifold with a Hermitian holomorphic vector bundle and its flag bundles, coupled with their respective universal bundles, now endowed with the induced metrics. A crucial aspect of our research involves establishing the validity, pointwise in Chern forms, of the universal push-forward formula for all universal bundles. A fundamental step toward our proof is explicitly determining, at each point of the flag bundle, the Chern curvature of the universal bundles, as endowed with their induced metrics. This leads to the development of an alternative approach to the Jacobi-Trudi identity using differential forms, as well as confirmation of the positivity of specific Chern forms for Griffiths semipositive vector bundles, thus partially supporting Griffiths' conjecture on characteristic forms of positive characteristic. This research presents an independent assessment, as it addresses and resolves issues arising from his first and second characteristic variants. Moreover, it refines and generalizes other conjectures and theorems related to the positivity of characteristic forms for vector bundles, as posed by El Kacemi-Laquerre and by Ottem. As concrete illustrations of our results, we present three applications encompassing well-known scenarios: when the vector bundle possesses a Hermitian metric with (plain) K\"ahler properties, positivity of the Chern curvature, or semi-positive Griffiths properties. Additionally, we outline an extension of the theory to characteristic $p>0$ in specific contexts, as illustrated by the works of T. Friedman and of El Kacemi-Laquerre. Lastly, we include an assessment of El Kacemi-Laquerre's and Ottem's conjectures in the light of our findings. As key elements of our analysis, we develop an original global identity for the Chern forms of the universal bundles, as well as establish their positivity properties. Importantly, our research demonstrates that these results can be translated to yield new proofs, as well as enhancements of existing theorems and conjectures, as exemplified by the extensions of Griffiths' conjecture, of Eisenbud and Griffths' conjecture, of Peternell van de Ven's conjecture, of El Kacemi-Laquerre's conjecture, of Friedman's conjecture, of Ottem's conjecture, of Schreier's conjecture, of Tomanek's conjecture, of Tu's conjecture, of Vesovski's conjecture, of Wu-Yau's conjecture, of Yeung's conjecture, of Yeung-Wu's conjecture, of Yeung-Tomanek's conjecture

Observations from the XMM-Newton telescope revealed how a clumpy stellar wind from a companion star in high mass X-ray binaries impacts the variable absorption and timing properties of the emitted X-rays. We analyzed a 7.22 day dataset from the Cyg X-1 Hard state Observations campaign and discovered notable changes in the source's X-ray properties in the presence of the wind. The wind's effects on variability decreased as wind density increased, while its hardness-ratio increased significantly during this period. Furthermore, the wind led to the development of quasi-periodic oscillations and spectral changes, which are not explained by established accretion flow models. The detected wind's complex behavior is consistent with previous models of wind evolution in high mass X-ray binaries. The observed phenomena can be attributed to the interaction between the accretion flow and wind, which forms distinct hot bubbles and shells that affect the timing and spectral properties of observed X-rays. The predicted implications of these interactions are substantial and point to the need for further models that incorporate feedback in the context of wind-accreting high mass X-ray binaries. We step away from prior strategies of integrating syntax and semantics parsing independently within a shared model and instead explore a new approach: a unified, two-part model that simultaneously guides syntax and semantics parsing with minimal adjustments. Our results from testing this model on the BEIR benchmark indicate that joint modeling leads to superior performance and increased efficiency. We also demonstrate the effectiveness of using contextualized representations to boost the precision of semantic parsing on the WSj datasets. Ultimately, our study delivers conclusive evidence that modeling syntax and semantics parsing together yields substantial benefits. To investigate this process, we run a two-way coupling simulation linking a general relativity-based simulation of a black hole and its surroundings to an MHD simulation of the ejected material. This coupled simulation reveals that mass ejection is influenced more greatly by the opacity of the outflow than by the properties of the central disk, allowing for a general explanation of the characteristic EM behavior of short gamma-ray bursts and possible kilonova events. Specifically, we find that mass ejection is enhanced when jets interact with the surrounding disk, forming a cocoon that breaks the outflow's momentum structure and makes it susceptible to further absorption. Additionally, we find that spin-dependent features in EM light can serve as reliable indicators of the properties of the central object. While a high-black hole spin results in more pronounced emission, a critical threshold exists beyond which emission increases significantly when the black hole spin increases. This complex relationship indicates that future observations at late times for both gamma-ray bursts and kilonovae events, as well as at early times for kilonovae events, would provide greater insight into the properties of the central object. Finally, we verify the previous claims of magnetically-driven jets being responsible for short gamma-ray bursts and possible supernovae through simulations involving a massive companion and a high-black hole spin. Observations indicated an accelerated rate of tidal features disappearance as their mass decreased in pairs. According to the results of N-body simulations, the tidal features features exhibited a substantial depth in their profile, a characteristic associated with features originating from dark matter halos.
