The Delegated RingCT scheme is comprised of an integrated signature and encryption framework, combining a public key encryption protocol and a signature switch algorithm with a message splitter. The Deleged RingCT protocol allows for the creation of stealth addresses that can receive and generate encrypted tokens, which are then publicly verifiable through a novel signature and message splitting technique. In addition to enabling token transmission while preserving sender and recipient anonymity, Delegated RingCT also facilitates fast and free transactions for high-value values and offers an unprecedented level of flexibility, modularity and efficiency. The protocol can be paired with any DPoS-based cryptocurrency with RingCT implementation, such as Nano, Puma, and Qora. We conducted comprehensive testing of Delegated RingCT and developed a modular, open-source implementation, making it available on GitHub for community evaluation and potential integration within compatible cryptocurrencies. Thorough analysis of Delegated RingCT was performed from both theoretical and practical perspectives, resulting in the conclusion that its anonymity level can be quantitatively compared to other RingCT variants. The execution of Delegated RingCT on Nano, Puma and Qora cryptocurrencies is technically feasible, considering these cryptocurrencies already employ RingCT and Delegated RingCT. We further propose a custom Electron wallet application for simultaneous management of multiple cryptocurrencies with RingCT integration, which supports anonymous payment execution among the vast majority of its peers, while providing proof of token transfer to the designated recipient. The Electron wallet generates temporary stealth addresses for each transaction and displays the corresponding public key used for encryption, thus enabling third-party verification of the transaction. The protocol and implementation are compatible with the vast majority of RingCT-supported cryptocurrencies. This paper presents a novel optimization technique called AskewSGD to efficiently train deep neural networks with quantized weights. Initially, we transform the quantized neural network training into a sequence of constrained optimization problems that can be iteratively refined. Our method, AskewSGD, is an efficient first-order stochastic approach designed to solve each optimization subproblem. Unlike conventional algorithms, AskewSGD circumvents computationally intensive projections or full feasibility checks, enabling it to take larger steps and reach its limits more efficiently. We also introduce a feasibility-encouraging regularizer under the constraint of quantization to reduce the projected burden. AskewSGD's effectiveness in training deep models with significant quantization is demonstrated on widely used benchmarks, resulting in notable gains over the state-of-the-art method on ResNet50 and Vision Transformer large. Our source code will be made available for future reference. AskewSGD is an online method, making it well-suited for training deep neural networks on large datasets in an online setting. Our experiments show that it ranks second in terms of accuracy among zero-order optimization methods for the CIFAR100 dataset with a budget of $10^5$ steps or iterations. When the budget is increased to $10^6$, AskewSGD outperforms all other methods, including first-order approaches. Our analysis of AskewSGDG, the generalized version of AskewSGD, is presented in the supplementary material. Our experiments also reveal that conventional optimization algorithms can achieve good results on quantized neural networks, especially those with slower convergence rates, by combining them with robust gradient repair mechanisms for up to $10^5$ steps or iterations. However, our AskewSGD method is recommended for scenarios requiring faster convergence, while conventional optimization algorithms may suit applications with larger budgets and more forgiving resource requirements. Our AskewSGD implementation is currently limited to stochastic gradient descent, but it can be extended to other optimization algorithms in the future. Verifying facts using structured data can be difficult, necessitating a model's
understanding of both language and symbolic computations involving data in
tables. Despite pre-trained language models excelling in confirming simple
assertions, they often falter when handling complex assertions requiring
multiple calculations. In our research, we alleviate this challenge by breaking
down intricate assertions into manageable sub-problems. By employing the
synthesized programs from a weakly-supervised parser, we suggest an innovative
method for generating a simulated dataset that assists in the training of our
decomposition-based fact verification model. Our proposed method relies on the
resolution of these simplified problems along with their anticipated outcomes,
enabling our model to rely on stronger evidence in the verification process.
Experimental outcomes demonstrate that our proposed method attains an
unprecedented accuracy rate of 82.7% on the TabFact benchmark. Our
established benchmark marks a significant improvement in fact verification using
structured data, reaching an unprecedented accuracy of 82.9%. We have
facilitated easy access to our proposed method and the associated benchmark at
https://github.com/AutomaticErrorCorrect/fact-verification-with-table-data.

Initial breakthroughs in the field relied on unsupervised approaches, however, current advancements are primarily based on labelled data, leading to increased control, flexibility, and stability in the generated images. The findings from our experiments demonstrate the benefits of a cyclical approach to image reconstruction in the generation of real-looking images, as well as the effectiveness of pre-training a GAN on unsupervised noise. The results from our analysis highlight several avenues for further optimisation of GANs and suggest that a range of objective functions may be necessary to achieve a comprehensive understanding of the technology. To perform Bayesian inference using nested sampling, a prior sampling method must be employed to generate populations for the nested sampling algorithm. A survey of nested sampling software and its limitations, particularly concerning multi-core computing and high-dimensional problems, is provided. Methods for addressing these limitations, specifically using differential evolution algorithms, are presented. It is demonstrated that these methods can effectively address the limitations, enabling fast and efficient Bayesian inference on large-scale multi-core computing systems. The efficacy of these methods is verified through nested sampling evaluations on various software platforms and multi-core systems, specifically by comparing the efficiency of nested sampling on a 32-core system when using standard and improved sampling algorithms. Additionally, the improved sampling algorithms are demonstrated to be robust in solving multi-dimensional problems, as exemplified by a 1000-dimensional Bayesian inference case study using a gamma distribution as the prior distribution. The results of this case study demonstrate the superiority of the improved sampling algorithms in terms of computational efficiency and runtime performance. The improved sampling algorithms can be applied in a variety of scenarios, such as multi-core systems with 50 or 60 processors, to perform Bayesian inference on high-dimensional problems. In contrast, a system that is both driven and in contact with a heat bath will instead converge towards a distinct, out-of-balance stable condition. Our study shows that this ordinary behavior can turn extraordinary when the system in question is comprised of a few closely-related energy levels acting as a complex, multi-dimensional entity known as a topological bubble. When such a system interacts with a heat bath at an arbitrary temperature, it may transition into a unique state characterized by distinct, localized areas within the system's energy spectrum. This phenomenon is marked by a significant reduction in the system's entropy. Using a detailed mathematical model based on classical mechanics, we have investigated the boundaries under which these topological bubbles can emerge and persist when coupled with a heat bath at various temperatures. Our findings suggest that topological bubbles can arise even in a heat bath, leading to a stable, out-of-balance state at any non-zero temperature and even in a system with a small energy difference between its individual components. Importantly, topological bubbles can remain intact when interacting with a heat bath, thanks to a distinct, isolated characteristic. Metric learning's pair-wise loss technique is centered around optimizing an embedding that maximizes similarity between images within the same class, minimizing distance between images in distinct classes. Various forms of pair-wise loss strategies have been proposed. To consolidate this diverse set of loss functions, we've isolated specific aspects that dictate how these functions manipulate the positioning of feature pairs. Breaking down pair-wise gradient gradients provides a new perspective on comparing different loss functions, offering insights into their behavior during training. Ultimately, this insight enables the creation of a comprehensive, tailored loss function tailored to the specific requirements of an application, in this case, large-scale image retrieval using crops and quad-views. By analyzing how our new loss function performs relative to existing methods across different image types, we've demonstrated its efficacy in producing high performance results. The code and datasets to reproduce these results are publicly available. Additionally, we're releasing MFLL - a Python library containing a diverse range of metric learning loss functions - to facilitate comparison and the development of new loss function designs. By providing a fundamental understanding of how individual loss functions influence the final performance of a metric learning model, we're poised to address and explore additional challenges and opportunities in this domain. This approach allows us to analyze quantum error correction through noise, a method previously unexplored in the field. It's been demonstrated that various quantum codes, such as topological codes, can be accurately modeled using noise-induced mapping, even under random noise, which contradicts a established hypothesis. The results show that noise-induced mapping is most effective for quantum codes with moderate bond dimensions on the boundary of their lattices, and their ability to correct errors also depends on the inherent stability of these codes. The implementation of noise-induced mapping for quantum codes is an innovative method that combines quantum error correction and quantum information processing, offering insights into their connection. Additionally, this approach provides a practical standard to evaluate the performance of quantum codes in scenarios where they function as expected, which is crucial for near-term applications. The results of our study also mark a significant advancement in the understanding of quantum error correction, specifically how these codes can correct errors, and what their connection is to, as it offers an entirely new perspective on this field. The approach and tools we've developed have the potential to be used in the future for practical near-term applications of quantum error correction to systems that are susceptible to noise. The computational methods employed here have previously been used in the context of DMRG for bulk properties but have never been used for the topological entanglement structure of quantum codes, which underlines the cutting-edge nature of this approach. Our study of magnetized radio filaments at the center of the galaxy utilizes MeerKAT data by examining the distances between groups of these filaments. A sample of 43 groupings containing 174 radio filaments was studied and their shapes were analyzed. Many grouped filaments were found to resemble harp strings or comets with looped tails, in addition to the expected fan-shaped configuration. Their orientation relative to the filaments' direction of extension is independent of their distance from the black hole, with filaments oriented perpendicular to the filaments' extension being the most common type. Their location in the plane of the galaxy, extent, and proximity to the filaments' putative drivers such as the supermassive black hole, the central molecular ring, the radio arc, the filaments themselves, and other grouped filaments, are recorded for future reference. Future 21 cm intensity mapping observations are proposed to assess the impact of these filaments on the galaxy's surrounding interstellar medium. Furthermore, the filaments may hold clues regarding the impact of an energetic event around 4.72 million years ago that impacted 20 million solar masses of gas near the galaxy's center, with regards to the origin of the energetic event and surrounding filaments' extent. Their precise origin remains to be determined through ongoing and future investigations.

A proposed paper suggests a new method of distributed leader-follower control for achieving conservation voltage reduction in unbalanced three-phase distribution systems by optimizing DERs through the scheduling of smart inverters. The method considers primary-secondary networks and loads influenced by voltage. The system complexity is minimized through creation of an obstacle-free path for information exchange among devices, resulting in a successive convex optimization problem with achievable sequential and near-real-time solutions. The effectiveness of the proposed method is demonstrated through an illustrative example. The methodology allows for the successful exploration of complex optimization problems in smart energy systems of the future. The application of the proposed method in real-world scenarios could contribute significantly to the achievement of an intelligent and sustainable grid. Numerical studies show that high voltage-related loads can be efficiently influenced through the scheduling of inverters, whereas non-voltage loads may require direct control. The scheduling of smart inverters also shows potential in reducing line losses, a key finding of this research. We investigate non-stochastic bandits and experts in a delayed context, where delays are contingent upon both the time and arm choice. While delayed settings with time-dependent delays have been thoroughly studied, considering arm-dependent delays is more reflective of real-world applications, but raises additional technical obstacles. In the experts scenario with complete knowledge, we create an algorithm achieving a first-order regret bound, highlighting the relationship between delays and losses. This algorithm also results in a first-order regret bound for bandits, given knowledge of missing losses. These are the first regret bounds established for delayed settings, taking into account the best arm's losses and delays only. When no additional information is provided in the bandit scenario, we modify Zimmert and Seldin's algorithm and prove a regret bound despite limited knowledge. The analysis relies on a new bound on expert regret and combines with existing bounds on lost confidence samples, yielding an improved regret bound compared to the best previous result. The modified algorithm also outperforms the existing approach in the experts scenario, especially for large delays. To achieve these results, we develop two new bounds: a first-order loss bound with delayed projection and a bound on expert regret with delayed projection, which are valuable in their own right. Theoretical assertions are supported by simulations. The proposed modifications even provide value in the non-delayed setting, especially for large time delays. Consequently, two algorithms are recommended in the absence of delays. The analysis and techniques developed are also applied to the competitive expert setting, yielding an algorithm with improved regret bounds, especially in the static context. The setting and bounds considered are broad enough to encompass various delayed problems, such as those with time-dependent delays, arm-dependent losses, missing rewards, delayed projections, and non-stochastic contexts, highlighting their connections and promoting their study. The code for the algorithm is available at https://github.com/PhamVanThang/FollowTheExperten. The study is the first to provide theoretical insights into delayed bandits and experts, opening new avenues for exploration. The resulting algorithm can be applied beyond bandits and experts to other fields, as the problems are common across different domains. The approach and bounds obtained are also applicable in the non-stochastic setting, underlining the relevance of previous work in this context. Following Quantum Chromodynamics' 1972 formulation, a breakthrough in its regularization came when Kenneth Wilson applied it to Euclidean lattices. This opened doors for in-depth numerical analyses of QCD's non-perturbative features, exemplified in the initial studies by Michael Creutz. Subsequently, investigations into the QCD phase diagram and the thermodynamics of hot, dense strong-interaction matter gained significant momentum. In this concise review, some key outcomes from over four decades of lattice QCD research on QCD thermodynamics are compiled. These findings include observations of hadronic phase transitions, the connection between QCD and other models for hot and dense strong-interaction matter, and the impact of lattice calculations on understanding the QCD phase diagram and extracting the equation of state for hot and dense regions. Moreover, recent developments in enhancing large-scale simulations via advanced computational methods are reviewed. Finally, the non-perturbative approximation methods initially employed in lattice QCD are briefly discussed. The primary goal of this summary is to provide a concise overview of the research, rather than in-depth explanations of the underlying physics, thus offering a brief historical perspective on the subject. This article is part of a broader review on Quantum Chromodynamics from the 'TASI 2018: Lattice Gauge Theory' course materials. An extensive, separate summary by the course instructor, Rajiv Vasudevan, covers three additional topics: an introduction to lattice gauge theory, an introduction to QCD simulations, and novel applications of lattice QCD. An alternative summary by Tanmoy Bhattacharyya covers topics including perturbative QCD, soft hadron physics, and numerical and phenomenological approaches. The original distribution list of the course materials includes contact information for the speakers and additional resources. The randomness inherent in turbulence and wave conditions makes the outcomes of simulations highly scattered. To capture this variability, a method based on ensemble of numerical simulations via Gaussian process regression is introduced. Notably, the model's determinate parameter is tied to the uncertainty in the simulations, allowing it to be calibrated using data from finite-element analyses or prototype testing. The model's effectiveness is demonstrated through its application to the load predictions of the Sopley prototype, showing that it outperforms traditional methods during the design phase, and its potential as an enhanced predictive tool. The model can also be used in conjunction with stochastic response prediction to obtain reliable probability estimates. To facilitate the use of this model, a Python implementation with the name HGSORE has been released, making it easily accessible to researchers and engineers. The model's source code and example usage are discussed in additional resources. By leveraging heterogeneous data from numerical simulations and prototype testing, our enhanced regression model offers a grounded probabilistic forecasting method that orients itself towards a reliable and efficient risk assessment strategy. A group G exhibits property $R_\infty$ if all automorphisms $\varphi$ of G produce an infinite number of twisted conjugacy classes. In such cases, we establish a precise count, given by $[G:\varphi^\infty G]=\infty$, and provide a specific definition of $R_\infty$-element $\alpha$ in terms of equations. Additionally, if G contains no torsion, the condition for property $R_\infty$ is defined in terms of conjugacy classes under automorphisms. This leads to various practical applications and examples. In general, if G is torsion-free, the condition for property $R_\infty$ can be defined in terms of twisted conjugacy classes, and this yields multiple new findings. Notably, in torsion-free groups, the property $R_\infty$ can be achieved for any non-trivial inner automorphism, and this results in a group of infinite class splitting. This implies that if two torsion-free groups, say G and H, have the same Abelianization, they will both exhibit property $R_\infty$ if and only if their Abelianization is a division ring. A new technique is developed to process time-sensitive data from ultra-fast experiments using an approach based on optimization in a pathway framework. This technique is successfully tested on data from experiments involving X-ray scattering and electron diffraction to analyze the breakdown of molecules. Results from applying the technique accurately match experimental findings and highlight key molecular movements, further aligning with other independent experimental evidence. What's more, this approach effectively considers the continuity of molecular structures and is resilient against noisy data. Moreover, this method opens up new possibilities for combining data from different experimental techniques, such as when combining laser experiments with electron and X-ray diffractometry. This breakthrough paves the way for a new time-resolved analysis technique that expands the scope of molecular structure determination. Contributions:
1. An innovative optimization-based approach for time-sensitive data analysis using a pathway framework without assuming a specific functional form for data.
2. Effective application and validation of this approach on experiments involving electron diffraction and X-ray scattering using samples of cyanoborazine and malononitrile molecules.
3. Development of a novel hybrid approach for combining data from different experimental techniques like diffractometry of X-ray lasers and electron experiments.
4. Determination of molecular structures in complicated systems using molecules of malononitrile in their gas phase.

This paper presents SceNDD: a novel naturalistic driving dataset derived from
instrumented vehicle data collected in downtown Indianapolis over the course
of 68 driving sessions with various drivers. Each session lasted approximately
20 minutes, totalling 40 hours of driving experience. We've made this dataset
available to the scientific community in a centralized repository and have
comprehensively documented it. SceNDD encompasses a diverse set of driving states
characterized by normal, turning, merging, and obstructed vision situations,
along with multiple instrumental data formats and expert-labeled driver states. 
Our hope is that this dataset will stimulate further research in instrumented
naturalistic driving datasets with similar properties and influence other
domains, such as medical body sensor streams. Also presented in this paper is
initial analysis of the dataset's instrumented driving data. Furthermore, this
paper compares and distinguishes different feature extraction methodologies for
deriving driving states from instrumental data. Evaluation of state-of-the-art
machine learning models has been conducted using driving data. Due to its unique
characteristics  we believe SceNDD is well-suited for various driving research
domains, such as driver state assessment and automatic driving guidance. 
Additionally it can serve as a testing platform to compare and evaluate
instrumented driving data extraction techniques and driving state estimation models. 
You can find the SceNDD dataset repository at https://github.com/crcc-usc SceNDD 
and the repository containing analysis code at https://github.com/crcc-usc sceNDD-Analysis.

In connection with the information paradox problem, theories such as BCFT and ICFT are gaining attention. As a contribution to this area of study, we have developed an approach to reflected entropy in the context of BCFT/ICFT. Starting with BCFT, we define left-right reflected entropy and establish its dual description using AdS/BCFT, specifically through the entanglement wedge cross section area. Additionally, we have worked out how to calculate reflected entropy in ICFT. With these tools, we are able to reveal a universal behavior of the Markov gap in the HaPPi RaT IoN scale. Furthermore, our work has helped to clarify the connection between BCFT/ICFT and the more comprehensive IPNG picture, a similar result which was previously proposed in the literature. In the process of our study, we have demonstrated that BCFT can be viewed as a type of restricted BCFT, a finding that is verified through an example in the middle critical regime. We also obtain a representation of the left-right reflected entropy in the middle critical regime, specifically for a type Sp(2/8) using the Iguro, Odock, and Yambe's work on the Iguro-Yambe basis and the Toda multiple Hamiltonian. We are able to express the ignored part of the left-right reflected entropy in the middle critical regime as the order Omega correction to the HaPPi RaT IoN scale. If the system reaches the deconformal limit, we find that the left-right reflected entropy reduces to the ordinary entropy. We are able to express the time evolution of reflected entropy in the Markov scale using the Toda kernel, a symmetric function that was first introduced by Iguro, Togashi, and Yambe. We are also able to give a physical interpretation of the time evolution in the context of BCFT. We are able to describe the time-evolving L functions in the context of the AdS space, specifically for various configurations of excitations in the additional scales Omega 1 and -1. Research on Reconfigurable Intelligent Surface (RIS)-assisted Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiplexing (OFDM) systems has intensified due to their potential for controlling the communication environment and combating multi-path interference effectively. Nonetheless, the precision of channel estimation in such systems is significantly compromised by the increased risk of underutilized subchannels resulting from additional reflection paths introduced by the RIS. To address this challenge, a novel energy-efficient multiple-subchannel parallel channel-peak-corrected least squares (PC-ML) algorithm is proposed to enhance the accuracy of channel estimation. The proposed approach leverages the correlation between adjacent subchannels to produce cleaner estimates, thereby decreasing the number of unnecessary subchannels and minimizing the impact of noise. The effectiveness of the proposed PC-ML approach has been evaluated in terms of channel estimation precision and computational complexity for a 4G-type RIS-assisted OFDM system. The results suggest that the proposed PC-ML approach yields a 7.14% improvement in average signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) compared to the conventional least squares (ML) algorithm while requiring only 55.56% of its computational resources. To facilitate practical applications, the proposed PC-ML approach has been integrated into a two-stage iterative channel estimation algorithm along with an analytical-based upper bound model to streamline the optimization process. The proposed approach has been shown to provide reliable channel estimation performance as the number of subchannels is varied. Moreover, the PC-ML approach yields a favorable performance-complexity balance for various system settings. Specifically, the results produced for 20, 32, and 64 subchannels respectively were 1.05%, 1.21%, and 1.34 dB higher than those of the ML algorithm while requiring 10%, 15%, and 20% more computations. To further optimize the channel estimation process, a novel two-stage approach is proposed to determine the optimal number of subchannels for a given system. The proposed approach yields an 86.67% reduction in computational resources compared to traditional methods while producing identical performance outcomes. The performance of the meter relies on the concept of resolution, which essentially captures the inherent uncertainties present in the system. Our aim is to establish that better resolution leads to more accurate energy measurements. In order to support this claim, we developed an expression for the expectation value of the energy that must be respected by any applicable measurement postulates. This postulate, in turn, is derived from the no-go theorem for standard postulates and a specific set of assumptions that pertain to the system and meter. These assumptions emphasize that the energy measurements are distributed around their mean value with minimal variance, a characteristic that is analogous to the system's being in an energy eigenstate. This go theorem research builds upon previous research by Death, Skotnicki, and Svetitski and is significantly expanded to cover a broader range of scenarios, including the use of meters with distinct dynamics that interact with the system. Our study indicates that the expanded go theorem research is effective in explaining the behavior of analog energy measurements obtained using meters with or without moving parts. In addition, it is consistent with existing research on the no-go theorem related to the use of ports. Moreover, it is observed that the expanded go theorem research offers novel equality claims for the performance of the meter that rely on the time it is being used. Lastly, it is demonstrated that the behavior of the analog energy measurements obtained using moving parts is consistent with those associated with quantum thermodynamic processes that feature non-equilibrium steady states, such as phonon-driven unidirectional pumping. Moreover, it is observed that the expanded go theorem research is applicable to the use of ports even when the moving parts are not present. We are exploring the deformation theory of G2-instantons on nearly G2-manifolds. A one-to-one connection exists between nearly parallel G2 structures and real Killing spinors, enabling the deformation theory to be formulated through the use of spinors and Dirac operators. We establish that the space of infinitesimal deformations for an instanton is equivalent to the kernel of an elliptic operator. With this approach, we prove that abelian instantons exhibit rigidity, and subsequently apply these results to define the deformation space of the canonical connection on nearly G2-manifolds with a normal homogeneous structure of four dimensions. This leads to a key conclusion regarding the rigidity of the canonical connection. Furthermore, our research expands to examining the deformation theory of the canonical connection on nearly G2-manifolds with a suspension of seven-dimensional spacetimes possessing a real Killing spinor. Similar to our previous findings, we discover that the deformation space of the canonical connection on such a scenario is finite-dimensional. Notably, these results contribute significantly to the solution of a long-standing open problem posed by Salamon and Semmelmann in 2006. Moreover, our study offers novel insights into the geometry of nearly G2-manifolds via the exploration of deformation theories, and offers a fresh perspective inspired by the work of Bryant and Salamon from 1995. The details of our methodological framework can be found in Chapter 7, along with three test cases presented in Appendix 8. We are proud to have been awarded the 2020 Heinz Iwanowski Prize for this research. Ultimately, the outcomes of this study are anticipated to open up new avenues for the investigation of nearly G2-manifolds. They may also be extended to the realm of nearly hypercomplex manifolds and the Blair decomposition of pseudo-Riemannian homogeneous manifolds. In fact, our study constitutes the first instance in which the deformation theory of the canonical connection on G2-manifolds has been explored. We are confident that the methods employed in this study will be universally applicable to other geometric scenarios. To build upon this research further, the reader is referred to the works of the first author, along with those of Salamon and Semmelmann. The global spread of the 2019 COVID-19 pandemic caused by SARS-CoV-2 has resulted in widespread losses and socio-economic disruption, with the rapid proliferation of the virus having far-reaching effects worldwide. As part of the effort to combat this crisis, contact tracing technology, known for its success in other outbreaks, has been widely adopted.  However, this technology poses significant concerns regarding user data security, as it entails data collection and analysis that can potentially reveal an individual's identity, location, health status, and daily activities. The primary goal of this research is to investigate the current status of contact tracing technology in order to assess users' data security level and provide an analysis of the risks involved. Furthermore, this study aims to examine contact tracing apps' compliance with essential security standards and to discuss the former with the latter. Ultimately, this research seeks to evaluate the safety and efficacy of contact tracing technology as a means to prevent the spread of COVID-19 through distance-based protection, while highlighting its implications on users' data privacy. The outcome of this investigation may guide policymakers and developers in this regard. The applications under consideration have been scrutinized regarding their data collection practices, which include merit and demerit lists in order to identify both positive and security-related attributes. The analysis was performed in two stages: an a posteriori review and a qualitative survey of reputable contact tracing apps' characteristics. The latter's results rely on literature reviews regarding data security and contact tracing technology. The results show that the use of contact tracing technology may bring about significant privacy risks, with primary concerns centred around the extent of data being collected, aggregation, and transmission processes. The study concludes by suggesting potential solutions to address these concerns and highlights areas for further research in this area. The ultimate goal is to provide guidance for users regarding responsible contact tracing technology use and to inform policymakers and developers on this critical topic. The outcome may also encourage further investigations and research to reveal additional data security risks and related challenges. The final outcome seeks to provide guidance on responsible contact tracing technology use and shed more light on this vital topic. The study can potentially contribute to other areas, including recommendations for future contact tracing systems, an discussion of relevant ethical considerations, and a detailed description of the designed distance-based model. The outcome may also provide an analysis of the perceived trust and performance of contact tracing technology. The final results obtained showed that contact tracing technology can be trusted to a certain degree, with user satisfaction being high, but this confidence comes at a cost due to existing security and privacy issues. The central nervous system's underlying physiological processes are thought to
emanate from fundamental electromagnetic interactions between brain cells, or
neurons. Despite the ubiquitous presence of electromagnetic interactions,
conventional neuroscience employs a non-quantum description to analyze brain
function and explain behavioral outcomes. However, when we measure the emergent
properties of brain function, quantum principles such as entanglement, where
correlated outcomes arise, may be relevant. To determine if this non-quantum
description is indeed sufficient, we developed a theoretical framework to
estimate typical correlation distances in biological systems, and applied these
criteria to the brain. We discovered that experimental measurements of brain
function, like those using functional magnetic resonance imaging, establish
correlations over short physical distances, corresponding to the size of brain
cells or neural clusters. However, these outcomes only make sense within a
non-quantum framework, as the underlying interactions are incoherent. Notably, if
we treat neural function as quantum mechanics, without additional structure,
correlation distances typically extend to double the size of biological cells.
This distinction suggests that electromagnetic interactions occur at a cooperative
level, generally exceeding individual cell dimensions, without necessarily
requiring quantum entanglement. To verify this hypothesis, we proposed a
significant modification to MRI techniques to detect potential quantum signals,
and we recommend that future neuroscience investigations, including fMRI studies,
be conducted in an quantum-enabled manner, allowing for both quantum and
non-quantum descriptions of brain function. By promoting this new approach,
our work may lead to a deeper understanding of electromagnetic interactions and
cooperative effects within biological systems, potentially revealing new
mechanisms underlying neuroscience and the science of complex life. Ultimately, a
grounded quantum foundation for neuroscience could unlock new frontiers at the
intersection of quantum and biological inquiry.

This research paper introduces a tool for automatically translating ACL2 representations of C code into executable C code and verifying its correctness through the creation of accompanying ACL2 theorems. This tool was utilized in the past to develop formalizations of two modules from the GNU Autoconf library. Additionally, the paper outlines a case study involving the formal verification of a modified, elevated layer on top of the C standard library, with the objective of ensuring the reliability of autoconf testing frameworks as an added value. We calculate rational T-equivariant elliptic cohomology of complex projective spaces derived from finite dimensional T-representations V. This is accomplished by establishing that the T-equivariant elliptic cohomology theory constructed in Gre05, and the T^2-equivariant theory in Bar22, share a key decomposition property. This key property enables us to apply the methods in both references to obtain the T-equivariant cohomology results. Under certain conditions, the T-equivariant cohomology results are found to be equivalent to the T-equivariant cohomology theory based on Chow rings, as found in Fu's work in EU19. Key to the method is a geometric decomposition of the finite dimensional T-representations V into a direct sum of tensor and symmetric representations. This decomposition geometrically interprets the T-equivariant cohomology results in terms of geometric T-actions on complex projective spaces and odd dimensional complex manifolds, and provides a direct relationship with complex lines in the space CP(V). Using this decomposition, we are able to prove that a T-action exists on CP(V) with a fixed point if and only if a T^2-action exists on C^2 such that the map {(z_1, z_2) to [z_1, z_2]} is T-equivariant. We further show that a T-action exists on CP(V) with a fixed point if and only if a T-action exists on C^(n+1) with a fixed point that fixes exactly one point, where n is the tensor part of the decomposition of V. The proof involves a fundamental theorem in Bar22 that links T^2-equivariant cohomology with T-equivariant cohomology. We leverage this relationship, and the decomposition of V, to provide a geometric interpretation of the T-equivariant cohomology theory based on an extension of the Schubert polynomial, as found in EU19. Under certain conditions, the T-equivariant cohomology theory based on the elliptic cohomology is found to be equivalent to the T-equivariant cohomology theory based on the Chow ring. By combining this equivalence with Fu's work in EU19, we are able to show that the rational T-equivariant elliptic cohomology of CP(V) has a dual structure to the rational T-equivariant cohomology theory based on the Chow ring. This dual structure enables us to obtain a bottle-beer idempotent and a Massey machine, as introduced in Mandell-Szymanski 07

Our online survey with 235 Signal users revealed that users can be divided into two categories: those who understand the function of PINs (enthusiasts) and those who do not (casual users). Surprisingly, only 14% of users declined to use a PIN, indicating successful encouragement of PIN adoption in Signal. While enthusiastic users predominantly employed complex PINs saved in password managers, casual users mainly used simple numerical PINs. To strengthen the security of casual users, enhancing awareness about the true purpose of PINs and the features they offer could be beneficial. Furthermore, Signal could consider integrating a option to remind users of their PIN that they have forgotten. Our survey also explored users' opinions on additional security features in Signal, including importing encryption keys, sharing encrypted messages, integrating Security Keys, and implementing multi-factor authentication. The results underscore the need for incorporating these features in Signal. Finally, we discovered that users are uncertain about the encryption method utilized by Signal and likely do not require an explanation. We recommend educating users about the benefits of sharing encrypted messages while preserving the anonymity of users in their community. In conclusion, while enthusiastic users possess a good understanding of PINs, there is a need for awareness about the function of PINs among casual users. We are eager to collaborate with the Signal team to implement additional security features in their application. The curvature formed by the Hessian matrix or its generalized Gauss-Newton approximation holds significant value in developing training algorithms for deep networks. However, current methods based on automatic differentiation and Kronecker-factored block diagonal approximations disregard noise in mini-batch datasets. Our new model, ViViT, capitalizes on the low-rank structure of the generalized Gauss-Newton approximation without introducing additional computational complexities, achieving an improvement of up to 75% in scaling compared to recent techniques. Training times have been reduced significantly, with benchmarks showing a 4 to 130 times speed increase on various image classification and generation tasks, including applying it to the ImageNet dataset. Our work includes an in-depth numerical analysis and showcases the effectiveness of ViViT through an embedding of the ViT Transformer in PyTorch. Moreover, it has also been successfully integrated with other loss functions in other deep learning frameworks. These integrations can be accessed at a dedicated repository. The ViViT PyTorch implementation can be found at https://github.com/danielkwu/vivit, with a public demonstration of its capabilities utilizing the ImageNet dataset at https://danielwu.ai/vivit-image-net-demo. A public meeting to further discuss ViViT can be accessed at https://danielwu.ai/vivit-meeting. Numerous languages attribute gender not just to living entities but also to inanimate objects. When such a gender-based distinction is present in a language, related words must conform to the noun's assigned gender, affecting how we interpret these inanimate objects. As inanimate objects sharing the same gender draw closer together in word representations, we observe this distinct categorization in these languages. However, conventional debiasing techniques have not proven successful in eradicating this distinction. To rectify this, we devised a novel approach to identify and eliminate inanimate object gender distinctions embedded within pre-trained word representations. For this purpose, we created a proprietary dataset of French inanimate words and designed a targeted word manipulation strategy which we then applied across multiple embedding spaces. Through experimental comparison with baseline approaches, we noticed that our method effectively eliminated gender distinctions among these inanimate objects, and this was supported by our own self-supervised evaluation metrics as well as an independent assessment of accuracy using contextual clues. Ultimately, by eliminating these gender distinctions, we observed increased similarity in the word representations of synonyms, and this was confirmed both from a semantic and syntactical perspective. The code for our approach has been made publicly accessible. Additionally, we released BabelScore, a publicly accessible resource and tool to quantify and analyze gender-based categorization in word representations across various languages based on different metrics. For the French language, we reported a gender discrimination threshold of 90%, indicating that more than 90% of the words in the dataset correctly adhered to their assigned gender. Based on our work using the BabelScore resource, we observed the following: (i) higher gender discrimination among verbs than monosyllabic nouns; (ii) the efficiency of the WNG\^e convention, a French grammatical gender detection tool, in detecting gender distinctions among polymorphic nouns but failing in the case of monosyllabic nouns. The BabelScore resource is designed to be language-agnostic and we encourage contributions that integrate additional languages; you can contribute by visiting the repository page on GitHub. Given the significant categorization present in many languages that attribute gender to inanimate objects, we firmly believe that our approach and the BabelScore resource will be invaluable not just in English but also in languages such as French, Spanish, German and many more. For instance, while the English language might not pose a notable challenge, Spanish and German explicitly assign gender to plural forms as well as singular. By leveraging these properties, it provides a versatile framework for simulating hypothetical scenarios and making predictions based on past actions. State-of-the-art radio interferometers such as the LOw Frequency ARray (LOFAR) and the Square Kilometer Array (SKA) have expanded our range of observable radio signals beyond traditional sources like compact radio galaxies and quasars to encompass pulsars, fast radio bursts, gravitational wave- induced fast radio bursts, and binary black hole mergers. However, the spectrum of radio emission from these novel transients is not yet thoroughly understood. This research delves into the distinct spectra produced by the aforementioned sources, utilizing the Grid Computational Intelligence JImmy tool to create teacher and student machine learning models. These models aim to leverage overlapping features from diverse sources to build reliable models for classification and prediction. An additional machine learning model is included that utilizes features specifically from rapid changes in radio bursts to identify fast radio bursts (FRBs). The analysis indicates that modern radio telescopes can discern FRBs from pulsars and gamma-ray bursts, achieving high accuracy (up to 99%) using the rapid changes in radio bursts feature set. While the model's overall precision for distinguishing between cosmic events and cosmic sources is not optimal (approximately 60%), the study indicates which sources share similar features that can be utilized for improved classification and analysis. Furthermore, it suggests using models trained on diverse sources to make predictions about unexplored sources, an area of research likely to experience significant advancements in the future as the SKA becomes operational. The development of novel machine learning models for analyzing, segmenting, and visualizing the discussed radio signals is also presented. These extensions include the use of computational intelligence for automatically identifying and categorizing cosmic sources and events, and for reconstructing two-dimensional images from the data. The analysis provides insights into the efficacy of modern machine learning strategies for distinguishing between diverse radio signals. The research outcomes have been incorporated into software tools that can be utilized for alternative forecasting or analysis on radio signals beyond traditional galactic sources. The corresponding implementation of these models is presented in the paper. The study provides an in-depth analysis of the diversity in the features of the various radio signals observed. The research suggests that future radio interferometers will be able to detect and analyze previously unexplored categories of radio signals. The paper includes recommendations for optimizing machine learning strategies and algorithms for improved analysis and segmentation of radio signals in the data. In recent years, advancements in machine learning and artificial intelligence have driven significant growth in photonics research, leading to cutting-edge photonic systems including traditional waveguides, nanoantennas, and metasurfaces. The innovative application of AI-driven methodologies empowers the development of smart photonic devices rooted in fundamental light-matter interaction principles. Artificial intelligence-based frameworks are effectively utilized for solving complex problems involving the optimization of light behavior at the source, transmission, or detection levels. Nevertheless, the application of AI methods in fundamental physics is relatively new, particularly when the underlying function's analytical form is unknown. This concept note aims to provide an overview of the current state of AI methods in photonic device design, address existing challenges, and propose future research directions that could lead to a potential 'AI-driven revolution' in light-matter interactions and photonic technologies. Furthermore, we highlight the potential of integrating the 'inverse design' approach, commonly used for AI-driven photonic design, into research on exotic photonic materials and metasystems. By integrating the 'first-principles' approach with advanced AI-based optimization tools, researchers may uncover new possibilities for enhancing photonic performance at the core of future information and communication technologies. These future advancements could, in turn, pave the way for groundbreaking photonic-based applications in fields such as fundamental physics research, cosmology, particle detection, and medical therapy, thereby opening up new opportunities for scientists and engineers. This concept note represents a starting point for exploring these opportunities and encourages discussion on the emerging interdisciplinary field of AI-driven photonic interactions. Throughout the document, we incorporate visual aids containing example code and illustrate the underlying concepts, thereby facilitating the next steps in this research area. To facilitate seamless comprehension, we have included a brief glossary in each section and concluded with an extensive reference list. We anticipate that this concept note will serve as a prompt for the 'AI in Photonic Revolution' working group to conduct market analysis, establish partnerships, leverage industrial expertise, and develop a comprehensive report based on the findings. Additionally, we include in the appendices key details regarding the 'AI in Photonic Research Group' and its activities, along with information about the working group's mission and composition. Lastly, we have included at the end of the document a brief overview of the 'AI in Photonic Research Group's' (aiphotonics.org) activities, founded by one of the authors (M. A.). Please note that the document contains 33 references at the end of the appendices for further reading.

Baryon creation is investigated using a quantized fragmentation model based on QCD strings. Baryons are generated through a process that is straightforward to understand, which involves a QCD string breaking up into causally linked parts. The resulting formula accurately predicts the ratios of nucleon densities at varying momentum values, closely matching the findings of lattice quantum chromodynamics. Additionally, the model provides a clear explanation for the phenomenon of baryon dimuon signatures. It also offers a potential connection to the 'anti-baryon like states' discovered in recent lattice simulations. Further discussion is given regarding how fragments of a single QCD string can form a triply connected object, which could serve as the foundation for an independent experimental discovery of baryon formation. Given that our process is irreversible, it might serve as a model for an irreversible aspect of quantum chromodynamics that needs to be addressed within lattice simulations. Since this discussion is broader, it is placed in an added section titled 'Implementation considerations'. Furthermore, in an additional section titled 'Alternative fragmentation mechanisms', it is explored whether our particular fragmentation mechanism is unique among all those consistent with the observed nucleon structure. It is suggested that if this is the case, then an independent experimental study of baryon formation in high-energy collisions could provide compelling evidence for quantum chromodynamics. Such an experimental study is discussed in an additional section titled 'Experimental investigations'. Lastly, in an additional section titled 'Generalized fragmentation mechanisms', it is demonstrated that if the ratios of nucleon densities predicted by our model are used as constraints, then a wide array of different fragmentation mechanisms can be identified, to varying degrees of approximation. In particular, it is found that a variant of this fragmentation process can also apply to the creation of di-baryons, an observation that might be explored through experimental investigations. These additional sections can be found at the end of this document. Further research into the topic is proposed in an appendix titled 'Proposed research'. In addition to this document, there are two separate documents titled 'Appendix A' and 'Appendix B' that contribute valuable information. Among other points, it is pointed out in 'Appendix A' that a generalized form of a process discovered by Andersson et al. can also apply to the creation of baryons, an observation that might be explored through experimental investigations. 'Appendix B' provides a summary of how fragments of a triply connected object can interact with each other. Such a summary is crucial in order to validate our model of baryon creation

A significant feature of commercial plenoptic cameras, the lenslet array captures spatial and angular light information in a single exposure. However, the resulting high data dimensionality, which contributes to light field capabilities, poses a significant challenge to data transmission and storage. This challenge has led to two primary issues: data compression and noise reduction, which necessitate further research. A novel approach for compressing and filtering captured light field data is proposed. The method utilizes a multi-scale representation and filter bank to isolate different detail levels, followed by a novel extension of the BLP2A compression algorithm to accommodate this new representation. The filters are then used to determine weights for sub-aperture images, which are subsequently arranged into a hierarchical, multi-resolution format and compressed using the BLP2A extension. The process is completed by performing inter-color and inter-frame entropy coding. The proposed system provides superior noise reduction and light field image quality while achieving a high data compression ratio, which significantly reduces storage requirements. The performance of the method is verified through comprehensive tests using the NTLK light field dataset and other commercial plenoptic camera datasets. interactive and non-interactive, prevail with synchronous and asynchronous 
query-document embeddings, respectively. Weighed against retrieval accuracy and 
computational efficiency, each approach excels and falls short. This study combines 
the benefits of these two frameworks through a novel, semi-interactive framework. 
Named 'interactive-to-interactive' (I2I) cross-lingual information retrieval, our 
approach generates document embeddings interactively but queries non-interactively, 
utilizing a deep neural machine translation model to map the source to target 
embbedding spaces. Empirical results on two prominent datasets validate the 
superiority of our proposed I2I framework and make the underlying code 
accessible-to-the-public.

This paper employs a refined hierarchical latent variable model to capture patterns within multi-period time series data, which exhibit dynamics governed by various time-sensitive factors. Traditional stacked RNN and DBN models lack the capability to incorporate tendencies spanning multiple periods and often overlook redundant input variables, which contribute nothing or negatively affect predictive power. In contrast, our HLVM model effectively models one-time series using a single latent variable shared across multiple periods, thus increasing the impact of relevant variables while diminishing the influence of irrelevant ones. To achieve dynamic modeling, we introduce a time-dependent probability factor in the likelihood function, enabling the capture of patterns spanning multiple periods. Two novel methods for introducing temporal continuity have been discovered and tested on multiple datasets, demonstrating the efficacy of our HLVM model in outperforming previous models in various tasks. In the experimental process, by manipulating the explanatory model's complexity, we demonstrated that our model's performance mirrors the description of the underlying data, thus providing a compelling model balance. Lastly, through ablation studies, we found that integrating a temporal continuity term significantly improved the model's capability to capture long-term dependencies in multi-period time series data. With time being an expensive commodity, we also assessed the scalability of our model at different levels and suggested potential future strategies for reducing model overhead. The remarkable effectiveness of deep learning has led to an array of applications raising significant ethical issues. A comprehensive framework to address these problems doesn't exist yet, so we've developed a practical and theoretical guide to identify, analyze and resolve the ethical implications of deep learning. We've identified two key areas: the inherent characteristics of deep learning and the broader societal context. Through case studies and a non-exhaustive analysis of real-world examples, we've demonstrated the application of our framework to various subfields like fairness, privacy, and the impact of bias. This research is an essential step towards creating a systematic approach to understand and tackle the ethical complexities of deep learning. The developed framework can be applied to different subfields, providing a foundation for educating individuals working with such technologies and fostering responsible innovation. The goal is to contribute to a deeper discussion about the ethical implications of deep learning and help advance responsible development. The document containing more detailed information and specific examples can be found at https://ethdeep.github.io. Despite significant advancements in object detection, current methods have limitations in detecting diverse object categories due to the labor-intensive task of creating training data with bounding-box annotations. Recent open-vocabulary object detection methods have emerged to overcome this limitation by training on a set of base categories, enabling detection of unseen object types. However, their effectiveness is restricted by the relatively small number of base categories used for training. To address this issue, we propose a general architecture framework called Object Nearest Neighbor Deformer (ONN-D) that can effectively combine multiple self-supervised object detectors without baseline constraints. ONN-D achieves this by leveraging an associative memory module to dynamically form associations between novel object instances and base categories during inference. Using this framework, we develop a series of simple and effective object transformers and demonstrate state-of-the-art performance on three challenging object detection benchmarks, significantly improving the detection accuracy by up to 8.9 points compared to previous state-of-the-art methods. Our model and training code are publicly available at https://github.com/ditnet/ONN-D.venir.

In lotteries with exceptionally high jackpots, as seen in Mega Millions and Powerball,
increasing bettor participation actually works to reduce the return on investment for each ticket.
The reason for this is a higher likelihood of multiple people winning with the same ticket.
In an attempt to boost the return on investment, some theorists suggest combining lotteries
into a single higher-stakes game.
Using probability theory and game theory, we've found this approach is both unwise and unnecessary. 
Instead, we've identified strategies to maximize the return on a single lottery ticket in the presence
of heavy betting. 
These strategies prioritize selecting a subset of popular numbers with minimal redundancy,
given the specific winning conditions and betting pool size.
By doing so, we've found the return on a single ticket can approach one-thousandth of the jackpot size. 
For Mega Millions and Powerball, this means the return on a single ticket can approach $3 to $4 million
given their respective jackpot sizes. 
This research provides a practical method for determining an optimal lottery ticket, at least in theory. 
The so-called 'optimal' tickets suggested here are unusually expensive, however, with prices
potentially exceeding $50 for Mega Millions and Powerball, given the specific combinations
suggested here, thus illustrating the sheer absurdity of lottery investing. 
Beyond the obvious absurdity, our findings also indicate a limit to how much people should be encouraged
to participate in heavy betting, as the return on a single ticket actually decreases as the betting pool grows. 
One potential application of this research is helping casinos use lotteries as a tool to draw in investors,
by offering higher returns on smaller stakes lottery tickets, rather than the traditional high-stakes versions.

By expanding the variational approach to cover moderately coupled regimes through a second-order perturbation theory, we find that the effective polaron mass exhibits a distinct point of transition from an initially lower to a remarkably higher mass compared to the non-interacting limit, occurring at a coupling strength corresponding to the mean square displacement of bosons equal to half a bosonic lattice constant. This transition arises from a polaron becoming locally centered within the trap field rather than center-of-mass moving as occurs in zero-range interactions, thus the transition corresponds to a phase shift from the ambient to the magnetized phase. Additionally, at the critical coupling strength, the variational ground state consists of both polaron and continuum components, both carrying the same quantum Hall vortices. Our findings offer significant insight into experimental investigations of 2D Fermi polaron matters where the transition could be observed. Moreover, our analysis expands the applicability of the variational approach to the nonlinear Bose-Fermi coupling regime, offering a new method to estimate the polaron mass in this case. Furthermore, our method may also be applied to explore the distinct point of transition in other types of polaron models. Furthermore, our effective action at low energies is similar to a spin-1 action. Graph polynomials hold significant value due to their potential to develop algebraic formulas describing various graph characteristics and encoding multiple graph invariants through their evaluation processes. Certain graphs, including complete and bipartite structures, can be identified through unique polynomial properties. For example, the chromatic polynomial evaluated at -1 counts the number of orientations with an odd number of edges, while its evaluation at 1 indicates the presence of a Hamiltonian path or cycle in a specific configuration. Recently, higher-order polynomial evaluations have been explored with insights into their meaning, such as indicating paths of a particular length or containing specific subgraph patterns. Although a comprehensive understanding of these higher-order polynomials remains limited, it has been established that for any N-1 order polynomial, its evaluation cannot surpass N. We address and resolve questions surrounding polynomial properties when evaluated beyond order N-1. We demonstrate that for various polynomial types, including the chromatic, connection, and flow polynomials, their evaluations beyond order N-1 provide information on the presence of specific subgraphs within the graph structure. In doing so, we introduce novel applications for polynomial evaluations and develop novel graph invariants based on these higher-order polynomial evaluations. Notably, in graphs meeting a particular criterion for these higher-order polynomial evaluations, we identify a relationship linking evaluations at negative values to the topological integers of related Moore spaces. Moreover, we employ the methodology developed in the last section to derive new interpretations for polynomial evaluations at orders two and three in specific graph types. We also introduce a novel approach for obtaining a graph's chromatic polynomial based on a particular two-graph structure association. Lastly, we provide a comprehensive understanding of polynomial evaluations at orders two, three, and four in the context of bipartite graph embeddings. The findings described hold significant value in the manipulation and understanding of graph structures. In addition, connections to other areas of mathematics, including topology and design theory, are discussed through examples. The approach employed allows for easy modification and application to various polynomial types, highlighting the broader potential of this method. Moreover, in the event that a polynomial type exhibits distinct evaluations beyond order N-1 for distinct values of N, it implies the existence of specific graph patterns within the graph structure, which can then be used to express independent graph invariants based on these higher-order polynomial evaluations. In general, the study addresses previously unexplored aspects of polynomial theory and expands our understanding of polynomial theory. In the process of this analysis, Moore spaces and 2-graph structure associations are explored, which provides additional insight into their properties.

We derive an expression for the pullback of the Hitchin connection, extending from the moduli space of genus two curves to a 10-fold cover of a Teichmueller curve, which was first found by Veech. Subsequently, we develop an expression in terms of iterated integrals that describes the monodromy representation of this connection. Consequently, as a secondary result, we determine the quantum representations of a vast array of pseudo-Anosov elements in the genus two mapping class group. Additionally, following from a key result established by Chen and Moeller regarding trace representations, our work implies that the pullback of the Hitchin connection yields novel, explicit, and computable linear combinations of matrix coefficients in the trace, that are specific to each pseudo-Anosov element, in the theta-stable locus of the Teichmueller space. Lastly, drawing upon a crucial discovery by Silverberg and Tamagawa, our calculations yield a novel, explicit, and computable formulation of the L-functions associated with each pseudo-Anosov element, that are specifically situated within the theta-stable locus. We are confident that our calculations can be extended to the hyperbolic iteration problem, which is an issue that is currently under separate investigation. Over time, the trend of companies adopting remote working has been on the rise, leading many to adapt Agile methodologies such as Scrum to cope with distributed teams. However, the global shift to fully remote working brought about by the COVID-19 pandemic was a unprecedented phenomenon. This research involves a two-phase, multi-method approach. Initially, it investigates how working from home affected Scrum practitioners through a qualitative survey. Subsequently, it proposes and empirically tests a theoretical framework using PLS-SEM with data from 202 employees. The results demonstrate the positive relationship between all constructs, specifically when comparing working from home to traditional office settings, and that working from home may be acceptable for Scrum team members as long as their needs for autonomy, relatedness, and competence are met. The findings highlight key recommendations that organisations working with Scrum in a remote environment should be aware of providing necessary resources and support to meet these fundamental human needs for enhanced team well-being, and that this can be achieved through adjusting Scrum practices. The study contributes to our understanding of remote working and its impact on Scrum teams. Furthermore, it offers practical guidance to organisations and managers on maintaining a productive and well-nurtured remote Scrum team. The final framework offers theoretical and practical implications for future research in this field. The study was conducted without any prejudice towards or against remote working, and its implications for both Scrum teams and organisations as a whole will be discussed. The participants' anonymity was respected throughout and the data obtained met the required regulations, specifically via a do-not-share policy with the data provider Prolific. The participants' data were shared via an informed consent form, and the results were analysed in accordance with the required protocol. The results were shared with the participants as outlined in the protocol, and the results were approved by the relevant committees. Leveraging techniques borrowed from image processing, we develop mathematically sound indicators to capture both fine-scale and broad-scale interplay among color categories. Our proposed methods enable fast computation by adapting techniques such as Delaunay tessellations and alpha-shapes for color mapping. Additionally, we introduce a novel procedure, alpha-strips, to explore the color patterns that result from different radius values and to extract the shapes of objects while handling noise and curvature. Our alpha-strips method also forms the basis for a new clustering algorithm that leverages a simplified model to achieve state-of-the-art results in computing chromatic surfaces. Furthermore, we introduce a procedure for computing the Voronoi tessellation of the complex color domain by first computing the color mapping using our alpha-strips approach and then optimizing the polygonal mesh through laplacian smoothing. Our proposed techniques are showcased through their application to a brain tumor dataset as well as the analysis of colors in a collection of sculptures by artist Jonathan Alger. Our quantitative analysis of the generated surfaces demonstrates that our algorithm produces accurate approximations of the color domain with minimal error. This enables the creation of detailed, precise models using only a few surfaces to capture the intricate color patterns, which are otherwise indistinguishable from the original data. Our techniques are documented in the Browser-based Geodesic Pattern Explorer, an interactive tool that facilitates exploration and analysis of the color patterns in three-dimensional point clouds. This tool has the potential to revolutionize the digital preservation and analysis of sculptural art by automating the generation of color surfaces, reducing the time and skills required for this process. In the future, our algorithm can be extended to make contributions to the field of medical imaging, particularly in the estimation of soft tissue surfaces. Our novel algorithm has already yielded impressive results in the analysis of a dataset from Duke University relating to brain shift estimation. This work utilizes the concepts from Statistical Learning Theory to tackle the problem of multi-user communication via optimal power control in order to derive the most efficient achievable rates when there are no constraints on the devices' power levels. It first presents a general method called "Optimal Power Control" (OPC) that can achieve the maximum possible rate for any number of users and level of interference. When OPC is combined with randomization, it successfully meets the constraints set by power limitations. Building upon this knowledge, a learning theory-based approach to determining extremal gains from optimal power control is developed. Interestingly, the research finds that the extremal gains become significantly reduced as the number of users increases, which means that larger networks may be able to accommodate more users under equal levels of interference. Additionally, the work introduces two novel strategies called "Identifiable Projected Optimal Power Control" (IPOC) and "Averaged Projected Optimal Power Control" (APOC), which not only have extremal gains that are comparable to those of optimal power control but also have more desirable properties as well. A proof is given of how these two strategies can be trained using regularized empirical risk minimization, which is a commonly used technique in the field of statistical learning theory. Finally, the research also provides a precise mathematical bound for the deviation between the achievable rates from these two methods and the maximum possible rates from optimal power control. A practical application of APOC is also demonstrated to a specific scenario, which is a cellular network with different power constraints. It is observed that when APOC is applied to this specific problem, its performance is very close to that of OPC, which shows that larger networks can achieve near-optimal rates even when they use simpler and more deterministic methods. A comparison is also made between the computationally expensive OPC optimization algorithm and the computationally efficient APOC algorithm, which uses stochastic gradient descent, which is another common technique in the field of statistical learning theory. A practical demonstration of how these two methods can be applied to each other is also given. Moreover, the work also theoretically and practically expands the principles of near-optimal risk minimization to other problems of multi-user communication with or without power constraints, which can achieve the maximum possible rates when the number of users is significantly larger than the number of dimensions. A practical application of this learning theory-based approach to a specific problem, which is a 3-user interference channel, shows that the near-optimal risk minimization can achieve rates that are very close to those of the optimal rate

Auditing business processes often requires categorization of complex data to ensure compliance with regulations like the General Data Protection Regulation. Traditional machine learning methods excel at categorizing transactions but struggle to provide transparency, making it difficult for auditors to understand decision-making processes. This lack of clarity is crucial, as auditors need to be able to trace decisions back to their underlying data elements. Our research introduces an novel, explainable categorization method that combines logical rules with machine learning. By integrating these two approaches, we created a model that not only accurately categorizes transactions but also provides clear, human-readable explanations for its decisions. These explanations are crucial, as they allow auditors to confidently verify our model's accuracy and identify potential errors due to incorrectly trained data. To address this issue, we also developed a method for detecting logical errors in the training data of our model. Our method could also be adapted to detect errors in the training datasets of traditional machine learning models used for auditing. This research demonstrates a new approach to categorization, showcasing how explainable models can significantly boost the accuracy and confidence of auditing processes. Our research was applied to the accurate categorization of business-to-business transactions and provides a concrete example of the potential for explainable models to revolutionize the field of auditing. Additionally, the research provides an in-depth analysis of the trade-off between the model's accuracy and logical error rate, allowing auditors to make informed decisions about minimizing logical errors to achieve maximum accuracy. Our methodology is highly adaptable and can be applied to a wide range of categorization tasks, making it an invaluable resource for auditors. Our team developed a free, open-source software framework to facilitate the research and can be accessed at: https://labc0ns.uniud.it/ExCat.
