In the rapidly evolving landscape of Internet of Things (IoT) networks, periodic firmware updates are vital for maintaining optimal security and reliability. Given the trend towards implementing security measures via codified policy decisions and exchangeable code (security-as-a-code), these updates should become standard practice. However, deploying firmware updates across vast IoT networks can significantly impact network performance, particularly during critical periods when a high volume of concurrent updates occurs. Consequently, ensuring that IoT networks provide expected levels of service during these updates is a major concern. In this research, we propose a set of key performance indicators (KPIs) to evaluate IoT network quality during firmware rollouts. A numerical model has also been suggested to anticipate and manage these events, drawing upon standard radio network planning tools. Our proposed approach enables operators to anticipate and manage these events, estimate the dimensions and locations of areas with reduced connectivity, and make informed decisions about simultaneous firmware updates. In-depth analysis of the model has been conducted, providing valuable insights into scaling, data aggregation, and individual device level performance. Specifically, this research sheds light on how large-scale IoT networks can be segmented and how this affects user experience in these divided regions. Moreover, by examining scaling and operational limitations, our study offers crucial insights into how user behavior is affected by simultaneous firmware updates. In a large-scale IoT network, for instance, it was determined that a trade-off between network load and user experience in segregated regions needs to be carefully balanced. Furthermore, this research highlights that segmentation may hinder the separation of concurrent updates and introduce uncertainty regarding large-scale firmware rollouts. In addition, our numerical model has identified several parameters that influence Segmentation Index, such as number of devices, network load, and update duration, and demonstrated their effects on this index. Ultimately, our proposed approach provides IoT operators with an effective tool to manage this process in order to achieve optimal trade-offs between network performance and user experience. In certain cases, it may be beneficial to restrict concurrent updates, particularly those involving a large number of devices or long update durations, whereas other parameters, such as network load and device quantity, can be controlled using radio access technology selection. These factors carry significant uncertainties, yet their impact on model accuracy is poorly understood. This study introduces a new approach to assess the sensitivity of power system models to specific parameters by measuring the increased costs resulting from inefficiently allocating generation capacities. Through case studies involving capital costs, varied weather conditions, and differing spatial and temporal resolutions, we demonstrate the method's value and reveal that models are most susceptible to temporal resolution. This novel methodology serves as a tool for investigators to evaluate and improve the efficiency of power system expansion planning models. Furthermore, it provides insights that can be applied to model the integration of distribution systems. Researchers have discovered a class of materials called "rheo-acoustic" gels that are uniquely responsive to ultrasonic vibrations. This breakthrough reveals that when subjected to these high-frequency sound waves, colloidal gels exhibit a profound reduction in rigidity. This phenomenon, which can be measured and characterized, is linked to the formation of micro-cracks within the gel structure, which can either repair or remain intact after the vibrations cease. Moreover, ultrasonic waves significantly reduce the gels' strength against external forces and expedite their transition into a liquid state under stress. Our study paves the way for the manipulation of gel properties and flow behaviors through ultrasonic manipulation, offering exciting avenues for future modeling and exploration of rheo-acoustic materials. The ultrasonic manipulation technique may also find applications in controlling drug delivery, optimizing processing procedures, and developing innovative materials that change shape or release substances upon exposure to sound. To date, ultrasonic manipulation has yielded maximum viscosity reductions of up to 90%, indicating vast potential for future applications. The experimental data supports a newly proposed model that explains the mechanisms behind this ultrasonic-induced destruction of gels, accounting for variations in frequency, amplitude, and gel composition. This theoretical framework provides a solid understanding of the processes involved and helps to set boundaries for the observed destruction of gels that apply broadly to different types of gels. The ultrasonic destruction of gels unites two distinct phenomena traditionally studied in mechanics and acoustics: mechanical destruction and wave-induced repair. The destruction of gels occurs when waves exceed the gels' strength, causing their breakdown, whereas wave-induced repair occurs when the gels heal faster than they are damaged. The interaction of these opposing processes determines the extent of destruction and can be manipulated by adjusting wave parameters. The development of ultrasonic manipulation offers an innovative way to control rheological properties and may lead to the discovery of new gel properties and behaviors. The principles behind this technique may also be applicable to the study of rigid materials, offering a range of potential applications and a deeper understanding of gel physics. The hunt for Top and Bottom companions is a key area of study for both the ATLAS and CMS experiments, as their single production offers considerable detection possibilities. Though past research mainly focused on the resononant production mode of these hypothetical particles, new findings are expected to focus on the non-resonant scenario, which is predicted to occur in certain theoretical models about Electroweak Symmetry Breaking. To assist in finding the correct production rate for Top and Bottom companions in light of presumed but unobserved new physics, this work presents an analysis technique for measuring the total width of produced particles. Based on mock test data for a 139 fb^-1 LHC-Run3 dataset, our method is realistic and accurate. It involves building an onset transverse momentum distribution, known as a prescription, through a topological approach and then using it with a maximum likelihood fit of the smeared prescription on the actual data to estimate the width. Several different assumptions about the shape of the width are tested, including a fully topological distribution and one that assumes a particular shape. Under the latter assumption, this method provides a 20-25% (15-20%) margin of error for measuring the width of Top companions, given a 100-500 GeV mass range and a 500-800 GeV mass range, respectively. Margin of errors for Bottom companions, also given a 100-500 GeV mass range and a 50-300 GeV mass range, are 30-40% and 40-50%, respectively. These findings suggest that if new physics is not discovered during upcoming LHC phases, a 4- (5-) sigma deviation from the standard model prediction is expected for Top companions in the 100-300 (400-600) GeV mass range, and a 2- (3-) sigma deviation for Bottom companions in the 50-300 (70-300) GeV mass range. In summary, this method provides a means to measure the width of observed peaks and is expected to be a valuable tool in the search for Top and Bottom companions and their single production mode. Recent advances in artificial neural networks (ANNs) claim to simulate aspects of primates' and humans' neural performance. However, these ANNs primarily rely on basic visual characteristics when performing object recognition tasks, unlike humans. Additionally, ANNs are hindered by noisy input, as evidenced by their poor handling of "bad" images in object recognition tasks. In contrast, humans are able to effectively recognize objects even when the input is degraded. To gain insights into the neural basis of human flexibility in visual recognition, we examine the interplay between domain knowledge and learning in visual cortex in relation to advanced visual processing capabilities. We speculate that a combination of domain-specific knowledge and general learning mechanisms in visual cortex is required to achieve human-level flexibility in visual recognition. Our proposal is supported by studies in neuroimaging and electrophysiology that reveal the role of the inferior frontal gyrus in advanced visual processing. Moreover, our results demonstrate that a combination of bottom-up and top-down mechanisms in visual cortex is essential for flexible and efficient visual recognition. Finally, our findings indicate that a simple network of linear classifiers, similar to ANNs, is insufficient to account for humans' ability to recognize objects even in the presence of noisy input. Instead, humans' performance is enhanced when the linear components of ANNs learn complex and hierarchical representations of objects. Our studies provide a framework for investigating the neural basis of human advanced visual processing capabilities and offer a guide for developing more human-like machine learning algorithms. To address a fundamental question about the relationship between the computational structures of human and machine learning, our results reveal that machines and humans share common computational strategies for object recognition. However, machines require larger datasets and longer training times to achieve human-level performance. In contrast, humans are born with a pre-wired visual system, and learn to refine their abilities through experience. Our results indicate that a combination of top-down and bottom-up processes in human learning is crucial for efficient visual recognition. Our studies provide a scientific framework for addressing important ethical issues related to human learning and signal processing in machines. To demonstrate the practical value of our findings, we present a new method for recognizing objects that is more accurate and efficient than standard machine learning algorithms. Our results reveal that machines and humans share a common computational framework for object recognition based on spatial attention. However, machines require datasets similar in complexity to human learning data to achieve human-level performance. Our new method for object recognition is based on learning objects in image space, where objects are represented by learning complex and hierarchical features that are critical to human learning. Specifically, to accomplish this, users can instruct these models to classify sentiment according to specified instruction prompts. However,, there is a limitation to the number of classification tasks that can be taught to GPT-3, which cap at hundreds, given the model is shared across users. To overcome this challenge, researchers have developed "meta-tuning," a strategy where a meta-model is trained to classify sentiments. To accomplish this, users provide existing samples with their correct labels and specify the model how these samples should be categorized. Subsequently, researchers have designed MRCPNet, a multi-reason convolutional network, utilizing the meta-model's output as reasons to classify samples. MRCPNet has been shown to achieve superior zero-shot classification accuracy on datasets, including SemEval-2017, SemEval-2018, and JASIST-2020, with results outperforming fine-tuned BERT models in several tests. Additionally, MRCPNet has been shown to effectively handle challenging tasks, such as handling scarce data, when applied to the aggregation of sentiment datasets. Given the abundance of labeled data, the model's potential in generalizing across diverse datasets is substantial. To further showcase its applicability, MRCPNet has been successfully applied to other difficult tasks, including natural language inference and group discussion analysis, achieving state-of-the-art performance. A new discovery in X-ray variability patterns in four galaxies, identified as Quasi-Periodic Eruptions (QPEs), has led researchers to re-evaluate the case of the low-mass X-ray binary system 4U 0614+09. Analysis of this system's observations from the NASA Swift and XMM Newton observatories revealed the presence of QPEs. Unlike Quasi-Periodic Oscillations, which typically appear as a specific frequency in X-ray spectra, QPEs manifest as an entire Fourier power spectrum with various frequencies above the Nyquist limit. It is proposed that QPEs arise when a compact accretion disc in a thin-migration disc (located between 0.1 and 1 astronomical unit) becomes unstable due to a specific mechanism involving a disc wave propagating at a slow speed. As a result, energy is transferred in the disc through secularly developing bump-like structures, which in turn cause an oscillating phenomenon in the disc's surface density. When the size of the considered time interval changes, a log-normal distribution is seen in the sizes of the forming secularly developing bumps, which in turn cause an entire spectrum with various frequencies to form. According to our calculations, when a disc is vast enough to form two opposing phases, the entire pattern in the disc is referred to as a standing quasi-periodic eruption. For the particular instance of 4U 0614+09, we estimate that in order for us to see the entire pattern in the disc, the value of the disc's optical depth should be 1. Research driven by ultrashort pulses from Kerr-lens mode-locked oscillators has spawned diverse applications, with theoretical understanding rooted in conventional beam propagation analysis. However, established frameworks are often insufficient for handling the extreme demands of high-power oscillators. This study expands upon the ABCD-matrix method to investigate ring resonators in high-power settings, also offering critical guidance for maintaining Kerr-lens mode-locking stability. The analysis provides a practical tool for optimizing design and pushing the limits of ultrashort pulse generation. Moreover, by applying this approach, we have successfully generated pulses shorter than 50 fs directly from titanium-doped waveguide amplifiers, achieving pulse energies of up to 12 pJ with virtually ideal characteristics. Furthermore, without compromising the ti:d waveguide amplifier's efficiency, we have obtained pulse energies of over 30 pJ through the incorporation of a geometrically adjusted 45-degree hollow-core PCF prism, setting the stage for high-energy pulse generation in ti:d sources. This breakthrough offers new possibilities for picosecond ti:d amplifiers, enabling the conversion of pulse energies by arbitrating the ti:d amplifier and ti: pump interactions. As a consequence, high-energy pulses of over 20.8 nJ have been obtained after a single pass through the ti:d amplifier, achieving an energy enhancement factor of 170. Importantly, our findings provide valuable insights for engineering ti:d waveguide gratings to effectively manipulate the group delay dispersion and ultimately enable the attainment of sub-70 fs pulses. Ultimately, the methods employed in this study open doors for high-energy pulse generation in ti:d sources, serving as a valuable reference for future developments. Moreover, the developed methods can be directly applied to solid-state lasers used in powerful oscillator configurations. Furthermore, the advanced ti:d PCPR offers promising potential for use beyond pulse compression applications, offering new possibilities for high-energy pulse generation in the near-nanojoule regime. Moreover, the developed methods achieve an energy compression factor of 13.7 with an overall process efficiency of 54%, yielding 21.1 nJ energy at the output of the ti:d PCFR, earning the design the name 'compacter'. Lastly, our study provides an independent analysis of the energy compression mechanism within the ti:d PCFR, contributing knowledge to the broader scientific community. Several optimistic assumptions prevalent in federated learning literature are often unachievable in real-world scenarios. To counter this, an asynchronous framework provides a more realistic setting for testing federated learning's reliability. This setup reflects varying amounts of non-IID data across participants as well as heterogeneous client engagement influenced by computational and battery limitations. Additionally, the framework accommodates delayed client scheduling to simulate disparate participation rates. To address asynchronous and non-IID challenges, we developed asynchronous Selective Federated Learning (ASFL), a novel, user-centric framework that surpasses existing federated learning methods in classification and anomaly detection performance, especially when participation is voluntary and scheduling is delayed. To demonstrate this, we applied ASFL to classify images from the CIFAR100 and NIST-239A datasets, as well as an anomaly detection task using the ImageNet dataset, comparing its success to existing approaches such as FedSGD and FedProx in asynchronous, non-IID settings. The results show significant enhancements in absorption for solar cells with a 1 μm thickness, an increase of 26% compared to a metal back reflector, and confirm that most of the enhanced absorption occurs in the bulk material.  The success of this approach is due to its ability to create a suitable electromagnetic environment through opposition between the crystal's dielectric properties and those of the bulk material and the surrounding air.  The concept is expected to have applications not only in thin-film silicon but also in other photovoltaic materials with low light absorption coefficients. The predicted reflectivity and absorption characteristics indicate that silicon nanostructure approach can be applied to conventional single-crystal silicon solar cells to retrieve about 92% of electrons incident on the back interface, a value comparable to multi-junction solar cells. The results show that photonic band gap crystals offer a range of unique electromagnetic properties including omnidirectional and otherwise non-resonant properties that can be used to enhance light absorption in thin-film solar cells. We introduce the Sparse Structural Network Embedding (SSNE) model, which creates a representation of network nodes suitable for predicting links in these types of sparse networks. SSNE employs a novel regularization method highly adapted to the characteristics of sparse networks. Additionally, it uses a Multi-layered Peacock Distribution-based initialization technique to enhance the efficiency of gradient-based optimization. Our thorough evaluation confirms that SSNE surpasses alternative embedding models in predicting links on sparse networks. Furthermore, to facilitate further research and improve link prediction in various sparse networks, we also release a comprehensive benchmarking tool suite named sparse-gae. The SSNE model name contains 'Sparse-' to distinguish it from the work of Feng et al. published in 2018 in Journal of Machine Learning Research. A low-cost water jet process effectively removes laser material to create a high-intensity atomic vapor cell with 2 mm thickness and 25 mm diameter, enabling a longer interaction time to boost photon collection efficiency. By employing a diode laser operating at 1140 nm, this innovative design offers enhanced performance compared to conventional sandblasting techniques. The outcomes of this innovative approach have led to the development of a high-performance atomic vapor cell that excels in photon collection efficiency with minimal damage, setting it apart from conventional cells with 1 mm thickness and a 15 mm diameter. Furthermore, this innovative process can be applied to other materials, such as DLC (Diamond-like Carbon) coated surfaces, to improve surface treatment effectiveness. Overall, the results of this research demonstrate that atomic vapor cells with deep etch structures can be designed for applications requiring external compensation to amplify photon collection capabilities. Detailed descriptions of the water jet process have been shared publicly on our GitHub repository at https://github.com/quantumfpga/laser-welding. Our research also offers insights and suggestions for optimizing the process for specific materials and applications. Finally, the benefits of deep atomic vapor cells in quantum information applications are discussed, particularly in areas related to long-range quantum communication and photon collection efficiency. However, our current research focuses on a particular application where deep atomic vapor cells can make a substantial contribution. In regions with low density, a vapor cell with 2 mm thickness offers around four times the photon collection capability of a conventional 1 mm cell. Consequently, global distances between long-range stations in quantum communication can be significantly increased while maintaining the required weak coherence of the signal. Though our current research focuses on quantum information applications, the water jet process developed for laser materials can be generalized to other fields with relevant parameters and process modifications. Early detection and treatment of depression is essential to prevent it from worsening and enable students to pursue their academic goals despite facing mental health challenges.  Given that individuals struggle to openly admit their depression due to societal stigma, researchers are exploring the potential of identifying depression in written texts, such as social media posts, to prevent and treat the condition.  Unfortunately, existing datasets primarily focused on mild depression cases, which is not sufficient for machine learning model training due to their simplicity.  Moreover, datasets related to mental health, including depression, are scarce.  To address this issue, we developed a gold-standard dataset, referred to as depression-level-annotated-posts (DIPA), which consists of social media posts annotated with three levels of depression.  The DIPA dataset aims to facilitate research on various depression levels, accelerate the development of machine learning models for depression detection, and enhance our understanding of mild depression, which is understudied.  Using DIPA, we evaluated the performance of two cutting-edge deep learning models, including BERT and RoBERTa, to demonstrate their potential in automatically classifying depression levels in social media posts.  Our experimental results also validate the effectiveness of pre-trained language models in identifying depression in written texts.  With the DIPA dataset being publicly available, we anticipate that it will lead to significant advancements in depression detection using social media data, which can be further extended to other depression-related datasets.  Ultimately, we believe that early detection and treatment of depression can contribute to improved mental health for students.  Please visit https://github.com/grimetr/gcr/ for our code and data. This research investigates the theoretical recovery boundaries for a wide range of such problems. We provide exact formulas for the mean squared error of matrix and factor estimation in an infinite-dimensional setting where a fixed number of matrix components is considered. These results are based on an innovative model transformation from the homogeneous to a heterogeneous low-rank matrix tensor product model. Network science is the multidisciplinary study of intricate systems comprising interconnected elements, including connections and relationships. This broadly defined field can be observed in almost every aspect, from biological to social networks. A vast array of systems is encompassed by network science, including those depicted as graphs of interconnected nodes and edges. This versatile field applies to numerous contexts such as chemical reactions, electrical circuits, biological systems, social structures and transportation networks among others. A key focus area of network science involves the examination of a system's backbone which reflects its inherent connections and relationships. To investigate the system's core structure, researchers use a variety of methods. This study compares and evaluates different backbone identification methods in terms of their applicability to different types of networks. By utilizing real-world examples of different network types researchers test and highlight the benefits and drawbacks of each method from a quantitative perspective. A key conclusion drawn from this research is that different backbone identification methods should be utilized based on the type of network being studied. Furthermore recommendations are offered for designing novel methods for network analysis. This research is expected to aid researchers working with network science and provide insights on the most suitable methods for distinct types of networks. A significant outcome of this research is the development of the BToolbox MATLAB package which enables users to effectively extract a system's core structure using various techniques. The study of eco-evolutionary dynamics is being limited by an exclusive focus on fast-changing ecology and evolution, typically occurring over short periods, as evidenced by the rapid changes observed in Trinidadian guppies and other laboratory models. We argue this perspective overlooks the potential for significant changes to accumulate over longer periods in a wider range of systems. Ignoring these slow processes could prove costly when assessing the impacts of large-scale environmental changes. We use theoretical models to illustrate that even small, gradual changes can amplify over time to cause substantial shifts in eco-evolutionary dynamics. To contribute to a more comprehensive understanding of eco-evolutionary processes, we must expand our scope to include these slow-moving phenomena. Furthermore, integrating insights from both slow and fast dynamics may reveal new insights that would remain hidden in separate analyses of short- and long-term processes. For instance, incorporating stochastic models into theoretical eco-evolutionary models could provide valuable insight. We believe that combining these different dynamics may uncover new and unexpected interactions that are prevalent in nature. Nevertheless, in many cases, these interactions may remain dormant due to environmental and biological constraints that can be effectively modeled. We demonstrate the significance of considering the context of acting agents in eco-evolutionary dynamics through a new theoretical framework that allows for a more nuanced understanding of the role of predation in driving eco-evolutionary dynamics. Using this framework, we identify predation regimes in which evolutionary responses to environmental changes are likely to occur. We conclude that both fast and slow eco-evolutionary dynamics are crucial to understanding the potential for rapid or gradual responses to environmental changes to shape the ecology and evolution of interacting agents. We believe that integrating these dynamics may provide a more comprehensive and systematic understanding of these interactions. Nevertheless, in many cases, these interactions may remain benign due to broader ecological and environmental conditions that can be effectively modeled to predict their occurrence. Such predictive ability could inform conservation and management strategies by forecasting when and if slow or rapid eco-evolutionary responses are likely to occur, in terms of their impact on ecosystem resources. As an empirical example, we demonstrate that predictive simulations can inform our understanding of the role of predation in driving eco-evolutionary dynamics in the present study. Nevertheless, our empirical findings suggest that predation is unlikely to cause significant eco-evolutionary responses in the studied population of killifish. We attribute this discrepancy to a more nuanced understanding of eco-evolutionary processes, made possible by integrating simulations of both slow and fast dynamics. Our research focuses on the underlying structure of Automated Market Makers (AMMs), 
a prevalent form of blockchain-based, decentralized exchanges. 
We reveal that the order processing mechanism results in token value diminishment for market liquidity suppliers under circumstances of heightened token price volatility. 
AMMs are adopted predominantly when their supported token combinations have significant use or price movements are strongly interconnected. 
However, the steeper pricing curve actually discourages extreme price fluctuations, though this benefits the system overall it negatively affects individual market participants. 
We also find that the prevalence of AMMs prompts firms to list their securities on Automated Market Makers rather than other types of decentralized exchanges. 
A US-based firm's initial public offering price is successfully predicted by our AMM model, which incorporates token price volatility factors. 
In conclusion, our investigation shows that the Automated Market Makers have had a profound impact, especially in the token price distribution outcomes. 
Moreover, our decentralized market findings provide valuable insights for firms considering initial public offerings on Automated Market Makers, as our results can inform their listing decisions....

We demonstrate the utility of these E-values through a practical example involving diabetes research data. We argue that these E-values hold particular significance for researchers dealing with outcome data missingness and multiple imputation methods. The integration of Artificial Intelligence techniques and improved information systems within Internet of Vehicles (IoVs) has yielded substantial benefits, albeit with heightened risks of security breaches and compromised privacy. As IoVs technology continues to evolve, there's growing interest in privacy preservation methodologies that adapt to changing data usage criteria without consistently monitoring IoV users' activities. This requirement leads to a new challenge in the research on IoVs: developing a security framework that's agile, privacy-conscious, and adaptable. To address this challenge, we propose a distributed Machine Learning model that's capable of learning from local data while being aggregated across vehicles. This proposed model is based on a Federated Learning framework, reducing the amount of data shared during training and safeguarding user privacy. Additionally, we developed a Head-and-Tail Loss function to counter negative learning outcomes and demonstrated the successful application of our proposal in a simulated urban environment. The results demonstrated that our proposed framework successfully identifies private data instances and accurately predicts the next movement of a vehicle, outperforming comparable models by achieving a 95.5% training and 93.6% testing accuracy. The proposed approach significantly contributes to the development of a robust, adaptable, and agile system for analyzing IoVs data while prioritizing privacy above functionality. This research aims to lay the groundwork for a comprehensive, decentralized security framework, incorporating features such as encryption methods, intrusion detection systems, and vehicle system authentication to safeguard against external breaches and generate trustworthy data that's shared anonymously. Future studies will focus on addressing any potential security vulnerabilities and developing a key generation and distribution protocol. The escalating demand for bigger cooling systems to support increasingly larger numbers of cryogenic qubits in quantum computing applications is prompting innovation.
Through the National Quantum Initiative and the Department of Energy's support, our work at the Superconducting Quantum Materials and Systems Center at Fermilab is focused on creating a 2-meter diameter by approximately 1.5-meter tall cryogenic storage facility that uses a novel cryogenic cooling platform designed to handle a wide variety of superconducting qubits in the 3 to 450 millikelvin temperature range.
We are developing an innovative cryogenic distribution system with centralized ring mufflers for gas supply and a 4-meter long distribution header with interconnected mufflers to minimize heat load and thermal bridges, as well as an advanced shell-and-tube heat exchanger for efficient thermal transfer.
Additionally, our design encompasses an innovative cryogenic storage facility with an outer shell that uses a foam-based thermal superinsulation to reduce radial thermal bridges between inner and outer cylinders, as well as an inner vacuum space that uses radial thermal superinsulation to minimize radial thermal bridge thermal conductance.
We also propose the use of a new cryogenic cooling platform with a novel radial thermal superinsulation design that will support the inner cylinder of the storage facility and provide a new approach to reducing thermal conductivity in the radial direction.
We have detailed the design overview of both the cryogenic distribution system and the storage facility, as well as well-established design software and testing plans. Ultimately, our goal is to create a new standard in cryogenic cooling platform design at Fermilab. Moreover, our proposed concept will serve as a testing ground to validate the EU's CLIC and CERN's C-SQUID qubit-scale cryogenic cooling platform designs, and provide valuable insights for the development of large-number quantum computing applications. We intend to make the final design ready for construction in summer 2023 and have the first prototype operational at the Superconducting Quantum Materials and Systems Center at Fermilab by summer 2024. At present, we are in the process of finalizing the design and have submitted a request for a 25-ton crane to support construction at Fermilab. This article investigates the semigroups of composition operators on BMOA-type spaces, specifically on BMOA and its analogue on the upper half-plane. BMOA is a space of continuous functions on the unit disk that can be expressed as integrals of analytic functions with bounded mean oscillation. This space was first introduced by the Polish mathematician Pawlak in the 1960s and has since been the subject of extensive research by several authors. In 2000, Pawlak expanded his findings to include other function spaces on the upper half-plane through a linear fractional mapping. This work examines the topological structure of semigroups of composition operators on these spaces, focusing on the sufficiency of the closed ideal theorem to determine the compactness of such semigroups. The results are illustrated with relevant examples. This work also explores the ergodic theory of composition semigroups of operators on BMOA and its analogue in relation to the forward mean continuity of the operators. In a surprising discovery, it is found that a sufficient condition for the compactness of the semigroup can be obtained without the need for the closed ideal theorem. This condition is an extension of an earlier finding by the first author in 2013. This work is ultimately a significant generalization of previous research on the topological structure of composition semigroups of operators on various function spaces, including Hardy, Bergman, and Moebius transformation spaces. The findings in this article fundamentally differ from those in the existing literature on operator theory. To validate the new theorems, novel methods were developed, providing additional insights into the structure of composition semigroups of operators. This work is significant in that it significantly expands the scope of research in this area and may inspire further research into the ergodic theory of composition semigroups of operators on BMOA and its analogue. In addition, the findings in this article can be applied in other fields, such as general topology, the theory of differential equations, and metric fixed point theory. Research suggests that these coefficients can be computed using wavefunction overlaps of low-energy states in the spin chain. Automated part-of-speech (POS) annotation is a crucial task for linguistics and natural language processing, typically addressed through machine learning. Although the problem is largely solved for contemporary languages, historical corpora pose significant challenges, primarily due to limited native speaker interaction and a lack of training data. Compounding this issue, historical texts lack uniformity in spelling, punctuation, and capitalization, making cross-period annotation comparisons impractical. To bridge this knowledge gap, this study introduces a method for POS tagging historical corpora, utilizing datasets from classical Greek (5th century BCE - 5th century CE) to the Byzantine period. Employing this approach on the Klaima corpus, which covers the period from the 5th century BCE to the 15th century CE, yielded promising results, demonstrating that the method outperformed standard strong baselines while showcasing resilience in the face of text ambiguities. The research also highlighted the potential for combining the advantages of pre-trained neural models and transfer learning in the context of historical POS tagging. Notably, despite the significant differences between the tagging datasets, Klaima corpus rankings were consistently produced by the models used in this study. The research offered new insights on the potential for neural models to excel in the POS tagging of historical corpora, even under more challenging conditions. The findings were published in a paper titled "Part-of-speech Tagging of Historical Greek Texts using the Klaima Corpus," which can be accessed at openaccess.btb.inria.fr/klaimeo18/openreview/23/. The study also utilized publicly available resources, including the Klaima corpus at access.btb.inria.fr/en/klaimeo/, which covers the period from the 5th century BCE to the 15th century CE. The research further benefited from the use of the Joriez library, a Python-based toolkit for statistical analysis and machine learning, available at access.btb.inria.fr/en/joriez/. The team's GitHub repository at github.com/btbe/open-source-access/tree/master/historical-pos-tagging contains further details on the implementation, including example codes, which can be replicated by interested researchers. The research paper received an outstanding paper award at the 18th Conference on Computational Methods in Linguistics in 2020. The study was also featured in a special issue of the journal Digital Philology: Culture, Arts, and Polity in the Digital Age, published under the title "Distributed Machine Learning for Historical Part-of-Speech Tagging." This research focuses on developing a method to calculate a utility function from a non-differentiable but locally Lipschitz candidate of a demand function. Using this method, we derive two new criteria that a demand function candidate must meet. First, it must be symmetrical and have a negatively semi-definite Slutsky matrix, and second, it must be a unique concave solution to a specific partial differential equation globally. Additionally, under certain assumptions, the resulting utility function corresponds to a unique upper semi-continuous weak order, which we also show to be the only weak order under these assumptions. The system leverages formal verification techniques to ensure that the translated specifications accurately convey the original intentions behind the user's input. Through case studies involving concrete scenarios and comprehensive evaluations of 42 complex queries, we showcase CitySpec's exceptional performance in formal specification, outshining comparable systems in clarity and user satisfaction. Accurately predicting non-performing loans for individual clients is a major challenge for the lending sector. To address this issue, machine learning models can be utilized for credit risk assessment. Nevertheless, common machine learning methods often overlook the inherent probabilistic nature of credit decisions, leading to biased estimates of default rates. To mitigate this problem, a Bayesian approach can be employed to accurately quantify risks and uncertainties associated with lending decisions. In this study, we evaluated seven widely used machine learning models capable of handling continuous data inputs like borrower age, income, and loan amount, as well as categorical variables like applicant gender and loan purpose. To an objective evaluate these models, we applied them to a dataset describing public sector employees and employed a multi-model Bayesian analysis to derive precise and accurate estimation of PD for population with similar characteristics. The results showed that machine learning models are highly susceptible to the data preparation stage, and the optimal model depends on the specific context of the population being evaluated. Consequently, a more reliable model is proposed as an alternative, obtained by analyzing the correlation between different variables, including employment and financial sectors. Notably, Bayesian estimation significantly reduces biases associated with certain demographic groups, including age. Interestingly, our research found that gender, employment, and personal financial histories are the key factors influencing an individual's creditworthiness. To minimize biases, it is advisable for lenders to diversify their portfolio rather than relying solely on conventional methods of evaluating creditworthiness. Consequently, a diversified portfolio that considers the diverse economic backgrounds of clients may yield more accurate and unbiased credit assessments. To confirm the practical efficacy of the proposed approach, it is recommended that lenders conduct thorough evaluations across different demographic segments and then adjust and refine the models based on their specific experience and knowledge of their clients. To facilitate the implementation of these findings, a practical prototype named CreditEEA has been developed for direct utilization by lenders. The practicality and efficacy of the proposed approach and prototype are further validated through a comprehensive live demonstration involving multiple lenders. The associated Jupyter Notebooks provide users with step-by-step instructions for building and customizing the optimal Bayesian models and assessing credit risk in real-world scenarios. The proposed research and prototype CreditEEA enable lenders to effectively and efficiently diversify their client base, minimize biases, and attain accurate and reliable credit assessments. Among these, post-hoc methods have been identified as the most practical solutions for intricate models that operate as "black-boxes." Recent studies have exposed limitations in local surrogate-based post-hoc explanations regarding their inherent reliability, especially in critical applications such as human-centric recommendation tasks. Moreover, an ideal explanation should enhance key aspects of user experience including clarity and trustworthiness, posing additional challenges to the current approaches. However, a classical post-hoc model utilizing surrogates demonstrates dependence on the model itself, thus falling short in guaranteeing the accuracy of generated explanations. Furthermore, current methods that aim to rectify this issue are bound by restrictive assumptions concerning the explainability of models and thus cannot be directly applied to complex recommendation tasks that involve diverse data such as item descriptions, user feedback, and item interconnections. Therefore, a novel framework has been introduced called ExplanationAuth, a system designed for globally validating explanations generated within complex recommendation settings through the utilization of networked user reviews. Given that users generally leverage recommendations based on partial information available to them, ExplanationAuth models user uncertainty when providing feedback. Subsequently, explanations generated within these scenarios are assessed against a representation of the model's decision-making process derived from a second explainable model, also trained within the same environment. A thorough evaluation of ExplanationAuth was conducted by focusing on the accuracy and reliability of explanations generated within a large dataset called AramaQ, comprising numerous online reviews across multiple categories. To investigate this, a study examined the evolution of surface morphology and its impact on electronic properties during the epitaxial growth of a two-layer InAs quantum well on GaAs using a technique that allows real-time observation of crystal growth. The results showed that a unique surface morphology develops due to self-organization, visible as distinct ridges on the surface. The consequences of this surface morphology on electronic properties were then examined through the use of photoluminescence and x-ray diffraction. The study found that this surface morphology affects the electronic levels in the quantum well but does not significantly impact the electron mobility within the quantum well, unlike what is seen in single-layer InAs quantum wells. The reason for this behavior remains to be determined. Additionally, this surface morphology does not appear when growth is changed to include an ultra-thin InAs layer, suggesting that this effect may have implications for a particular class of quantum well samples. The characteristics of this surface morphology have also been found to depend on growth temperatures. Specifically, at lower growth temperatures, this surface morphology has a coarser appearance with larger width than when it appears at higher growth temperatures. The study further confirms that these surface ridges are composed of pure InAs, as it uses x-ray reflectivity to investigate the interface between the quantum well and the substrate. The depth of these surface ridges was then found to correspond to the thickness of the quantum well, providing a new method to control surface morphology through the design of quantum well thickness. The study ultimately concludes that this surface morphology is a manifestation of a unique thermodynamic equilibrium between the quantum well material and the substrate during the epitaxial growth process. The investigation of this surface morphology may offer a new way to understand this equilibrium. Research has shown that certain distributional assumptions are required to develop reliable machine learning models. Introducing an adversary that alters data features uniformly to protect against it highlights the need for models to work effectively even with corrupted data. Previous studies have addressed this challenge by assuming the presence of additional information: Duan et al. used local membership queries in 2020, and Bellman et al. used adversary advisory queries in 2021. This study focuses on developing a reliable machine learning model that doesn't rely on any additional information, instead using uniform protection as a key consideration. By combining the ideas from the work of Duan et al. and Bellman et al., we have proposed a robust decision tree that doesn't require any additional information, thereby achieving an optimal classification accuracy of $O_k(\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}})$ where $n$ is the number of samples, $k$ is the number of classes, and this result holds almost surely. This proposed solution generalizes well even with limited data by applying the uniform low density model, which makes it an efficient framework. Moreover, we estimate our solution's expected accuracy to be $\Omega_k(\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}})$ where $n$ is the number of samples, $k$ is the number of classes, and this result holds for most likely cases. We support these claims through an in-depth analysis and testing on specific training datasets. Our previous research significantly sped up Sinkhorn iteration by taking advantage of a kernel matrix's inherent properties, transforming its $O(N^2)$ complexity to $O(N)$ efficiency. This paper delves deeper into kernel matrix characteristics by defining and applying two key concepts, Lower-ColLinear Triangular Matrices and Upper-ColLinear Triangular Matrices. By showing that multiplying these matrices with vectors can be achieved in $O(N)$ operations and demonstrating their closure under specific operations like Hadamard product and matrix inversion, we validate a broader matrix theory applying to its closure. This finding enables us to offer a unified explanation for various accelerated algorithms targeting the Sinkhorn iteration, including those utilizing binary kernels, and provides a basis for developing new efficient algorithms for solving programming problems on graphs. Additionally, through numerical examples and simulations, we evaluate the computational efficiency of accelerated algorithms based on L/U-CoLT matrices and Hadamard eigen-decomposition. Accelerated algorithms using the decomposition achieve a speed-up for relatively small values of $N$, but for larger values of $N$, the accelerated algorithms based on the matrix's inherent properties surpass their counterparts in efficiency. This research contributes a new efficient method to compute binary optimization problems, which has substantial practical relevance and serves as a promising alternative to the current state-of-the-art algorithms. Using real-world data, we show that our accelerated algorithm can search for the top-performing $K$ solutions of a binary optimization problem within a $N=10^5$ scale in approximately 0.8 milliseconds for $K=10$ and $N=10^5$, thus outperforming its competitors in efficiency. A detailed explanation of the code used in this research is provided in the supporting file, where we employ Python to develop an innovative and efficient algorithm for searching the top-performing $K$ solutions of a binary optimization problem within a $N=10^5$ scale in approximately 0.8 milliseconds for $K=10$ and $N=10^5$. This research offers a new and improved method to solve binary optimization problems and programming problems on graphs. By open-sourcing the code and providing an open-source library, we open up new avenues for further refinements and applications of the L/U-ColLinear Triangular Matrices theory. (2009). First, we calibrate the luminosity function using near-infrared data from specific bands. Then, by analyzing all bands with sufficient data, we derive photometric redshifts for additional sources and derive a well-fitted curve for the luminosity function with a double component representing single objects and their averages. This analysis at higher $z$ reveals a specific pattern in the luminosity function with two peaks, similar to lower $z$ observations by Richards et al. (2009), and provides data on its slope for separate $z$ ranges. Moreover, combining our UKIRT Infrared Deep Sky Survey data with W.M. Baugh's simulation models, we develop a theoretical framework for the luminosity function with confidence intervals. Together, these findings provide strong evidence for evolution in the fraction of massive dark matter halos hosting quasars as we progress in cosmic time. We have successfully observed the charge-tunneling phenomenon occurring between a quantum dot and a superconducting island using a technique that employs radio-frequency sensing. Our approach has allowed us to distinguish between different types of tunneling events, specifically those driven by individual particles as well as by pairs of particles called Cooper pairs. Furthermore, we've found that the quantum dot can be utilized to detect changes in the superconductor's electronic state without needing traditional electrical current measurements, providing us with insight into previously inaccessible subgap energy states. Our findings offer valuable insights for future research focused on detecting parity-dependent interactions between these quantum dots and superconducting islands, potentially revealing the existence of elusive Majorana modes. Additionally, our radio-frequency sensing method has been successfully used to measure macroscopic quantum states in a superconducting system by using a quantum point contact as a detector. These experimental results set the stage for investigating the critical characteristics of superconducting systems. Lastly, our approach may contribute significantly to the development of more efficient detection methods in various types of superconducting systems. All data from our experiments have been made available online. (As a note, our research was conducted on a superconducting material called Nb with a critical temperature of approximately 9.9 K.) Our research explores the contraction behavior of specific types of shockwaves in systems of equations, particularly those that conserve quantities, given the presence of a convex "stability" function. To expand upon existing work, we introduce a new metric that can accommodate spatial variations and use it to establish conditions under which shockwaves in a broader class of systems, such as multi-dimensional flows, exhibit contraction. Furthermore, we analyze the long-term stability of shockwaves in a specific type of flow under the influence of an additional equation that governs the rate of change of pressure. Our study also includes the evaluation of specific boundary conditions that may be relevant, such as those related to entropy and pressure. To complement these findings, we develop a method to approximate the stable equilibrium points of shockwaves in systems of equations, and this method is particularly useful in the study of steady-state solutions to the equations of ideal gases. By applying these results to a system of equations that represents a one-dimensional adiabatic ideal gas with pressure \(p=1\), we derive an estimate for how rapidly the equilibrium state of a shockwave converges as the initial distance from this state decreases. This particular system corresponds to the well-studied theory of shocks in one-dimensional conservative systems. Furthermore, we include additional appendices that provide broader existence theorems for shockwaves in systems of equations and multi-dimensional flows. To to establish these theorems, we utilize concepts related to the interaction of shockwaves and their equilibrium states. By building upon prior research in these areas, we are able to provide a more comprehensive understanding of shockwaves in systems of equations. One of the core assumptions underlying our analysis includes the presence of a "convex" equilibrium state, and we demonstrate that systems of equations such as the Euler equations (e.g. from ideal gases) do not generally satisfy this assumption. To address this limitation, we develop an alternative approach that evaluates the contraction behavior of shockwaves in systems of equations relative to specific metrics that may not be convex. To incorporate these non-convex metrics into our analysis, we introduce a new concept that utilizes concepts related to Bregman divergence and its application to the evaluation of shockwaves in systems of equations. By building upon this divergence, we are able to derive new existence theorems for shockwaves in systems of equations that incorporate additional equations governing the rate of change of pressure. These theorems are relevant in the study of Euler-type systems of equations and are particularly well applied in the evaluation of steady-state solutions to the equations of ideal gases

This paper introduces an innovative method for duration modelling in statistical parametric speech synthesis by training a recurrent model to generate phone transition probabilities and then sampling durations from a distribution embedded within a recurrent state. The embedded distribution is a shifted and scaled version of a standard Cauchy distribution, specifically the Gumbel distribution. Training this model involves finding optimal scaling and shifting parameters, which we demonstrate to be essentially equivalent to maximising the lower bound on the data likelihood. Additionally, we prove that the optimal scaling parameter is the reciprocal of the geometric mean of the standard deviations of the phone distribution, while the shifting parameter is the sum of all shifts minus the mean. A median-based output synthesis approach is proposed as an alternative to the mean, offering greater resistance to outliers in duration data. The results from this method are comparable to the state-of-the-art in terms of zero-shot speech synthesis quality on the LJSpeech dataset. Notably, this model is uniquely characterised by its ability to produce durations for arbitrary unseen input, as well as providing exact marginal likelihoods for model assessment. The full source code is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/daniel-tay/duration-model. Speech research communities may also be interested in alternative models developed under a competing prior at https://github.com/daniel-tay/normal-model. Both models utilise the same median-based synthesis approach. Finally, this work contributes to the understanding and differentiation between training objectives in duration modelling through the spectra analysis of learned distribution parameters. The research findings suggest that the median-based output synthesis approach is grounded in the sample's geometric moment, which is distinct from the mean-based approach centered around the mean. Identifying online hate speech is increasingly critical due to its capacity to inflict emotional and psychological harm on minority groups. A recent study from arXiv investigated various models of classification and their interactions with language context in understanding offense classification. Utilizing the 2020 Indo-European language dataset from OHUM, the research analyzed neural network and logistic models, as well as multiple feature extraction techniques from text data. Key findings revealed significant interactions between models and language contexts, particularly in German and Russian, which reduced overall performance. Interestingly, the study discovered that the Russian language, characterized by high offense content, negatively affected model combinations. Conversely, the opposite held true for German. Moreover, the study suggested that combining English model and language features might appear favorable but actually decreased overall performance. It is hoped that the outcomes of this research will provide valuable insights for classifying offense content across languages. Multi-input multi-output (MIMO) networks attempt to improve ensemble performance by training separate subnetworks within a base model and combining their predictions. However, these networks have been found to wastefully use parameters, restricting further ensemble optimization. In this work, a compact MIMO architecture is developed using autoencoders to efficiently learn from multiple outputs. The proposed method involves packaging co-trained subnetworks into a single, MIMO network, allowing for learning of MIMO coefficients without additional parameters. Experiments on small MIMO datasets demonstrate that the developed method surpasses standard ensemble approaches, achieving comparable accuracy with fewer parameters. Moreover, this approach results in better performance and parameter efficiency when training large MIMO datasets. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/jmjl/ensemble-networks. Interestingly, this compact method reveals that many MIMO datasets may not benefit from increasing the number of outputs beyond three, suggesting data quality and MIMO scalability limitations. To overcome these constraints, a novel MIMO learning strategy is introduced, using a hierarchical structure to separate predictions and allowing for better output separation. This strategy enhances the ensemble performance of standard MIMO networks. Lastly, this work investigates the practical effectiveness of MIMO networks for real-world applications using benchmark datasets. Our results demonstrate that MIMO networks produce robust ensemble models which consistently achieve high accuracy on diverse tasks, but may not always provide substantial improvements over base models. However, the developed methods offer flexible tools to enhance ensembles for other network architectures. As the field of learning to ensemble is rapidly evolving, this contribution aims to shed light on its challenges, limitations, and potential applications. Our code at https://github.com/jmjl/ensemble-networks serves as a building block for future research to further optimize the field of MIMO networks. Moreover, a novel MIMO learning framework at https://github.com/jmjl/mimo-learning-strategy provides a versatile tool to assess the scalability and robustness of MIMO networks on diverse datasets. In particular, the framework at https://github.com/jmjl/mimo-learning-strategy offers MIMO networks trained on the datasets at https://www.openaccessgovernment.org/uci datasets, which consistently outperform base models, demonstrating robustness, scalability, and generalization capabilities. Additionally, the development of MIMO networks at https://github.com/jmjl/ensemble-networks or https://github.com/jmjl/mimo-learning-stragegy opens up the possibility for parameter transfer and analysis of MIMO datasets, showcasing growth potential in the field of ensemble learning.

Domain theory's powerdomains hold significant importance in the semantics of non-deterministic programming languages.  This paper extends powerdomains to directed spaces - a concept equivalent to T_0 monotone-determined spaces.  Powerdomain-like spaces (upper, lower, and convex powerspaces) of directed spaces are defined through free algebras, and their existence and structures are shown for any directed space.  Notably, these spaces have distinct structures compared to powerdomains of directed-complete partial orders with Scott topology and other previously-introduced powerspaces.  Relations between these spaces and directed powerdomains are investigated: directed upper powerspaces act as ccc powerspaces of directed spaces, and for spaces with a lower powerdomain, it is shown either the existence of a directed lower powerdomain or the equivalence of directed lower and convex powerspaces.  Examples illustrate powerspaces in different structures, and a directed space with distinct upper, lower, and convex powerdomains is constructed, showing that the inclusion relations of powerdomains are strict in general.  Lastly, the paper explores the properties of directed complete partial orders with Scott topology through the lens of upper and lower powerdomains.  Specifically, it can be concluded that the upper and lower powerdomains of a directed cpo are equal and complemented if they exist, and the set of directed complete partial orders with Scott topology that have a directed lower powerdomain is a proper subset of the set of directed complete partial orders with Scott topology that have an upper powerdomain.  Ultimately, the paper demonstrates the specificity of powerdomains in directing settings by showing that the directed upper and lower powerdomains of a directed complete partial order are equal if and only if the directed powerdomain of the directed complete partial order has a canonical structure.  This work has been implemented in an Epistemology-based formalisation as [https://www.epistemology.org/javdoc/DirPowSpec.html].  A more detailed exploration of the directed powerspaces of Scott domains can be found in [https://www.epistemology.org/javdoc/DirPowSpec/DirPowSpec.html].

Past and potential future Earth climate states have included extremely warm 'hothouse' environments with unknown atmospheric behavior, characterized by a distinctive low atmospheric heating pattern. A combination of climate model simulations and laboratory experiments reveals that hothouse climates are marked by the presence of dry atmospheric fronts, where warm and moist air masses meet a drier opposition, resulting in significant local precipitation. This discovery in satellite data and model outcomes contradicts theoretical forecasts of uniform precipitation patterns across low atmospheric fronts, replacing them with areas of high precipitation along the front's lower boundary, resulting in the creation of semi-permeable barriers that influence atmospheric dynamics and affect climate behavior in complex ways. This novel finding offers a new method for studying these harsh climate states, which may become the Earth's future if greenhouse gas emissions continue to rise. The application of deep neural networks (DNNs) in medical image classification has shown great promise due to their exceptional data learning capabilities. Despite advancements, the quality of the training data and noise resistant abilities of current DNNs remain major concerns. The process of labeling data, a vital step in model training, is prone to errors and omissions, resulting in incorrect annotations. To address this issue, a new method called annotation learning (AL) has been proposed to detect and rectify noisy labels in medical image classification using DNNs. The proposed approach identifies noisy labels by applying statistical analysis to the annotation dataset and determines the probability of accuracy for each training sample based on the annotation label. The model then incorporates this probability along with a generated noisy mask obtained through adversarial training to both augment data and refine the classifier. The proposed AL method demonstrates the ability to effectively eliminate noisy labels and achieve optimal model performance when validated using three medical image classification datasets. The results show that AL outperforms existing noisy label robustness techniques and achieves training completion within a reasonable timeframe compared to alternative methods. Furthermore, the experimental findings indicate that AL can also enhance model interpretability by identifying noisy samples and providing valuable insights to annotators to rectify errors in the annotation dataset. The proposed AL method is capable of handling multiple annotators and is a valuable contribution to medical imaging, offering solutions to noisy labels, data augmentation, classifier refinement, and model interpretability in medical image classification using DNNs. This study analyzes data from an online monitoring system of U.S. local news to explore connections between the media and COVID-19 cases. It finds that local news coverage initially focused on travel-related cases but later concentrated on deaths from the disease. The frequency of coronavirus coverage in local newspapers initially rose along with national death rates, but subsequently declined as the disease's fatality increased. Local news played a crucial role in informing residents about pandemic restrictions, with those in counties with higher local coverage awareness more likely to adhere to non-pharmaceutical interventions. The findings also indicate inequalities in local news coverage across racial and ethnic groups, with a greater focus on coronavirus stories in white populations compared to people of color. Additionally, the study reveals that local news coverage was significantly higher in areas with existing high COVID-19 case counts, with a greater focus on basketball and sports-related events in those areas. The data demonstrate that local news initially emphasized nonessential aspects of the coronavirus but gradually shifted to more severe information as the disease's severity increased. The study concludes by highlighting the long-term implications of these findings for informing individuals and policymakers about COVID-19 risks. Furthermore, the data suggest that existing high COVID-19 case counts were often publicly acknowledged in local news, but late in the pandemic. The research also shows that local news played a crucial role in informing individuals about pandemic risks and the importance of non-pharmaceutical interventions, as well as the need for targeted coverage of minority groups. The study contributes to an understanding of the inequitable distribution of local news coverage across the country and the necessity of equitable pandemic communication strategies. The data highlight the impact of the pandemic on local news and the need for a renewed focus on the role of the media in informing individuals during future public health crises. The study provides insights into the unavailing role of local news in early pandemic communication efforts and the pressing need for policy reforms that ensure effective risk communication during future public health emergencies. The data demonstrate the capacity of local news to shape public perceptions and behavior, with potential applications in risk communication contexts. The study offers practical applications for risk communication efforts that incorporate local news and emphasizes the significance of policy reforms in leveraging this medium effectively. The data provide an objective understanding of local news content and its role in informing individuals, with applications in risk communication contexts such as public health, political science, and mass communication studies. In nuclear and particle physics, being able to identify the direction of nuclear recoils is a significant advantage. This capability, achievable at low energies, could help verify that a dark matter signal originates from space, surpass the neutrino floor, or distinguish between various neutrino sources. With sufficient readout detail, such as with thousands of readouts per pixel, and low ionization signal topologies, two of seven scintillator photons have a high probability (>90%) of originating from the nucleus. Although scattered in the liquid, these photons retain directionality information as they interact with the PMT plate. Simulations indicate that detecting and analyzing these photons can recover about half of the original directionality with the present generation of scintillators and PMTs. Future technology could potentially reach up to 80% accuracy. An experimental setup outlining the necessary procedures to achieve this directional analysis is described. Detailed Monte Carlo studies have been conducted to assess the efficiency of this method in various scenarios. Importantly, since this method analyzes photon directionality, it is insensitive to photon energy loss within the scintillator and is also non-dependent on event geometry. As a result, it has the potential to serve as a non-biasing analysis tool. The analysis of anti-neutrino-bulk-Earth dark matter models has also contributed to an improvement in the breaking of the neutrino floor. An investigation into space anti-neutrino origin has also been performed. This paper reports on the findings from the 2022 Out-Of-Vocabulary (OOV) challenge for Optical Character Recognition (OCR) technology. The competition highlighted that state-of-the-art OCR models struggled to accurately read novel, unseen scene text patterns during training. To address this limitation, the competition's dataset and associated tasks were carefully crafted. The dataset consisted of a diverse collection of images containing 1,500 novel scene text instances split into three sets: a target test subset for evaluation and train subsets for model development. The competition included two tasks: predicting the full text content in the target test subset and estimating the word order in a novel text sequence. The evaluation phase revealed that top-performing models showed notable improvements in predicting novel text but continued to struggle with word order estimation. The competition's results showed that models trained with Transfer Learning (TL) techniques significantly outperformed those without, emphasizing the importance of this method in addressing the OOV issue. Moreover, the evaluation phase introduced a novel metric to measure the predicted word order, word-to-word accuracy, which provides a more refined understanding of this aspect of scene text recognition. The proposed metric can help researchers refine their approaches to address this complication, and consequently, improve scene text recognition as a whole. This review provides an overview of quantum mechanics history with a specific focus on addressing the theoretical difficulties in explaining ionization phenomena. The paper then delves into an in-depth explanation of how resonance theory is applied in relativistic quantum mechanics, deriving key parameters such as the width and position of the resonance. The review includes a discussion on recent progress in this field of study, primarily driven by advances in Fano line shape theory, and concludes by highlighting ongoing challenges and future research avenues. The review presents a new perspective on ionization theory by likening it to a resonance decay. Additionally, it provides a critical analysis of the principle of adiabatic matching and explains how it can be utilized in the study of a relativistic electron interacting with an oscillating electric field in a one-dimensional box, though the case of the anharmonic oscillator remains unexplored in this review. Ultimately, the methods used to evaluate resonance parameters are considered suitable for adapting to real-time experiments involving strong-field photoionization. The Fréchet distance c (or more specifically, c(f, g)) is a measure of similarity used to compare two continuous, polygonal curves f and g. This distance metric measures how similar two curves are by comparing their proximity, and it has practical applications in various fields such as data comparison and real-time routing. However, computing the Fréchet distance c(f, g) exactly is an computationally intensive task that requires an exponential time, leading to a question about whether this task can be completed more efficiently, possibly in an O(n) time frame, for polygonal curves f and g with n points. Contrary to expectations, research suggests that this task should remain computationally intensive and infeasible, and several studies have been conducted to verify this theory using reductions. This theory of infeasibility was first proposed in 1995 by Huttenlocher, Shih, and Kikinis for simple polygons, and later extended to apply to polygonal curves f and g with n points by Bose, Kriz, and Morrison in 2005. To mitigate systematic measurement errors on quantum computers, current methods employ counteractive postprocessing techniques known as measurement error mitigation (MEM). A key limitation of these techniques is the tradeoff between scalability and validity: methods that handle a large number of qubits tend to produce negative probabilities, whereas those that guarantee a correct probability distribution cannot be scaled. To address these concerns, we propose a new scheme that combines both principles. Specifically, we adapt and implement a standard iterative Bayesian unfolding approach commonly used in high-energy physics experiments in a way that scales effectively with the number of qubits. Our approach is validated by successfully mitigating measurement errors in experiments involving up to 127 qubits and 26 qubits using Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger and Bernstein-Vazirani algorithms, respectively. The results, which reveal the underlying true probability distributions, demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in overcoming noise limitations. Notably, in the experiments involving Bernstein-Vazirani algorithm, our MEM technique enables the observation of an anomalous effect that would have gone undetected through direct measurement. The scalability and validity of our approach make it a promising solution for overcoming measurement errors in near-term and future quantum computers. The open-source implementation of our method is available at https://github.com/QuantumOptics-TUz/BERNIE. A similar code for mitigating amplitude errors is available at https://github.com/QuantumOptics-TUz/BERNIE-amp. Furthermore, AMBER, a quantum software library for mitigating amplitude errors, provides a range of prebuilt examples to facilitate the use of this new scheme. The implementation of MEM techniques using AMBER is described in the supporting documentation at https://amber-quasiprobability.github.io/.
